docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Batch-level fusion (one kernel covering many rows of a four-step pass): the next lever before multi-core, per the N=4096, B ≥ 128 numbers.
  • Native registration (#80): nki_op for every kernel, register_autograd, and no torch_xla on the native path. In progress as draft PR #88.
  • Four-step beyond 4096, where per-stage Stockham launches remain the time limit (trnsci#35 capacity sweep).
  • Phase 2 — precision (Kahan/Neumaier for long Bluestein chains), including the open BF16 FAILs and kahan characterisation on silicon
  • Phase 3 — plan reuse, streaming large FFTs, NEFF cache, where #82 and #83 live
  • Phase 4 — multi-chip large-N FFT. Multi-rank nki.collectives were bit-exact at 2 and 4 ranks in trnsci#35
  • Phase 5 — trn2 larger-SBUF path

Suite context: trnsci.dev, the roadmap, the suite-wide tracker. Siblings face the same floor: trnblas's batched-pair kernel and trntensor's homogeneous batching were built around the old 100 ms one, and trnsci#35 flags both for revisiting.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: When a launch has a fixed price, an FFT plan costs its launch count; FLOPs barely enter. On Trainium the cheapest way to cut launches is to hand the transform to the Tensor Engine as one GEMM (two for four-step) and let FP32 PSUM accumulate, which also proved more accurate than the staged plan. The same accounting shows up at the large-n end: the fix for an overflowing kernel was more launches, chosen so their shapes repeat. None of it makes a standalone FFT beat the CPU. It makes the FFT cheap enough to leave on the device when the surrounding pipeline already lives there.

docs.title: trnrand: from byte tiles to full words on Trn2
docs.text: The byte-tile post argued that storing each Threefry word as four (128, 1) byte tiles was the representation the architecture preferred. On Trn2 with NKI 0.7 that design was correct and slow: the kernel was bound by instruction issue, because every instruction did 128 elements of work. Widening the tiles to (128, F ≤ 512) and moving the 32-bit adds onto GpSimd's native integer path takes trnrand.normal() at 4M elements from 934 ms to 15.9 ms with bit-identical output. That result shipped in trnrand v0.8.0 via PR trnsci/trnrand#62. Aten randn is still about 11× faster, and the host CPU still wins at every size measured.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
trnrand is the suite's cuRAND analog. Its default on-device generator is Threefry4x32-20, chosen in April because it needs only add, XOR and rotate. The 2²⁴ exact-integer ceiling reported in aws-neuron-sdk#1308 had ruled out Philox's 32×32 multiply. That post's answer was to keep every intermediate below 2²⁴ by working in bytes.

The Trn2 window in October ran trnrand on the public Neuron SDK 2.33.0 (torch-neuronx 2.14.3, NKI 0.7.0, neuronx-cc 2.28.7631) through TorchNeuron's native neuron device (trnsci/trnsci#35). The first latency numbers were bad enough that they got their own issue, trnrand#60: normal(4M) took 9.2 s. Two rounds of host-side fixes came first. Routing bulk draws through the 32-tile streaming kernel cut 8,192 launches to 256, and keeping inputs and outputs on the device (commit caa9aec) cut the copies from 1,792 to 7. Together they brought 4M to 934 ms.

Then the curve stopped bending. At caa9aec, cost was linear at about 0.23 ms per 1,000 elements. That is roughly 800× behind aten randn at 4M, and launches and copies were already near their floor. A cost that scales with element count after the launch overhead is gone lives inside the kernel.

docs.title: What the architecture suggests
docs.text:
A NeuronCore tile has two axes. The partition axis is 128 lanes. The free axis is how far each instruction sweeps along every lane. A CUDA habit maps one thread to one counter, and the April design did the Trainium equivalent: one partition lane per counter, free dimension of 1. Each instruction did 128 elements of work when it could have done 128 × F for the same issue cost.

Reading the caa9aec kernel made the cost concrete. A byte-sliced 32-bit add is four byte adds, three carry adds, three shifts and four masks: 14 instructions for 128 words. One 512-value tile of Threefry-20, with key injections, came to about 1,700 instructions. That explains why the cost was linear, and why removing launches and copies stopped helping.

The second axis is the engine. The four-engine post argued that RNG belongs on GpSimd and the Vector Engine, not the Tensor Engine. NKI 0.7 makes that literal for integers. Its documentation says nisa.tensor_tensor with all-int32 or all-uint32 operands runs on GpSimd with native integer arithmetic. The bitwise ops XOR, shift and OR already handle full 32-bit patterns on the Vector Engine. Only the add ever needed the byte workaround, and GpSimd now does that add natively.

flowchart TB
  subgraph before ["caa9aec: byte tiles, host-looped"]
    direction LR
    B1["4 × (128, 1) byte tiles per word"] --> B2["add = 14 instr / 128 words"]
    B2 --> B3["~1,700 instr per 512 values"]
    B3 --> B4["one launch per 16,384 values,\n256 launches at 4M"]
  end
  subgraph after ["fd77a8c: full words, one launch"]
    direction LR
    A1["iota builds counters in SBUF\n(128, F ≤ 512) uint32"] --> A2["add: GpSimd tensor_tensor int32\nxor/rotate: Vector bitvec"]
    A2 --> A3["Box-Muller in the same kernel\n(chunk stays in SBUF)"]
    A3 --> A4["one DMA per chunk,\n≤ 16 chunks = 4M values per launch"]
  end

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
The fix took two commits, each validated separately on device.

f4e8af5: widen the tile. The same byte arithmetic now runs on (128, F) tiles, with F up to 512. Each launch handles up to 16 chunks, so one launch covers 16 × 512 × 512 = 4,194,304 values. Counters are built in SBUF with nisa.iota instead of shipped from the host. Box-Muller stays fused in the kernel, and each chunk leaves with one DMA. That alone gave 4.3× to 29× over caa9aec.

ea3800e, then fd77a8c: widen the word. ea3800e added two opt-in widths under TRNRAND_LIMB_BITS. The 16-bit width splits each word into two limbs, so every add stays below 2¹⁷ and is exact even through fp32. The 32-bit width uses whole words with the adds pinned to GpSimd. The NKI docs promise exact integer results. They don't say whether the add wraps mod 2³², and Threefry depends on that wrap. The simulator can't settle the question, so hardware did. All three widths matched bit for bit at 1; 16,385 (offset 2²⁴−5); 1,048,577 (seed 2⁴⁰+3); and 4,194,305 elements. fd77a8c then made 32 the default.

The deliberate tradeoffs:

  • Bit-identity over a cleaner stream. The full-word kernel keeps the byte-era stream layout: 24-bit key halves from the seed, and batch counters masked to 24 bits. A native 32-bit layout would be simpler, but it would change every existing stream for a given seed.
  • Bounded shapes over perfect fit. F is capped at 512 by SBUF, since about 16 live (P, F) state tiles plus temporaries share each partition. C is capped at 16 because chunks are unrolled, so C bounds instruction count and compile time. Both come from a small bucket set, so a few NEFFs serve every request size.
  • The byte path stays. TRNRAND_LIMB_BITS=8 is the documented fallback. The XLA/Trn1 lineage never uses the bulk kernels and is unchanged.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Every add in the round function now goes through this helper. It replaced the 14-instruction byte add (from trnrand/nki/dispatch.py on branch perf-60-fullword):

def _add32_w(x, y):
    out = nl.ndarray(x.shape, dtype=nl.uint32, buffer=nl.sbuf)
    nisa.tensor_tensor(out, x, y, op=nl.add, engine=nisa.engine.gpsimd)
    return out

def _rotl32_w(x, rot):
    return nl.bitwise_or(
        nl.left_shift(x, rot, dtype=nl.uint32),
        nl.right_shift(x, 32 - rot, dtype=nl.uint32),
        dtype=nl.uint32,
    )

def _mix_w(a, b, rot):
    a_new = _add32_w(a, b)
    b_new = nl.bitwise_xor(_rotl32_w(b, rot), a_new, dtype=nl.uint32)
    return a_new, b_new

The counter setup inside the kernel body is where the free dimension gets used:

col = nl.ndarray((P, F), dtype=nl.uint32, buffer=nl.sbuf)
nisa.iota(col, [[1, F]], offset=0, channel_multiplier=0)
...
for c in nl.static_range(C):
    start_w = _pack_bytes_wide(_b_split(start_ref[:, c : c + 1]), zero)
    c1_w = nl.bitwise_and(_add32_w(col, start_w), 0xFFFFFF, dtype=nl.uint32)

On the host, _bulk_plan picks (F, C, launches), and the chunk count rounds to a bucket of powers of two plus their quarter steps:

def _chunk_bucket(chunks: int) -> int:
    chunks = max(1, int(chunks))
    if chunks <= 4:
        return chunks
    p = _next_pow2(chunks) // 2  # chunks in (p, 2p]
    step = p // 4
    return min(_BULK_CHUNKS_MAX, -(-chunks // step) * step)

docs.title: What didn't work
docs.text:
The byte-tile premise was half wrong. The April post said NKI routes 32-bit tile arithmetic through a float32 path. For the ops trnrand called, that held. The general conclusion did not. On NKI 0.7 the 2²⁴ limit came from how trnrand used NKI. nl.add and nl.multiply with a (P, 1) operand lower to tensor_scalar_arith, which is float-only. An int32↔uint32 nl.copy is a saturating value conversion, not a bitcast (trnrand#56). The Philox tests that had been marked xfail against #1308 were failing on the saturating copy. With tensor_tensor and NkiTensor.view() bitcasts, Philox is bit-exact on Trn2, 512 of 512 words, so the four-engine post's Philox gate now passes. The byte tiles solved a real problem, but they were the wrong fix for most of it.

torch.compile was not the lever. Before the kernel was rewritten, the compiled counter-mode path gave 1.5× at 16k (7.61 → 5.24 ms) and 1.1× at 262k. At 1M, compilation failed:

[F137] neuronx-cc was forcibly killed

The graph inlined every per-tile nki_op launch, and neuronx-cc's walrus_driver reached about 50 GB RSS before it was killed. Compiling a slow kernel mostly yields a slow kernel and a large compile.

Compiling at all required changing the stream. trnrand#61 found two blockers. Dynamo cannot proxy the torch.Generator argument ("Failed to convert args/kwargs to proxy"). The workaround, opaque torch.library.custom_ops, passed on CPU backends and then failed on backend="neuron" with "failed to legalize operation 'torch.operator'". The Neuron backend lowers the whole FX graph to StableHLO, and only aten ops and nki_op kernels survive. Default seeding draws each key from the host Mersenne Twister, and a graph can't express that. The result is an opt-in Generator(key_mode="counter"), which fixes the key from the seed and advances only a counter tensor. It compiles with zero graph breaks and matches eager bit for bit, but it produces a different stream for the same seed. The default stays "draw". That work shipped in v0.8.0 via PR trnsci/trnrand#63, on top of

Power-of-two buckets had a cliff. f4e8af5 rounded chunk counts up to a power of two, so 2²⁰ + 1 elements cost 1.7× as much as 2²⁰ (15.43 vs 8.86 ms). The quarter-step buckets above bring 1M+1 to within 1.1–1.15× of 1M.

Fit, stated plainly. Counter-based RNG is integer-heavy, branch-free and has no contraction. That suits the partition-and-free-axis shape once both axes are used. It never touches the Tensor Engine, which is most of the silicon. Aten randn at 4M is about 11× faster, and that gap is not yet explained. Threefry-20 spends 20 rounds of add, rotate and XOR plus five key injections on every four outputs, so it may simply be more work than whatever aten runs. trnrand's case on device is reproducibility (counter streams, partitioned multi-chip draws, bit-identity across cores) more than speed.

Upstream ask. The NKI 0.7 docs say GpSimd tensor_tensor integer arithmetic is exact, but not that the add wraps mod 2³². The docs also don't collect which integer ops are exact on which engine, so the nl.add float lowering and the saturating nl.copy had to be found on hardware. The new comment on aws-neuron-sdk#1308 asks for docs that say which integer ops are exact on which engine. (AWS closed the issue in April once the workaround shipped, noting that native int32 arithmetic support is on their list.) One table of op × engine × dtype, marked exact, wraps, saturates or via-fp32, would cover it.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: The partition axis is not where the parallelism ends. A (128, 1) tile leaves the free axis idle and makes every instruction pay full issue cost for 128 elements. The April design fixed correctness by working inside one engine's limits. The October fix came from using the second tile axis and from moving the integer adds to the engine with native int32 arithmetic. On Trainium, choosing the shape and the engine is the main decision in the kernel, and it is not a later tuning step.

docs.title: trnsolver: what torch.compile can't lower, and a 20-second eigh
docs.text:
trnsolver's Cholesky, LU solve and QR now compile under torch.compile(backend="neuron", fullgraph=True) on Trn2, and eigh at n=128 dropped from 20.8 s to 1.17 ms. Neither is the triumph it sounds like: first calls of the compiled factorizations take 13–259 s because their loops unroll, and the 1.17 ms eigh runs on the host CPU, which is where aten's linalg_eigh executes for a neuron tensor. The lesson for anyone putting dense linear algebra inside a compiled Trainium graph: a whole-graph, static-shape compile model turns pivoting into cheap data movement, but has no answer yet for convergence loops.

Code status

Everything below shipped in trnsolver v0.16.0 via trnsci/trnsolver#43 (branch fix-42-eigh-latency). The rejected blocked variant is kept on branch repro-ncc-inla001-blocked as an upstream reproducer only.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
The suite-wide move to native TorchNeuron puts every trnsci library on the Neuron SDK 2.33.0 stack: the TorchNeuron public beta (torch-neuronx 2.14.3 on PyTorch 2.14), NKI 0.7.0 and neuronx-cc 2.28.7631, on a trn2.3xlarge. Eager ops run on a neuron device; torch.compile(backend="neuron") hands a whole FX graph to neuronx-cc and gets back one NEFF.

cuSOLVER's model is a library call per factorization (potrf, getrf, geqrf) with an info code for failure. The naive port is to call torch.linalg.* and trust the backend to lower it. A compile coverage spike over trnsolver's public API (B6 in trnsci#35, recorded in trnsolver#41) showed what that trust buys today:

call under fullgraph=True result on SDK 2.33 cholesky, solve Higher-order operation 'with_effects' not implemented in the FxImporter (tried '_import_hop_with_effects') cholesky_ex Neuron has no lowering for this op solve_ex failed to legalize operation 'torch.operator' that was explicitly marked illegal qr failed to legalize operation 'torch.aten.linalg_qr' eigh (n=128) 26 graph breaks (Tensor.item(), guard x < 1e-20) cg 4 graph breaks (guard x < 1e-15)

The with_effects failure is the instructive one. torch.linalg.cholesky decomposes into linalg_cholesky_ex plus aten._linalg_check_errors(info), a side-effecting op that only raises; PyTorch wraps it in the with_effects higher-order op, which the Neuron FxImporter can't import. Error checking broke before the factorization did.

A separate latency spike (B7, trnsolver#42) found the second problem: trnsolver's NKI eigh on device-resident inputs took 391–413 ms at n=16 and 20.8 s at n=128, while torch.linalg.eigh on the same device took about 1 ms.

docs.title: What the architecture suggests
docs.text:
The Neuron compile model wants the whole computation at once, static shapes, and no host round trips. A solver written like a host-side LAPACK caller violates all three.

flowchart TB
    subgraph E["Eager, host-driven (trnsolver eigh before #42)"]
        direction TB
        E1["device op: tiny update"] --> E2["host: .item() read<br/>(sync, round trip)"]
        E2 --> E3["Python branch on value"]
        E3 -->|"next step: another launch"| E1
    end
    subgraph T["Traced, unrolled (compiled factorizations)"]
        direction TB
        T1["step 0: argmax, gather, mm, where"] --> T2["step 1: same ops, new constants"]
        T2 --> T3["... n steps, no host contact"]
        T3 --> T4["one NEFF: slow compile,<br/>1–9 ms warm"]
    end

Data-dependent data movement fits. Partial pivoting looks like control flow but is a data choice: argmax over a column, then gather with a permutation index. Nothing leaves the device and the graph shape doesn't depend on the answer.

Data-dependent trip counts don't fit. QR iteration in eigh and the residual test in cg stop when a value crosses a tolerance. With no loop higher-order op (while_loop, scan) in the Neuron FxImporter, a convergence loop either syncs to the host every iteration or can't be traced.

Static loops fit, at a price. A fixed-length loop unrolls at trace time into n copies of the step: a straight-line NEFF with no host contact, whose size and compile time grow with n. Same NEFF-cache economics as the Jacobi post and the Schur post: pay once to compile, win only if the same shape runs many times.

One hardware rule reaches up into plain PyTorch: partition accesses must start at partition 0, 32, 64 or 96 with matching spans. trnsolver hit it in its own kernel (#40), then in a graph with no NKI code at all (below).

None of this uses the Tensor Engine well. Each unrolled step is a rank-1 update, an (n×1)@(1×n) mm with a contraction dimension of 1, against a 128-row systolic array. The compiled path removes host round trips; it doesn't turn a factorization into a GEMM.

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
Factorizations: traceable implementations under compile. When torch.compiler.is_compiling() is true and the input is real, cholesky, solve, solve_spd, inv_spd and qr take implementations built from elementwise ops, where masks, mm, sqrt, sum, argmax, gather and cat. The rules are: no .item(), no data-dependent Python control flow, no in-place slice assignment (every per-column restriction is a row or column mask), and a static loop over n. Eager calls are unchanged and still call torch.linalg.

The deliberate tradeoff is error reporting. _linalg_check_errors is the op that broke, so the traceable paths don't raise: compiled cholesky on a non-SPD input returns NaN, and compiled solve on a singular matrix returns inf or NaN instead of LinAlgError. Callers who need the exception call eagerly.

Convergence loops: eager-only, labeled as such. eigh's NKI path and cg/gmres run under torch.compiler.disable: one graph break instead of 26. Under fullgraph=True that break is an error, which is the honest answer.

eigh latency: a cutover and host QR.

flowchart LR
    A["eigh(A), nki backend"] --> B{"device is neuron<br/>and n below TRNSOLVER_EIGH_NKI_MIN_N (512)<br/>and not TRNSOLVER_REQUIRE_NKI?"}
    B -->|yes| C["torch.linalg.eigh<br/>(aten; runs on host,<br/>result copied back)"]
    B -->|no| D["NKI Householder tridiag"] --> E["QR iteration on CPU copies"] --> F["NKI apply_reflectors"]

The default routes every size the single-tile NKI path supports (n ≤ 128) to aten. TRNSOLVER_REQUIRE_NKI=1 bypasses the cutover so the hardware suite still exercises the kernels.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The GEPP solve shows pivot-as-data-movement: the row swap is a gather with a permutation built from argmax, and elimination runs on the augmented [A | B], so no L factor or pivot vector exists. From trnsolver/factor.py:

def _solve_lu_traceable(A: torch.Tensor, B: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    n = A.shape[-1]
    batch = torch.broadcast_shapes(A.shape[:-2], B.shape[:-2])
    M = torch.cat([A.expand(*batch, n, n), B.expand(*batch, n, B.shape[-1])], dim=-1)
    rows = torch.arange(n, device=A.device)
    for k in range(n):
        mag = torch.where(rows >= k, M[..., :, k].abs(), -1.0)  # (..., n)
        p = torch.argmax(mag, dim=-1, keepdim=True)  # (..., 1)
        perm = torch.where(rows == k, p, torch.where(rows == p, k, rows))  # (..., n)
        M = torch.gather(M, -2, perm.unsqueeze(-1).expand(M.shape))
        factors = torch.where(rows > k, M[..., :, k] / M[..., k : k + 1, k], 0.0)
        M = M - factors.unsqueeze(-1) * M[..., k : k + 1, :]
    return _solve_triangular_traceable(M[..., :n], M[..., n:], upper=True)

Cholesky writes column k into L with a mask, not L[:, k] = ...:

    for k in range(n):
        d = torch.sqrt(S[..., k : k + 1, k : k + 1])  # (..., 1, 1)
        col = torch.where(rows >= k, S[..., :, k : k + 1] / d, 0.0)  # (..., n, 1)
        L = torch.where(cols == k, col, L)
        S = S - col @ col.transpose(-2, -1)

In _householder_qr, LAPACK's "skip the reflector if the sub-column is zero" branch becomes a where on tail_sq > 0:

        active = tail_sq > 0
        denom = torch.where(active, alpha - beta, one)
        tau = torch.where(active, (beta - alpha) / torch.where(active, beta, one), 0.0)
        v = torch.where(rows == k, one, tail / denom)
        w = (v.transpose(-2, -1) @ R) * (cols >= k)  # (..., 1, n)
        R = R - tau * (v @ w)

The eigh fix in trnsolver/eigen.py is a cutover predicate plus moving the QR iteration onto host tensors:

def _eigh_aten_cutover(A: torch.Tensor) -> bool:
    if _REQUIRE_NKI:
        return False
    if A.device.type != _NATIVE_DEVICE_TYPE:
        return False
    return A.shape[-1] < _eigh_nki_min_n()

# in _householder_qr_eigh:
    host = torch.device("cpu")
    eigenvalues, Q_right = _qr_iterate(
        diag.detach().to(host, copy=True), subdiag.detach().to(host, copy=True), tol
    )
    Q_right = Q_right.to(A.device)

docs.title: What didn't work
docs.text:
Switching to *_ex only moved the wall. The first fix (5baa5cf) called cholesky_ex and solve_ex directly to keep _linalg_check_errors out of the graph. with_effects disappeared; Neuron has no lowering for this op and failed to legalize operation 'torch.operator' replaced it. The backend has no linalg decomposition lowerings at all, so the traceable rewrite was the only route that didn't wait on upstream.

Blocking didn't shrink the graph, and it found a compiler bug. A third round (616bd39) tried right-looking blocked variants with panel width 32. The graph node count stayed O(n), since the panels still unroll column by column. At n=64 blocking helped solve_spd, inv_spd and qr and hurt cholesky and solve:

op, n=64 first call unblocked (1b3d819) blocked nb=32 (616bd39) cholesky 12.8 s 14.5 s solve 47.2 s 61.5 s solve_spd 44.6 s 27.3 s inv_spd 49.8 s 27.6 s qr 46.0 s 33.3 s

At n=128 every blocked op failed inside neuronx-cc 2.28.7631:

[INTERNAL_ERROR] [NCC_INLA001] Unhandled exception with message: === BIR verification failed ===
Reason: Pattern accesses 96 (> 32) partitions starting at partition 32
Opcode: GenericCopy
Instruction Source: (GenericCopy: I-21761), tensorizer(output tensor: float32<96 x 96> , id: 21761)

The 96×96 tensor is the trailing submatrix A[32:, 32:]: one copy starting at partition 32 and spanning 96, the same 0/32/64/96 rule as #40, reached from ordinary aten ops. Blocking was rejected. It doesn't fix graph size, and an internal compiler error isn't worth working around.

A correction belongs on the record. The first draft of the upstream report, in a trnsolver#41 comment, said a plain slice x[32:, 32:] of a 128×128 tensor triggers NCC_INLA001. It doesn't. x[32:,32:]*2, the trailing update x[32:,32:] - x[32:,:32] @ x[:32,32:] and that update reassembled with cat all compile correctly at n=128. The bug needs the large fused graph, so the filed reproducer is the whole blocked branch, not a ten-line script. The same comment had left blocked qr at n=128 unchecked; it fails the same way.

The 20-second eigh passed every test. The hardware suite passed 20/20 while eigh took 20.8 s at n=128, because the suite's inputs live on the CPU. The NKI kernels weren't the cost. _qr_iterate/_qr_sweep moved diag, subdiag and Q back to the input's device and ran scalar Givens code element by element there: about 20 device ops per rotation over about 1.25·n² rotations, roughly 400k tiny ops at n=128. Hence ~4× per doubling of n, O(n²) wall time for an O(n³) algorithm. The benchmark was counting launches, not FLOPs.

The #40 fix earlier in the window had its own wrong first guess. The issue blamed the Jacobi kernels for Expected 'src' partition start in {0, 32, 64, 96} for a 1-partition access, but got 6. The culprit was apply_reflectors_kernel in the Householder path, slicing row k of an SBUF-resident Vᵀ. Loading each row with nl.load_transpose2d so it lands at partition 0 took the suite from 1 passed / 19 failed to 20 passed.

Upstream asks, filed:

  • aws-neuron-sdk#1438: support with_effects in the FxImporter, or drop the _linalg_check_errors effect on Neuron. Add lowerings for linalg_cholesky_ex, linalg_solve_ex/LU, linalg_qr, triangular_solve and, if possible, eigh; a host fallback with a graph break beats a hard failure. Document which aten.linalg_* ops run on the host in eager.
  • aws-neuron-sdk#1441: the tensorizer should split copies at legal partition starts instead of emitting an illegal pattern. Reproducer: branch repro-ncc-inla001-blocked at n=128.
  • Not yet filed: a loop higher-order op (while_loop/scan) in the Neuron FxImporter, the one change that would make compile time independent of n and let a convergence loop trace.

docs.title: Fit: where this lands today
docs.text:
The eigh cutover is the right default, and it puts no work on Trainium. The profiler shows aten::linalg_eigh on a neuron tensor going through aten::_to_cpu: TorchNeuron computes eigh on the host and copies the result back. The 1.17 ms at n=128 is host LAPACK with device-resident I/O, and trnsolver's on-device eigh adds nothing at these sizes. Even with host QR, the NKI path loses by 100–1000× at n ≤ 128, because tridiagonalization still makes n−2 host-driven steps with about six .item() syncs each. Until that stage stops syncing, eigh on Trainium means "run it on the host."

The compiled factorizations fit narrowly. Warm calls of 1–9 ms up to n=256 suit a fixed-shape graph that runs thousands of times, such as an SCF loop at constant basis size; 13–259 s first calls rule out one-off or variable-n use. Against training graphs this workload is under-indexed: data-dependent loops at small n, where the Tensor Engine wants large static GEMMs.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
All measurements: trn2.3xlarge, Neuron SDK 2.33.0, native neuron device. Compiled factorizations use fullgraph=True, dynamic=False on 1b3d819. First call includes the neuronx-cc compile; warm is the steady state.

op n=64 first / warm n=128 first / warm n=256 first / warm cholesky 12.8 s / 1.0 ms 49.8 s / 1.3 ms 91.5 s / 3.0 ms solve (GEPP) 47.2 s / 2.4 ms 143.4 s / 4.3 ms 258.9 s / 9.0 ms solve_spd 44.6 s / 1.2 ms 76.1 s / 2.1 ms 227.5 s / 5.1 ms inv_spd 49.8 s / 4.0 ms 73.3 s / 2.6 ms 223.6 s / 7.5 ms qr 46.0 s / 1.9 ms 70.9 s / 1.9 ms 159.8 s / 4.2 ms

Compiled results match eager on the device to at most 9.3e-6 relative error (GEPP solve at n=128, fp32 roundoff from different pivot tie-breaks and accumulation order); every other case is at 2.8e-6 or below. Inside the B6 coverage harness, compiled solve at n=128 took 528 s. No CPU baseline was taken for these ops, so the table compares compile against warm, not Trainium against CPU.

eigh, warm median. "Before" is the NKI path on device-resident input (0efaf9f/1b3d819); CPU is torch.linalg.eigh on CPU tensors from the same spike:

n before cutover (default) aten on neuron NKI path, host QR CPU 16 391–413 ms 0.52 ms 0.42 ms 68.9 ms 0.016 ms 32 1.45–1.87 s 0.61 ms 0.42 ms 145.9 ms 0.05 ms 64 5.5–6.2 s 0.54 ms 0.52 ms 394.6 ms 0.15 ms 128 20.8 s 1.17 ms 0.95 ms 1112 ms 0.56 ms 256 — 2.73 ms 2.70 ms n/a (NKI path is n ≤ 128) —

The CPU column is the uncomfortable one: CPU-resident eigh is 2–33× faster than the cutover, a gap consistent with the cutover's device-to-host-to-device copies. Relative error against FP64 is 2.0e-7 to 3.7e-7 for the cutover and 1.3e-6 to 2.1e-6 for the NKI path. With TRNSOLVER_REQUIRE_NKI=1 the hardware suite passed 20/20 on the final head, twice, and results stay on neuron:0.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• trnsolver#43 is merged. Everything above shipped in v0.16.0.
  • On-device tridiagonalization. One kernel per panel, no .item(), so NKI eigh stops paying O(n) host syncs: the step that would give it an on-device reason to exist. Recorded as Phase 3 work on #42; in progress as draft PR #45.
  • Phase 3 — preconditioned iterative solvers + NEFF cache reuse, with NEFF compile-cache reuse in examples and benchmarks as the near-term lever on 50–260 s first calls.
  • Phase 4 — parallel Jacobi sweeps across NeuronCores.
  • Phase 5 — trn2 rotation-block tuning.
  • Upstream: aws-neuron-sdk#1438 and #1441. A loop higher-order op would replace unrolling.

Siblings hit the same launch-count lesson in the same window: trnrand cut normal at 4M elements from 934 ms to 15.9 ms with one launch per request (trnrand#60). The suite-wide picture is in the migration tracker, the suite tracker and the roadmap.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: Under Trainium's compile model, the line that matters in a solver is whether the data decides which values move or how many times the loop runs. Pivoting is the first kind: argmax plus gather traces cleanly, and a compiled GEPP solve runs in 2–9 ms warm. Convergence is the second kind, and today it can't stay on the device: eigh at 1.17 ms is fast because it runs on the host. The way forward is to remove host syncs from stages with fixed trip counts, starting with tridiagonalization, and to ask the toolchain for a loop primitive for the stages without them.

docs.title: trnsparse: from 14/30 to 30/30 on NKI 0.7
docs.text: trnsparse's block-sparse attention and screened-SpMM kernels had run under nki.simulate for six months, then failed 16 of 30 hardware tests the first time they ran on the native neuron device under NKI 0.7.0. The fixes are small: a reciprocal-multiply where a divide used to be, an explicit partition broadcast, and two host-side gather bugs, one of which had been blamed on the simulator since April. The compile fixes say a lot about how the engines want per-row scalars and partition counts expressed. The branch passes 30/30 on Trn2. It shipped in trnsparse v0.7.0 via PR trnsci/trnsparse#31, and anyone moving NKI 0.3-era kernels to the native PyTorch path should read it before starting.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Neuron SDK 2.33.0 brings the TorchNeuron public beta (torch-neuronx 2.14.3, NKI 0.7.0, neuronx-cc 2.28.7631). Tensors live on a native neuron device rather than an XLA device. The suite-wide migration is tracked in trnsci/trnsci#35, and trnsparse's share of it is trnsci/trnsparse#29.

The first experiment was deliberately lazy. The existing XLA-path hardware suite ran unchanged on a trn2.3xlarge. A test-only stand-in mapped the torch_xla device and sync calls onto the native device. The result was 14 passed, 16 failed. Plain SpMM and BSR SpMM held parity. The failures landed in the code the earlier posts were proudest of: the two-pass block-sparse attention kernels from the attention-mask post and the v0.6.0 post, and the fused Schwarz-screened SpMM. Fourteen were kernel compile failures. The other two, in the SpMM/BSR differentiability tests, were a host-side float != double mix.

The second problem is the one cuSPARSE users would hit first. cuSPARSE assumes the sparse matrix lives on the device: row pointers, column indices and values are all device arrays, and every routine takes device handles. TorchNeuron has no sparse CSR tensors on the neuron device (trnsci/trnsparse#30). A naive port that calls .to("neuron") on a torch.sparse_csr_tensor stops right there.

docs.title: What the architecture suggests
docs.text:
The three distinct compile errors from #29 read like a short manual for the NeuronCore datapath:

error: 'nisa.tensor_scalar_arith' op unsupported op0 'divide'
error: 'nisa.tensor_scalar_arith' op 'operand0' partition total elements 128 != 'dst' partition total elements 1
s3s3d3_tt_valid_op   (neuronx-cc ISA validation, tensor_tensor divide)

A (128, 1) operand is a per-partition scalar. Softmax normalisation divides a (128, 128) tile of exponentials by a (128, 1) row denominator. NKI lowers that to tensor_scalar_arith, the instruction form that broadcasts one value per partition along the free axis. In neuronx-cc 2.28 that form has no divide. The datapath supports reciprocal followed by multiply, and that is also the cheaper shape on paper: the denominator is constant across every K-block of a block-row, so 128 reciprocals per block-row replace a divide per element of every block. The trnrand work in #35 found the integer side of the same rules: (P, 1) tiles take a float-only path (aws-neuron/aws-neuron-sdk#1308), and integer tensor_tensor needs matching operand dtypes.

Partitions are lanes, not a broadcast axis. NumPy happily broadcasts (128, 1) * (1, 128) into an outer product. On a NeuronCore the first axis is the 128-lane partition dimension, and an instruction's operands and destination have to occupy the same partitions. A 1-partition operand cannot quietly fan out to 128 lanes inside an arithmetic instruction. The broadcast has to be its own step.

Sparse structure does not need to be on the device at all. The thesis of the tile post was that the Tensor Engine consumes dense 128×128 tiles, so BSR at block size 128 is the native format. Followed to its end, that means the device never needs row pointers. It needs dense blocks, already gathered and padded into the shape nc_matmul consumes. The index metadata is a scheduling input, and scheduling already happens on the host.

flowchart LR
    subgraph CU["cuSPARSE: everything on device"]
        direction TB
        cu1["CSR on device<br/>(row_ptr, col_idx, values)"] --> cu2["device kernel<br/>per-nnz indirect gather"] --> cu3["dense result<br/>on device"]
    end
    subgraph TS["trnsparse on TorchNeuron: split by role"]
        direction TB
        h1["host: CSR / BSR structure<br/>(block_row_ptrs, col_grid)"] --> h2["host: gather + pad<br/>dense 128x128 blocks"]
        h2 -->|"dense tensors only"| d1["neuron device:<br/>nc_matmul per block, PSUM accumulate"]
        d1 --> d2["dense result"]
    end

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
The fixes in PR #31 follow those three readings literally:

Rule (NKI 0.7 / neuronx-cc 2.28) Where it bit Fix on fix-29-nki07 No divide in tensor_scalar_arith softmax in _attn_out_kernel, _attn_bwd_dq_kernel, _attn_bwd_dkdv_kernel nl.multiply(exp, nl.reciprocal(row_denom)), hoisted per block-row in forward and dQ Operand/dst partition counts must match (128,1) * (1,128) Schwarz outer product; (1,1) threshold nl.broadcast_to to (128,128) and (128,1) tensor_tensor divide fails ISA validation screened-SpMM soft mask reciprocal-multiply No fp64 datapath; native device downcasts silently PyTorch-level backward under fp64 gradcheck kernels always get fp32; results cast back to caller dtype

The deliberate tradeoff is in the fourth row. Hardware gradcheck tolerances moved from eps=1e-6, atol=1e-4 to eps=1e-2, atol=rtol=1e-2. With an fp32 forward, an fp64-sized eps measures fp32 rounding, not the gradient. The ops are linear in each input, so the larger step adds no truncation error, and a wrong adjoint would still be off by O(1). The cost is that the tests now prove the adjoint is structurally right, not that it is accurate to fp64.

For sparse structure, #30 records the design rule and leaves the implementation open: CSR and BSR structure stays on the host, or travels as plain dense index and value tensors that trnsparse's own kernels consume, and never as torch.sparse_csr_tensor on neuron. The BSR and attention paths already work this way, since their host-side gather emits dense padded tensors.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The softmax change in _attn_out_kernel (diff from git diff main...fix-29-nki07):

        for m in nl.affine_range(M_tiles):
            row_max_m = nl.load(row_max[m, :, :])  # (128, 1)
            row_denom_m = nl.load(row_denom[m, :, :])
+           # NKI 0.7: tensor_scalar_arith has no `divide`; multiply by the
+           # reciprocal of the (128, 1) softmax denominator instead.
+           row_denom_inv_m = nl.reciprocal(row_denom_m)
            ...
            for ki in nl.affine_range(K_max):
                ...
                stable = nl.subtract(score, row_max_m)
-               weights = nl.divide(nl.exp(stable), row_denom_m)
+               weights = nl.multiply(nl.exp(stable), row_denom_inv_m)

The partition-count fix in _screened_spmm_kernel:

+       # threshold_sqrt is a (1, 1) HBM tensor. NKI 0.7 rejects a 1-partition
+       # scalar operand against a 128-partition tile, so broadcast it to a
+       # (TILE_M, 1) per-partition scalar once, up front.
+       thr = nl.broadcast_to(nl.load(threshold_sqrt), shape=(TILE_M, 1))
        ...
                    q_k = nl.load_transpose2d(q[k_off : k_off + TILE_K, :])  # (1, TILE_K)
-                   pair_bound = nl.multiply(q_m, q_k)
+                   q_k_b = nl.broadcast_to(q_k, shape=(TILE_M, TILE_K))
+                   pair_bound = nl.multiply(q_k_b, q_m)
-                   relu_diff = nl.relu(nl.subtract(pair_bound, threshold_sqrt))
-                   mask_f = nl.divide(relu_diff, nl.add(relu_diff, 1e-10))
+                   relu_diff = nl.relu(nl.subtract(pair_bound, thr))
+                   mask_f = nl.multiply(relu_diff, nl.reciprocal(nl.add(relu_diff, 1e-10)))

After the broadcast, the multiply is a plain (P, F) × (P, 1) tensor-scalar op, which is the form the instruction supports. The full diff, including the new tests/test_nki_compile.py, is on PR #31.

docs.title: What didn't work
docs.text:
The simulator was the wrong gate. Every one of these kernels passed nki.simulate. The simulator does not run the MLIR verifier, so a kernel can pass the whole simulator suite and still fail to compile. nki.compiler.frontend.source_to_mlir(...).verify() catches the first two errors on a CPU host with no device. It does not catch the third: a tensor_tensor divide passes verify() and fails later, in neuronx-cc's ISA validation. Getting full coverage takes a ladder of checks:

Check (CPU unless noted) Catches Misses nki.simulate Python-layer and shape errors all three compile errors above source_to_mlir(...).verify() tensor_scalar_arith divide, partition-count mismatch s3s3d3_tt_valid_op Full NEFF compile (neuronx-cc on PATH) ISA validation numeric bugs neuronx-cc BIRSim (trn2) the 49% forward mismatch, bit-for-bit screened SpMM (exit code 70, see below) Trn2 hardware everything that remains —

test_nki_compile.py now runs the verify and NEFF steps for every kernel on both trn1 and trn2 targets: 60/60 on CPU at 60faa05.

Five failures survived the compile fixes, and they were trnsparse's bugs. At 60faa05, the hardware run was 25/30. All five remaining failures were numeric and all were in attention. The local-window forward and head_dim 256 forward had about 49% of elements mismatched. Backward local, backward dilated and head_dim 256 backward had about 99%. The investigation in #29 routed the device path through neuronx-cc's BIRSim for trn2 on a CPU host. test_local_window_parity reproduced exactly: 15,954 of 32,768 elements wrong, max abs error 0.2599. The backward failures also reproduced under nki.simulate. With hand-built inputs, the dQ kernel matched a NumPy reference under BIRSim to 4.8e-6. That cleared the kernels and the 0.7 rewrites, and pointed at the host-side gather. Two bugs were sitting there, older than the branch and hidden on hardware behind the compile failures:

  1. Padded k-slots. Rows with fewer than K_max blocks are padded with sentinel slots, and those slots gathered column block 0. Block 0 then leaked into the softmax and weights @ V of every padded row. With a local window of 2 across four block-rows, rows 0 and 3 are padded, which accounts for the ~49%. Dilated and global masks have no padding, which is why they passed. The fix zeroes K/V (or Q/dO) in padded slots and drops their stats from _attn_host_reduction.
  2. dO gathered by column. _attn_bwd_gather gathered dO by column block when dP = dO_m @ V_ki.T needs the row block dO_m. dQ was wrong whenever a row attended to any block other than its own. dK and dV were already correct.

The second bug has history. The v0.6.0 post reported a "dQ backward systematic error in the simulator" and guessed at floating-point reordering. trnsci/trnsparse#28 went further and filed it as a simulator PSUM-accumulate bug. Both were wrong. The two xfails it explained were this gather bug, and on the fix branch they pass. A third host-side bug, fixed earlier at 60faa05, was in the same family: the ndim <= 3 and shape[-1] == b heuristic that picks which backward stats to unsqueeze also matched Q/K/V whenever head_dim == 128. Stats are now selected by name. New CPU regression tests in tests/test_attn_gather.py pin both gather bugs.

fp64 is downcast silently. On the native device, fp64 operands reach the kernel as fp32 and come back as fp32, with no warning. The host-side backward then mixed float and double. The dispatch layer now casts explicitly in both directions.

An unexplained harness gap. Screened-SpMM tests fail under BIRSim with neuronx-cc compilation failed with exit code 70, although the plain NEFF compile passes and the tests pass on Trn2. It is treated as a BIRSim harness limitation and has not been investigated.

Fit. Block-structured sparsity fits this design well: once structure is on the host, the device workload is dense tiles and PSUM accumulation, which is what Trainium was built for. Irregular CSR fits less well than before. With no device CSR, the CSR SpMM path builds its operands on the host and ships dense data across. Sparse structure that changes on the device, as in iterative pruning or graph rewiring, would need a host round trip. Under torch.compile(backend="neuron", fullgraph=True), no trnsparse op worked in the B6 coverage spike, because the inputs were device CSR. A re-run is on #30's checklist.

Upstream asks. Both are filed: aws-neuron-sdk#1442 (sparse CSR on neuron) and aws-neuron-sdk#1443 (simulator and verify() parity with the hardware compile).

  • Sparse CSR on neuron. aten::_to_dense and aten::addmv.out have no SparseCsrneuron implementation, and from_dense on a device tensor fails with Values and crow_indices need to be on the same device. Either kernels, or a documented host fallback with an error that says so.
  • Simulator parity with the hardware verifier. An nki.simulate option that runs source_to_mlir(...).verify(), and ideally ISA validation, would have flagged every kernel behind the 14 compile failures before any hardware time.
  • A hint in the divide error. unsupported op0 'divide' could name the reciprocal-multiply form.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: NKI 0.7's compile rules are not arbitrary strictness. They describe the datapath. A (128, 1) tensor is a per-partition scalar, the scalar form multiplies but does not divide, and partitions are lanes that have to line up. Writing kernels in that vocabulary (reciprocal once per block-row, broadcasts made explicit) is closer to what the hardware does than the NumPy-shaped code it replaced. The same reading extends to the data structure. If the Tensor Engine only ever sees dense 128×128 tiles, then the sparse pattern belongs with the scheduler on the host, and TorchNeuron's lack of device CSR costs BSR almost nothing.

docs.title: trntensor: the mock all-reduce meets four real ranks
docs.text: trntensor's reduce-parallel einsum now sums its partials with a real multi-rank all-reduce, either torch.distributed or an NKI nki.collectives.all_reduce kernel, across all four logical NeuronCores of one trn2.3xlarge, shipped in trntensor v0.17.0 from three stacked PRs, and the first write-up of the four-rank result claimed a bit-exactness it didn't have. Architecturally, the collective is an instruction inside an NKI kernel operating on HBM rather than a library beside the compute, and the rules it enforces (which cores may form a group, which HBM buffer type returns correct values) expose the chip's topology. Anyone planning multi-core contractions on Trainium, or arriving from NCCL, will want those rules before writing a launcher.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
The v0.10.0 post introduced _mock_allreduce, a named CPU stand-in that let reduce-parallel sharding run in CI. Reduce-parallel means the sharded dimension is a contracted index, so every shard produces a partial of the full output and the partials have to be summed. The v0.12.0 post added mixed output- and reduce-parallel dispatch on top of the same mock. Both posts ended the same way: on hardware, HAS_NKI=True raised NotImplementedError pointing at "nki.collectives, Neuron SDK 2.30+," and the swap was promised as "one function call."

On NVIDIA, the cuTENSOR family splits this work between two products. cuTENSORMg handles distributed contractions, and NCCL is the communication layer under most multi-GPU code. A direct port would treat the all-reduce as an external library call made between kernels on a separate communicator. The awkward part on Trainium is that no such separate library exists to call. The collective is something an NKI kernel issues itself.

There was a second, less glamorous problem. A reduce-parallel result is only as trustworthy as each rank's single-core result, and the same hardware window that produced the collectives data also found two precision promises trntensor was not keeping (below). Those fixes come first in the PR stack, and the collective work sits on top of them.

docs.title: What the architecture suggests
docs.text:
nki.collectives.all_reduce(srcs, dsts, replica_group, op) is called from inside an @nki.jit kernel. Its operands are HBM tensors, and the transfer is carried out by the device's own DMA and collective-communication machinery, not by a host-side library. Each rank is a separate process pinned to one logical core, and every rank compiles the same NEFF. In other words, the collective is just another instruction in the kernel's DAG, with HBM as the meeting point.

flowchart LR
  subgraph Mock["v0.10–v0.12: _mock_allreduce (one process)"]
    direction TB
    MA["A[:, J0..J3]"] --> MP0["partial 0"] & MP1["partial 1"] & MP2["partial 2"] & MP3["partial 3"]
    MP0 & MP1 & MP2 & MP3 --> MS["torch.stack(...).sum(0)\nsequential, one device"]
  end
  subgraph Real["phase4 branch: one process per rank"]
    direction TB
    R0["rank 0 · core 0\nA[:, J0] @ B[J0]"] --> S0[("shared_hbm src")]
    R1["rank 1 · core 1\nA[:, J1] @ B[J1]"] --> S1[("shared_hbm src")]
    R2["rank 2 · core 2\nA[:, J2] @ B[J2]"] --> S2[("shared_hbm src")]
    R3["rank 3 · core 3\nA[:, J3] @ B[J3]"] --> S3[("shared_hbm src")]
    S0 & S1 & S2 & S3 --> AR{{"nki.collectives.all_reduce(op=add)\nReplicaGroup [[0,1,2,3]]"}}
    AR --> D[("shared_hbm dst\nsame bytes on every rank")]
  end

Two constraints follow from this design, and both turned out to be physical rather than API trivia. Replica groups have to match the hardware's pairing of cores: cores 0–1, 2–3 and 0–3 form groups, and 1–2 does not. Buffer placement also matters. At LNC=2 each logical core is two physical cores, and shared_hbm buffers reduce correctly while private_hbm buffers do not. A GPU programmer reaches for a communicator and a stream. On Trainium the questions are which cores the collective hardware can join and which HBM the kernel is allowed to name.

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
The design keeps one rule from the mock era: the einsum dispatch does not know which all-reduce it is using. _execute_sharded now hands a compute_partial(i) callable to reduce_partials, which picks a backend:

Backend When auto picks it Who computes what mock no process group, world_size == 1, or n_shards != world_size every partial, in this process, summed by _mock_allreduce torch multi-rank group with any non-neuron c10d backend (e.g. gloo) rank r computes shard r; torch.distributed.all_reduce(SUM) nki multi-rank "neuron" process group rank r computes shard r; nki.collectives.all_reduce(add) on shared_hbm

TRNTENSOR_ALLREDUCE=mock|torch|nki|auto or set_allreduce_backend() overrides the choice.

The deliberate tradeoff is that an explicit torch or nki request that cannot be honored raises RuntimeError instead of falling back. A silent fallback to mock under a multi-rank group would have every rank compute every shard. The answer would still be correct, but all the cost of distribution would be paid for none of the benefit, and nothing would look wrong. The library also requires world_size == n_shards, so shard r always belongs to rank r. Supporting more shards than ranks would be more flexible, but it would add a scheduling layer that nothing in Phase 4 needs yet.

The torch backend stays even though auto prefers nki. It is the baseline the NKI kernel is checked against, and it is the path that runs under gloo in the CPU pre-flight.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The collective kernel, from trntensor/nki/collectives.py:

@nki.jit
def trntensor_all_reduce_add(x, replica_group):
    src = nl.ndarray(x.shape, dtype=x.dtype, buffer=nl.shared_hbm, name="trntensor_ar_src")
    dst = nl.ndarray(x.shape, dtype=x.dtype, buffer=nl.shared_hbm, name="trntensor_ar_dst")
    out = nl.ndarray(x.shape, dtype=x.dtype, buffer=nl.shared_hbm)
    nisa.dma_copy(dst=src, src=x)
    ncc.all_reduce(srcs=[src], dsts=[dst], replica_group=replica_group, op=nl.add)
    nisa.dma_copy(dst=out, src=dst)
    return out

# invoked per rank:
y = wrap_nki(_kernel)[(lnc,)](x, ReplicaGroup([list(range(world))]))

Backend resolution and the rank-local split, from trntensor/parallel.py:

def reduce_partials(compute_partial, n_shards):
    backend = allreduce_backend(n_shards)
    if backend == "mock":
        return _mock_allreduce([compute_partial(i) for i in range(n_shards)])
    import torch.distributed as dist

    local = compute_partial(dist.get_rank())
    if backend == "torch":
        return _dist_allreduce(local)
    from .nki.collectives import nki_all_reduce_sum

    return nki_all_reduce_sum(local)

scripts/run_reduce_parallel_multirank.py launches its own workers. It sets NEURON_RT_VISIBLE_CORES before torch is imported, then calls init_process_group("neuron"), and it refuses unaligned layouts before anything compiles:

if not _CPU and not args.allow_unaligned:
    for w in worlds:
        if w > 1 and args.core_start % w != 0:
            sys.exit(
                f"cores {args.core_start}-{args.core_start + w - 1} are not an aligned "
                f"{'pair' if w == 2 else 'group'} (core_start % world != 0); replica groups "
                "like cores 1-2 fail ('no_hier no_mesh'). Use --core-start "
                f"{args.core_start - args.core_start % w} or --allow-unaligned."
            )

That check exists because the runtime's own message did not explain the problem (below).

docs.title: What didn't work
docs.text:
Waiting for a primitive that already existed. The v0.9–v0.12 gate said nki.collectives would arrive in SDK 2.30. A spike on 2.30 found that, per the NKI release notes, it had been there since NKI 0.2.0. The function is also all_reduce(srcs, dsts, replica_group, op=nl.add), not allreduce(list, op=SUM). The v0.12.0 post's upstream ask was a request to make the real API match a guess. The first single-rank all_reduce kernel then failed with a tracing error. The working form needed a genuine multi-process replica group, plus three rules now recorded in the kernel's docstring: collectives cannot read or write kernel IO tensors (hence the two dma_copy calls), collective buffers need name= (otherwise NCC_IBIR440), and every rank must pass an identical shape and dtype.

private_hbm returns wrong values at LNC=2. At both 2 and 4 ranks, the private_hbm src/dst all-reduce failed on every rank, even though the NKI docstring says either buffer type is allowed at LNC=2. shared_hbm is bit-exact.

The unaligned-group error names the wrong coordinates. Ranks on cores 1–2 fail at process-group setup with:

ENC:enc_init_comm failed to init a collective algorithm. reason: no_hier no_mesh replica-group:[0,1]

The group it reports is [0,1], the rank IDs, while the problem is the physical placement on cores 1 and 2. Nothing in the message says that the pair straddles an alignment boundary, which is why the launcher now checks core_start % world itself and quotes the failure in its own error.

The world-4 note overclaimed. The first world-4 comment on trntensor#30 reported each result as "bit-exact to the fixed-order host reduction." It was not: bitexact[fixed_order=False] was in the log. At two ranks the collective's sum and the sequential sum p0 + p1 are the same operation. At four ranks the collective most likely associates as (p0+p1)+(p2+p3) while the reference computes ((p0+p1)+p2)+p3, so the last bits differ. The structural-determinism principle survives in a narrower form. Results are reproducible run to run and rank to rank, and they match a serial reference bit for bit only at two ranks or fewer. The follow-up is to make the reference use the collective's tree order rather than to loosen the claim further.

Precision promises found on the same window. On NKI 0.7, per-call use_sr is a no-op (trntensor#41). Stochastic rounding is process-wide, controlled by NEURON_RT_STOCHASTIC_ROUNDING_EN=1 and read once at runtime init, with round-to-nearest-even as the default. So precision="sr" silently did no stochastic rounding, and with the variable set, every downcast in the process becomes stochastic. It now warns once when the variable is missing. Separately, target_forward_error accepted targets below output roundoff, and precision="kahan" was not really fp64 on the device, which has no fp64 datapath (trntensor#42). Both are fixed and quantified below.

One honest suite failure. The native-device suite is 17/18. The failure is test_matmul_stays_on_xla (expected xla, got neuron:0). The test stand-in maps the old XLA device to neuron (the real native port is draft PR trntensor#46), and the to_xla()/from_xla() helpers it exercises are slated for deprecation. It reflects the harness, not the numerics.

Fit. All four logical cores of one chip share one chip's HBM, so on this instance sharding adds no memory capacity, and no sharded-versus-single-device timing at these sizes has been broken out yet. The case Phase 4 actually targets, THC/Tucker tensors larger than one chip's HBM, needs a trn2.48xlarge or an UltraServer, and neither was available. These results are a correctness milestone, not a scaling result. The communication-free contrast is the suite's data-parallel check (B8), which reached 3.99× aggregate throughput with four independent copies.

Upstream asks for the Neuron team:

  1. Document private_hbm collective semantics at LNC=2. Either it should work as the docstring says, or the docstring should say it does not.
  2. Document the replica-group alignment rules (which core pairs and quads are legal at LNC=1 and LNC=2).
  3. Make enc_init_comm say why a group is rejected, and report physical cores alongside rank IDs.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Shipped in v0.17.0: trntensor#43 (NKI 0.7 fixes, SR warning) → #44 (honest bounds, host fp64 for kahan) → #45 (reduce-parallel on a real all-reduce). All three are merged.
  • Phase 4 — sharded contractions across chips (trntensor#30): multi-chip reduce-parallel on trn2.48xlarge or an UltraServer, a tree-order fixed reference, and sharded CP/Tucker.
  • Phase 5 — trn2 fused multi-contraction paths (trntensor#31).
  • Sibling work: the same launch pattern is the prerequisite for trnfft's multicore collectives, which would extend the batch-split design in the NeuronCore is the unit of parallelism.

Hardware-window record: trnsci#35. Live roadmap: trnsci.dev/roadmap/. Suite tracker: trnsci/trnsci#1.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: The "one function swap" promised in v0.12.0 held at the dispatch layer: _execute_sharded changed by one call, and the mock still runs in CI. Underneath, the swap brought in topology. On Trainium the all-reduce is an instruction inside an NKI kernel, operating on HBM buffers the kernel names, within replica groups the core layout allows. That is why the useful rules are about alignment and buffer placement, not communicators. Determinism holds as reproducibility across runs and ranks, and as bit-identity to serial order only up to two ranks.

docs.title: trnblas: the 92× that was 1.8×, and the DF-MP2 win that holds up
docs.text: trnblas published a 92× speedup for its fused pair-energy kernel on Trn2, and it was wrong: the aten baseline had slowed because device memory was filling up, and against a fair baseline the kernel is 1.8× faster. What survives is narrower and more useful. GEMM routes to aten, a fused kernel keeps the energy step where it avoids work aten can't, and the metric Cholesky moves to the host, which makes density-fitted MP2 1.1–1.8× faster than aten on the molecules where the device beats the CPU at all. The post is for anyone benchmarking TorchNeuron eager code, and for chemists deciding which DF-MP2 stages belong on Trainium.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
DF-MP2 is trnblas's flagship workload. On CUDA it is a cuBLAS story: three-index transforms, a metric contraction and a pair-energy reduction, all GEMMs with elementwise work bolted on. The odd-shape cliff post ended with a warning sign: on the native TorchNeuron neuron device, aten's own matmul beat the trnblas NKI GEMM at every size measured.

trnblas#55 measured that properly. All runs were on a trn2.3xlarge with the public Neuron SDK 2.33.0 (torch-neuronx 2.14.3, NKI 0.7.0, neuronx-cc 2.28.7631), restricted to one LNC=2 logical core (NEURON_RT_VISIBLE_CORES=1), in fp32. aten was 2.4–3.2× faster than the NKI GEMM at every shape, including the DF-MP2 energy chunk (12928×1536×28672: 32.2 ms against 77.5 ms). The older fused energy kernels did worse. batched_pair, the subject of the batched pair energy post, took 7.8 s against aten's 207 ms at nocc/nvir/naux = 64/448/1536. That post's 3.6× was a win over the XLA path's roughly 100 ms dispatch floor. On the native device the floor is about 0.2 ms, and two GEMMs per pair through load_transpose2d have nowhere to hide.

So: what is a cuBLAS-equivalent for, when the framework's own GEMM is faster?

docs.title: What the architecture suggests
docs.text:
On Trn2 the suite-wide answer is that hand-written kernels win where they avoid work aten can't, not on raw GEMM. For DF-MP2 that points at the energy step. aten evaluates it as a chunk of T = B[i] B[j]ᵀ, written to HBM, then read back for the T(2T − Tᵀ)/Δ reduction. An NKI kernel can keep T on-chip:

  • SBUF holds the operands and T. B is pre-transposed on the host, so every load is a plain DMA with no load_transpose2d. B[i]ᵀ and B[j]ᵀ are loaded once and stay resident in SBUF. The kernel's live set is budgeted at 144 KiB of Trn2's 192 KiB per partition.
  • PSUM accumulates over naux. Each 128-row strip of T fills a fresh PSUM tile, and the result is copied into SBUF.
  • The Tensor Engine does the transpose. Tᵀ blocks come from nc_transpose of the SBUF-resident T, which is bit-exact on NeuronCore-v3. That replaces the second GEMM the old kernel ran per pair.
  • An LNC=2 logical core is two physical cores. A one-program kernel uses half the silicon aten uses. The pair window should split across both.
  • Pair symmetry is free to exploit. Because e_ij = e_ji, row i only needs j = i+d (mod nocc) for d = 0..nocc/2.
flowchart LR
  subgraph ATEN["aten: chunked GEMM + torch reduction"]
    direction TB
    B1[("B in HBM")] -->|"mm per i-chunk"| T1[("T chunk in HBM<br/>default budget 1.5 GB")]
    T1 -->|"read back: permute,<br/>2T − Tᵀ, ÷Δ, sum"| E1["energy"]
  end
  subgraph SYM["trnblas::pair_energy_sym, one launch per row i"]
    direction TB
    B2[("B[i]ᵀ, B[j]ᵀ in HBM<br/>pre-transposed")] -->|"plain DMA, once"| S2[/"SBUF: B[i]ᵀ, B[j]ᵀ"/]
    S2 --> TE["Tensor Engine<br/>nc_matmul"]
    TE -->|"accumulate over naux"| PS[("PSUM")]
    PS --> TS[/"SBUF: T strip"/]
    TS -->|"nc_transpose"| TT[/"SBUF: Tᵀ block"/]
    TS --> VE["Vector Engine<br/>T(2T−Tᵀ)/Δ, row sums"]
    TT --> VE
    VE --> EP[("HBM: (128, ND) partials")]
  end

The other half of the answer is less glamorous: the host is a resource too. The metric J is naux×naux, 71 to 555 on the molecules measured. On the device its factorization is an aten Cholesky plus a triangular solve, a chain of small ops that each pay launch and sync costs. A float64 LAPACK call on the host, with one copy each way (20 KB at naux 71), can beat that, and is more accurate.

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
trnblas now routes each DF-MP2 stage by where its operands live and how much work each launch carries:

stage (native path, device-resident inputs) runs on switch plain GEMM family (gemm, batched_gemm, syrk, trsm trailing updates) aten TRNBLAS_NATIVE_GEMM=auto\|nki metric factor X = L⁻ᵀ (metric_inv_half) host fp64 LAPACK if naux ≤ 1024, device otherwise TRNBLAS_METRIC_SOLVE=auto\|host\|device pair energy (nki_batched_pair_energy) pair_energy_sym at ≥ 3 GFLOP per row launch and within the SBUF budget, aten below TRNBLAS_PAIR_ENERGY=auto\|sym\|aten\|legacy

Host tensors, the Trn1 XLA path and the simulator are unchanged.

One launch per occupied row. The sym kernel launches nocc times, so it pays nocc launch floors. That is why aten wins below the threshold: at 16/128/384, aten takes 1.9 ms and the kernel 5.5 ms. But the single-launch version compiled for 734 s at 64/448/1536, against 3–45 s per row launch. Compile time won.

The metric threshold sits at the tie, not the speed optimum. At naux 1024 the routes measured 38.9 and 40.2 ms (42.6 and 43.2 on a repeat). The host route's residual max|XᵀJX − I| is 100–300× smaller, and it never compiles; the device route compiles for 33–210 s per new naux at 1024–6144.

The threshold assumes two host threads. Every host number was measured on 2 cores pinned with taskset -c 4,5. More cores would move the crossover up; that hasn't been measured.

The GEMM routing decision shipped in trnblas v0.7.0. The host metric factor (trnblas#57) and the LNC=1 fix (trnblas#58) are in v0.8.0.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The GEMM routing rule is short:

# excerpt from trnblas/nki/dispatch.py
def _gemm_via_aten(*tensors: torch.Tensor) -> bool:
    """True when a plain GEMM on these operands should run as aten on the device."""
    if _use_simulator() or not _on_neuron_device(*tensors):
        return False
    return _native_gemm_policy() == "auto"

Inside _pair_energy_sym_kernel, the core split and the Tensor Engine transpose look like this:

# excerpt from trnblas/nki/dispatch.py, _pair_energy_sym_kernel
n_prog = nl.num_programs() if nl.program_ndim() > 0 else 1
if ND % n_prog != 0:  # ND is even, so this only guards n_prog > 2
    n_prog = 1
pid = nl.program_id(0) if n_prog > 1 else 0
NJ = ND // n_prog
...
                    # T.T[a-strip, b-strip] = (T[b-strip, a-strip]).T
                    ptt = nl.ndarray((TILE, TILE), dtype=nl.float32, buffer=nl.psum)
                    nisa.nc_transpose(
                        dst=ptt, data=t_all[0:TILE, b * NVIR + a_off : b * NVIR + a_off + TILE]
                    )
                    tt = nl.ndarray((TILE, TILE), dtype=nl.float32, buffer=nl.sbuf)
                    nisa.tensor_copy(src=ptt, dst=tt)
                    t = t_all[0:TILE, a * NVIR + b_off : a * NVIR + b_off + TILE]

The host metric factor has two details that decide whether it is faster at all:

# excerpt from trnblas/nki/dispatch.py, _host_inv_chol_factor
Jd = J.detach().to(device="cpu", dtype=torch.float64)
L, info = torch.linalg.cholesky_ex(Jd)
...
# solve_triangular returns a column-major result; make it row-major on the
# host. Uploading the strided tensor costs ~3.8 ms at naux 71 on trn2
# (the device materialises the layout), against 0.06 ms contiguous.
return torch.linalg.solve_triangular(L.T, eye, upper=True).contiguous()

The other detail is in the docstring: torch's own LAPACK, not SciPy's, because a second BLAS thread pool on 2 pinned cores made the interleaved torch LAPACK calls several times slower.

docs.title: What didn't work
docs.text:
The 92×. #55 measured aten's chunked energy at 96/672/2304 at 63.0 s, against 0.69 s for the sym kernel. It suggested 672 = 5.25×128 as the cause and flagged the number as "pathological" and "worth a TorchNeuron repro". Then it published 92× anyway: in the PR's verdict, in a trnblas#50 summary and in the v0.7.0 CHANGELOG. An aten time 300× the one a row above it, for 2.5× the work per row, should have been checked before it went anywhere.

Torch-only repros in #57 cleared 672 (chunk GEMMs at 640, 704 and 768 took 39–55 ms, with no 672 effect), slicing and sync placement. What reproduced the slowdown was holding memory on the 24 GB logical core:

tensors already held on the logical core warm 12-chunk aten loop at 96/672/2304 0 GB 1.22 s 8 GB 1.22 s 10 GB 35 s 14 GB 64 s 18 GB about 5 min, then Failed to load model, Invalid NEFF, instruction, or input

docs.title: 57 attributes #55's 63 s to that 10–14 GB band, which is what a full 768/96/2304 DF-MP2 working set occupies. Against the fair 1.22 s the sym kernel is 1.8× faster. The code comment, docs/benchmarks.md, the CHANGELOG and the suite tracker now carry it. The 1.34× end-to-end result at 512/64/1536 was never affected.
docs.text:
One footnote: part of the kernel's real advantage is that it never writes T to HBM, so the pressure doesn't reach it. A full 768/96/2304 DF-MP2 run takes 25.0 s on aten with the default 1.5 GB chunk budget, 1.55 s with 0.75 GB chunks, and 948 ms on trnblas. Quoting 26× would repeat the mistake; the fair figure is 1.6×. Shrinking the aten fallback's default budget is an open follow-up, because it changes the baseline.

A faster NKI GEMM that still loses. A spike launched the same GEMM loop as an LNC=2 grid with a pre-transposed A. It came within 8–15% of aten at 2048³ and above (4096³: 4.71 against 4.09 ms; energy chunk: 34.8 against 32.2 ms). So the one-program launch and the DMA transposes were most of the gap. The spike didn't ship: closing most of a gap still leaves a loss.

kernel[2] at LNC=1. The sym kernel first launched as an explicit two-program grid, which fails at LNC=1:

NKI kernel '_pair_energy_sym_kernel' is configured with LNC=2, but neuronx-cc is using LNC=1.
... Remove any bracket syntax from NKI kernel calls (for example, kernel[2](...)); this is being deprecated.

For once the error message said exactly what to do. #58 launches the kernel gridless and splits by nl.num_programs(), the same pattern trnrand adopted in trnrand#66. Timing nearly doubles at LNC=1 (Numbers), which confirms that the second physical core was doing half the work.

A transposed matmul over 4 GiB. DF-MP2's half-transform C_occ.T @ eri_flat aborted the process at 768/96/2304 with NRT status: 1203, A DMA engine encountered an unrecoverable error. It fails only with a transposed-view left operand and a right operand over 2³² bytes (4.29e9 works, 4.30e9 aborts; a contiguous left operand works at 5.44e9), which suggests 32-bit offset arithmetic somewhere in the transposed-operand DMA path. gemm now copies the small left operand to row-major first.

OMP_WAIT_POLICY. With the default OpenMP wait policy, torch's thread pool spin-waits on the same 2 pinned cores the Neuron runtime threads use. A 20 KB upload that takes 0.06 ms under OMP_WAIT_POLICY=PASSIVE took about 4 ms after a host LAPACK call. The policy is worth 3–6 ms on every device path for small molecules (H₂O/cc-pVDZ: 8.4 to 3.1 ms). trnblas can't set it at runtime, so docs/benchmarks.md documents it. With spare cores it matters less; pinned to two, it decides whether the host route wins at all.

Upstream. Both runtime issues are filed with minimal repros and exact versions: aws-neuron-sdk#1447 (the eager loop slows 30–50× as HBM fills, then fails to load a model where an OOM was expected) and aws-neuron-sdk#1448 (transposed-LHS aten::mm with an RHS over 4 GiB). The ask for #1447 is a prompt, legible out-of-memory error, or a warning when the allocator starts thrashing. A silent 30–50× slowdown at 40–60% HBM occupancy is exactly what ends up published as a speedup.

Fit. DF-MP2's GEMMs are the Tensor Engine's home turf, which is why aten, using both physical cores, already does them well. trnblas's NKI value on Trn2 is the energy fusion, and only above about 3 GFLOP per row launch. That threshold wasn't reached on any real molecule measured. Molecules with nocc ≥ 32 and an RI aux basis weren't run; PySCF SCF on 2 host threads was the limit. So the real-molecule gains come almost entirely from moving a small, precision-sensitive factorization off Trainium. At nocc 5 the device as a whole loses: about 3 ms of launches and syncs against a 0.4–2.4 ms CPU run.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
All runs used one LNC=2 logical core and fp32. Host work ran on 2 cores (taskset -c 4,5), so the CPU column is a floor, not a CPU-node baseline. Other libraries' window-2 performance work ran on the same box, and the device Cholesky stage was noisy (5–26 ms) before #57.

Plain GEMM, warm, device-resident:
