docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Phase 2: double-double FP64 GEMM (trnblas#22), the path from the 1e-7 Ha FP32 regime to nanohartree.
  • Phase 4: tensor-parallel GEMM across NeuronCores (trnblas#24). The LNC=1/LNC=2 timing is the smallest case of the same idea.
  • Phase 5: trn2 FP16-accumulate GEMM path (trnblas#25).
  • Follow-ups listed in #57: a free-memory-aware aten chunk budget, overlapping the host factor with the half-transform, and the metric crossover with more host threads.

Earlier trnblas posts: the fused MP2 energy kernel, the profiler that found its Amdahl ceiling, batched pair energy and the odd-shape cliff. Suite context is at trnsci.dev, on the roadmap and in the suite tracker.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: On Trn2, a BLAS library earns its place by deciding where each stage runs, not by out-writing the framework's GEMM. trnblas keeps the pair energy in SBUF and PSUM across both physical cores, avoiding an HBM round trip aten can't. It hands plain GEMMs to aten and sends a small fp64 factorization back to the host, where it is faster and 100–300× more accurate. The 92× showed that a memory-pressured eager device can make a baseline arbitrarily slow. When one row of a table is two orders of magnitude off its neighbours, the baseline is the first suspect.

docs.title: trnfft: batch fusion, and the first FFT result that beats the CPU
docs.text:
trnfft's four-step FFT now runs a whole batch in one NKI launch. At N=4096 with 1,024 rows, the device goes from 10.1 ms to 0.93 ms, against 11.0 ms for a 2-thread host CPU. The previous post found the CPU winning every cell and called batch fusion "the next lever". It was, though the time it recovered wasn't launches: it was a DMA transpose repeated on every tile of every GEMM. The CPU still wins at B ≤ 128 and at N=256, so this matters for batched transforms on device-resident data, not for single calls.

Status

Merged in PR trnsci/trnfft#91 (follow-up to #82) and tagged in trnfft v0.24.0, along with the native TorchNeuron dispatch (#88) and the bf16_refined fix (#87). The tag is not on PyPI yet. Measurements: trn2.3xlarge, public Neuron SDK 2.33.0 (torch-neuronx 2.14.3, NKI 0.7.0, neuronx-cc 2.28.7631), native neuron device, NeuronCore 3, OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 for both the device and CPU runs, on a box shared with other work.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
The launch-cost post cut trnfft's plan to as few launches as the dispatch allowed: one complex GEMM up to N=1024, and the four-step (Bailey) factorisation from there to N=4096, run as two GEMMs, one twiddle kernel and three transpose pairs. Its batched table ended with an observation: at N=4096, device time grew roughly linearly with B above 128, from 3.0 ms at B=128 to 11.7 ms at B=1024. That pointed to per-batch work, not dispatch.

Timing each stage in place, with torch_neuronx.synchronize() between stages, located the work:

B T1 transposes GEMM1 twiddle T2 GEMM2 T3 sum (ms) 16 0.39 1.04 0.59 0.39 1.02 0.47 3.9 128 0.45 1.94 0.58 0.42 1.97 0.42 5.8 1024 0.50 5.46 1.13 0.56 5.42 0.78 13.9

The synchronizes inflate the sum (a free-running call is 10.1 ms at B=1024), but the shares are clear. At B=1024, 78% of the time is in the two _complex_gemm_kernel launches. That kernel is a general complex GEMM: it DMA-transposes A (load_transpose2d) into the stationary layout on every one of 512 M-tiles, and at N1 = N2 = 64 each transpose feeds a moving operand only 64 wide, an eighth of the 512 maximum. At B=16 the picture differs: about nine device ops at roughly the 0.3 ms dispatch floor each. Host Python (about 1.6 ms per call) overlapped with the device and was not the bottleneck.

The four-step had been assembled from a general GEMM and general transposes, library-style. Each piece was reasonable alone. Together they wrote the batch back to HBM between every stage and transposed it again on every tile.

docs.title: What the architecture suggests
docs.text:
A NeuronCore matmul contracts over the partition axis of its stationary operand, so the question for any layout is whether data arrives with the contraction axis on partitions. For four-step it does, written the right way round.

View row b as an (N1, N2) matrix, X[n1, n2] = x[b, N2·n1 + n2]. A plain strided DMA puts n1, step 1's contraction axis, on partitions. Step 1 yields Y[n2, k1] with n2, step 2's contraction axis, on PSUM partitions. Step 2 yields O[k2, k1]: the output in natural order. Every transpose in the unfused driver was an artefact of calling a GEMM that expected another layout.

Second, the tile. The PE array is 128 × 128 and N2 = 64 fills half of it. Two rows side by side fill it, if step 2 stays one matmul. A block-diagonal W2 (P copies of W_N2) contracts P rows at once without mixing them. Block-diagonal matrices usually waste FLOPs; here the zeros are free, because the array costs the same full or half empty.

Third, PSUM accumulates in FP32 and SBUF holds the intermediates, so Y never returns to HBM. The batch is read once and written once.

flowchart LR
  subgraph OLD["Before: unfused four-step (9 device ops)"]
    direction TB
    a1["HBM (B, N)"] --> a2["transpose ×2"]
    a2 --> a3["GEMM1: load_transpose2d on each of 512 M-tiles, 64-wide moving"]
    a3 --> a4["HBM"] --> a5["twiddle kernel"] --> a6["HBM"] --> a7["transpose ×2"]
    a7 --> a8["GEMM2 (same kernel)"] --> a9["HBM"] --> a10["transpose ×2"] --> a11["HBM out"]
  end
  subgraph NEW["After: four_step_fft_kernel (1 launch)"]
    direction TB
    b1["HBM (B, N)"] -->|"1 strided DMA per component"| b2["SBUF: X_re, X_im stacked on K = 128"]
    b2 --> b3["Tensor Engine: one K=128 matmul → PSUM [Y_re | Y_im]"]
    b3 --> b4["Vector Engine: twiddle on 128 partitions"]
    b4 --> b5["Tensor Engine: block-diag W2, 4 matmuls → PSUM"]
    b5 -->|"1 strided DMA per component"| b6["HBM out, natural order"]
  end

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
four_step_fft_kernel does the whole transform for a group of rows in SBUF and PSUM:

  • No transposes. The (N1, N2) row view is loaded directly as the stationary operand of step 1.
  • Packed rows. P = 128/N2 rows share one stationary operand, and step 2 uses a block-diagonal W2, so the twiddle and both matmuls run on all 128 partitions. Each group of rows is loaded with one strided DMA per component and stored with one.
  • Complex step 1 as one real matmul. X_re and X_im are stacked on the contraction axis against the real block matrix [[W1r, W1i], [-W1i, W1r]], so one K = 2·N1 = 128 matmul writes [Y_re | Y_im] side by side in PSUM.
  • Groups sized to PSUM. Q = 512/N1 packs per group fill one 512-wide FP32 PSUM tile.

Each step was measured on its own, in one process, kernel only, at N=4096, B=1024:

Kernel variant Time (ms) One row per stationary 3.13 Packed rows 1.31 Two-matmul step 1 0.88 One K=128 matmul (shipped) 0.79

A load/store-only probe with the same strided access pattern takes 0.62 ms. The shipped kernel is within 0.17 ms of moving the data and nothing else: it is DMA-bound, and matmul tuning has little left to give.

The deliberate tradeoff is generality. The kernel needs N1 ≤ 64, P·N2 ≤ 128 and Q·N1 ≤ 512, so it covers power-of-2 FP32 transforms from 512 to 4096 and nothing else. It also replaces the single DFT-GEMM at N=512 and 1024, which it beat at large B. N=256 keeps the single GEMM. TRNFFT_FOUR_STEP_BATCH_FUSED=0 restores the old dispatch for A/B.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The core of a group, from trnfft/nki/four_step.py on main:

            # PSUM tiles are zeroed and every matmul accumulates, the pattern of
            # _complex_gemm_kernel. Starting groups with accumulate=False on
            # column slices of one PSUM tile lost accumulated terms on Trn2
            # (only the last row of each group was right).
            y = nl.zeros((PN2, packs, 2, n1), dtype=nl.float32, buffer=nl.psum)
            for q in nl.affine_range(packs):
                st = xs[:, q, :, :].reshape((2 * n1, PN2))  # (2*N1, P*N2) stationary
                yq = y[:, q, :, :].reshape((PN2, 2 * n1))
                # Step 1: [Y_re | Y_im] = X^T W1 for P rows, K = 2*N1.
                nisa.nc_matmul(dst=yq, stationary=st, moving=w1b, accumulate=True)
            y_r = y[:, :, 0, :]
            y_i = y[:, :, 1, :]

            # Twiddle: A = T * Y (same formula as _complex_mul_kernel(T, Y)).
            t_r = tr[:, 0:width].reshape((PN2, packs, n1))
            t_i = ti[:, 0:width].reshape((PN2, packs, n1))
            ar3 = nl.subtract(nl.multiply(t_r, y_r), nl.multiply(t_i, y_i))
            ai3 = nl.add(nl.multiply(t_r, y_i), nl.multiply(t_i, y_r))
            ar = ar3.reshape((PN2, width))
            ai = ai3.reshape((PN2, width))

            # Step 2: O = blockdiag(W2)^T A (contraction over the P*N2 partitions).
            o_r = nl.zeros((PN2, width), dtype=nl.float32, buffer=nl.psum)
            o_i = nl.zeros((PN2, width), dtype=nl.float32, buffer=nl.psum)
            nisa.nc_matmul(dst=o_r, stationary=w2r, moving=ar, accumulate=True)
            nisa.nc_matmul(dst=o_r, stationary=w2n, moving=ai, accumulate=True)
            nisa.nc_matmul(dst=o_i, stationary=w2r, moving=ai, accumulate=True)
            nisa.nc_matmul(dst=o_i, stationary=w2i, moving=ar, accumulate=True)

The constants are built on the host and cached on the device. This is from _four_step_fused_consts in trnfft/fft_core.py:

    w1_blk = torch.cat(
        [torch.cat([W1.real, W1.imag], dim=1), torch.cat([-W1.imag, W1.real], dim=1)], dim=0
    )
    out = (
        w1_blk,
        t_re.repeat(pack, packs),
        t_im.repeat(pack, packs),
        torch.block_diag(*[W2.real] * pack),
        torch.block_diag(*[W2.imag] * pack),
    )

four_step_pack_rows picks P per call: the largest power of 2 ≤ 128/N2 that divides the batch, so an odd batch gets P = 1 and runs with less of the array filled rather than failing. That removes an old limit: the unfused N=4096 path's twiddle kernel asserted for any B > 16 not a multiple of 16 (B=38, say).

docs.title: What didn't work
docs.text:
The PSUM trap. The first version began each group with nc_matmul(..., accumulate=False) on column slices of one shared PSUM tile, the obvious way to say "this slice starts fresh". On Trn2 it lost terms: only the last row group of each tile came out right. nki.simulate got every group right. The pattern that works on hardware, zeroing the tile and always passing accumulate=True, is what _complex_gemm_kernel already did, and the simulator warns that it is undefined. So the simulator accepts the pattern that fails and warns on the one that works. This is a comment on aws-neuron/aws-neuron-sdk#1443, which already collects simulator/hardware mismatches from trnrand and trnsparse. The ask: document what accumulate=False on a slice of a larger PSUM tile means, or make the simulator model the hardware, and move the warning to the pattern that actually fails. Until then, verify() plus a hardware run are both needed; neither catches everything.

Spreading the twiddle across engines. Moving part of the twiddle from the Vector Engine onto GpSimd and the Scalar Engine looked like free parallelism. It measured slower and was dropped. The cause wasn't isolated; SBUF port sharing is a plausible explanation, not a measured one.

Compile time grows with B. The kernel body is unrolled per row group, so first-call compile grows with the batch: 3 s at B=1024, 17 s at B=8192. It is the unrolling reported in aws-neuron/aws-neuron-sdk#1440, and the workaround is borrowed from the row-chunked Stockham launches of #85: TRNFFT_FOUR_STEP_FUSED_MAX_ROWS (default 4096) splits larger batches into launches that share one compiled shape.

Not bit-identical. The fused kernel differs from the unfused driver by up to 6e-5 absolute on outputs of order 10², about 1 ulp, because step 1 sums its K = 2·N1 terms in one PE pass instead of two. Error against FP64 is unchanged at N=2048 and 4096 and slightly lower at 512 and 1024. Each path is deterministic, and chunked and single-launch outputs are bit-equal. Golden outputs pinned against v0.23.0 will change.

A refinement that never refined. The April PSUM-refinement post said bf16_refined drives error "to ~1e-6". On Trn2 it measured about 2e-3 against a promised 1e-5 (#86), no better than plain bf16. The fault was the algorithm, not the device: CPU emulation reproduces the Trn2 numbers to three digits. The residual r = x − IFFT(X̂) used the BF16 inverse GEMM. With W̃ = W + E and W̃′ = W⁻¹ + E′, the correction cancels the forward error and adds the inverse's, which is the same size, so more steps don't help either. #87 reconstructs with the FP32 DFT-GEMM instead, now validated on Trn2 (table below). The cost: each step is 2 BF16 GEMMs plus 1 FP32 GEMM, more than "fast" alone, and the docstrings say so. A CPU regression test now holds bf16_refined below bf16/100, which would have caught the April claim.

precision N Trn2 before #87 Trn2 after #87 bound bf16_refined 128 2.029e-3 4.61e-6 1e-5 bf16_refined 256 2.078e-3 4.74e-6 1e-5 bf16 128 / 256 2.058e-3 / 2.091e-3 2.06e-3 / 2.09e-3 2e-3 → 3e-3 (restated)

Fit. This is the first trnfft result where the device beats the host, and the reason is architectural: a batch of N ≤ 4096 transforms is a stack of 128-partition matmuls with FP32 PSUM accumulation, once the layout stops fighting the array. The kernel is now DMA-bound, and under it sits the ~0.27–0.35 ms eager dispatch floor that no kernel change moves. Small batches and N=256 are too little work per launch; a CPU finishes them in tens of microseconds. That matches the suite-wide Trn2 finding: hand-written kernels win where they avoid work aten can't (here, intermediate HBM passes and per-tile transposes), not on raw GEMM.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• The small-B floor. What is left at B ≤ 128 is dispatch, at about 0.3 ms per call. The two options in #82 are fusing the FFT into a larger on-device graph (STFT, or a torch.compile region) and lowering the per-launch cost.
  • Beyond N=4096. The kernel's N1 ≤ 64 limit comes from stacking re/im on 128 partitions. Larger N still goes through per-stage Stockham launches.
  • Multi-core. Still after the dispatch-floor work, per #82.
  • Phase 2 — precision, including whether bf16_refined stays, is deprecated, or points users to ozaki on Trn2 (an open decision in #87)
  • Phase 3 — plan reuse, streaming large FFTs, NEFF cache
  • Phase 4 — multi-chip large-N FFT
  • Phase 5 — trn2 larger-SBUF path

Suite context: trnsci.dev, the roadmap, the suite-wide tracker, and the Trn2 window scoreboard trnsci#35.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: The launch-cost post found that the unit of cost was the launch. Once launches were few, it was layout. The unfused four-step spent most of its time transposing data into the shape a general GEMM wanted, when the FFT's own index structure already put the contraction axis on partitions. Reading the rows in place, packing two per stationary operand with a block-diagonal W2, and keeping everything in SBUF and PSUM turned 10.1 ms into 0.93 ms, within 0.17 ms of the DMA floor. The April observation that FFT is a GEMM still holds, with a condition: it has to be a GEMM laid out for this array, not a call to a general one.

docs.title: trnrand: the 2× floor of bit-identical Threefry
docs.text: trnrand v0.9.0 takes the full-word Threefry kernel from 5.0 to 2.5 ms at 4M normals on Trn2. It also brings trnrand.normal(4M), measured end to end to a host tensor, to 5.5–8.1 ms, below CPU randn at 11.5–15.6 ms. Most of that gain came from moving host work off the critical path and from noticing the kernel had been running twice. The part worth writing about is the kernel's floor, which sits at about 2× aten randn for a reason the four-engine post did not anticipate: on this silicon, GpSimd and the Vector Engine cannot overlap. Anyone planning to spread an integer workload across Trainium's engines and expecting the engine times to overlap should read the profile below first.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
trnrand is the suite's cuRAND analog. Its on-device generator is Threefry4x32-20, and its contract is bit-identity: for a given seed and counter_offset, every kernel width and every launch plan must produce the same values. That contract shaped the byte-tile post in April, and the full-words post from the first Trn2 window. That post ended with normal(4M) at 15.9 ms, about 11× behind aten, and a guess about the reason: Threefry-20 "may simply be more work than whatever aten runs."

The guess was aimed at the wrong place. The 15.9 ms was measured through the threefry_normal_nki host wrapper. On v0.8.0, a device profile of one 16-chunk launch and some instrumentation of the host path in the second window split the 4M call like this (warm, 2 CPU threads, from trnrand#66):

step (v0.8.0, normal(4M) to host) ms bulk32 kernel launch, incl. sync ~5.3 6 host→device input copies (one was 2.7 ms in situ) ~4.6 device→host copy, 16 MB 1.3–4.7 host reorder _bulk_tile_order 2–7 out * std + mean, out of place on the CPU ~9 total 20–28

The biggest single item was a scale-and-shift that allocated two fresh 4M-element tensors on the CPU, even for std=1, mean=0. The kernel was about a fifth of the total. The profile also showed that the 4.56 ms of device time was not even spent once. The kernel was gridless, and a gridless NKI kernel at LNC=2, the Trn2 default, runs in full on both physical cores of the logical core. Both cores computed every value and both wrote the same output.

docs.title: What the architecture suggests
docs.text:
The four-engine post drew RNG on Trainium as a pipeline: counter rounds on GpSimd, Box-Muller on the Vector Engine, and output staying in SBUF for the next consumer. The diagram did not say the stages overlap, but the argument depended on it. Separate engines were supposed to mean separate throughput. The Trn2 profile tested that and it did not hold.

Per core, before the fix:

engine active instructions doing Vector 4.14 ms 4,295 rotate/xor, ~160 per chunk GpSimd 3.03 ms 1,402 int32 adds, 65 per chunk at ~2.9 µs each ScalarE 0.37 ms 519 LN, SQRT, SIN; 78 activation-table loads DMA ~2%

Three things in that table contradict the April picture.

The integer stage spans two engines, not one. GpSimd is the only engine whose int32 add is exact. The rotate and XOR are bitvec ops, which run on the Vector Engine. Every Threefry round therefore crosses between GpSimd and Vector.

The transcendentals are not on the Vector Engine. LN, SQRT and SIN lower to ScalarE activations, and ScalarE is about 8% busy. The engine April assigned to Box-Muller is busy with rotate/xor. The engine that does run Box-Muller sits mostly idle.

GpSimd and Vector serialize. A Vector rotate or xor takes 0.41–0.69 µs when it runs alone. Issued while a GpSimd add is in flight, it stretches to about 2.95 µs, the length of the add. The two engines share the SBUF port. This is why Vector shows 4.14 ms active for work that should take a fraction of that.

flowchart TB
  subgraph assumed ["Assumed (April): engines as pipeline stages"]
    direction LR
    G1["GpSimd<br/>Threefry rounds"] --> V1["Vector<br/>Box-Muller"] --> S1[/"SBUF<br/>consumer"/]
    G1 -. overlaps .- V1
  end
  subgraph measured ["Measured (Trn2, NKI 0.7): one shared SBUF port"]
    direction LR
    G2["GpSimd<br/>int32 add, ~2.9 µs"] <-->|"same SBUF port:<br/>Vector op stretches<br/>0.41–0.69 → ~2.95 µs"| V2["Vector<br/>rotate / xor"]
    V2 --> SC["ScalarE<br/>LN / SQRT / SIN<br/>~8% busy"]
  end

Profiling settles the obvious next idea before it is written. Double-buffering Threefry on chunk k+1 against Box-Muller on chunk k would only help if the engines could run at the same time, and for GpSimd and Vector they cannot. That limit comes from the hardware, not from the bit-identity contract. With overlap ruled out, three levers remained: issue fewer GpSimd adds, issue fewer Vector instructions, and stop running the whole kernel twice.

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
trnrand#66 made five changes. All of them preserve bit-identity, and the kernel changes apply only to the full-word kernels (TRNRAND_LIMB_BITS=32, the native default).

  1. Both LNC=2 cores, split by program_id. If the chunk count C is even, each core gets whole chunks. Otherwise each core gets half the columns of every chunk. Per-core tiles are never wider than before, so SBUF use does not grow.
  2. Hoisted key injection. x0 = lane + ks0 is the same for every chunk, and x2, x3 are just the key words. That removes three GpSimd adds per chunk.
  3. One instruction for u24 → uniform. (x & 0xFFFFFF) feeds a single tensor_scalar that multiplies by 2⁻²⁴ and clamps at 1e-7. The implicit uint32→fp32 cast inside it is exact below 2²⁴.
  4. Output in final order. The kernel writes (C·P, F, 4) so that the flat output is already in per-tile order. The host reorder is gone, and each partition leaves in one contiguous DMA.
  5. Host path. One packed host→device copy per call instead of six, a device-cached lane tile, and an in-place affine.

The deliberate tradeoff is the one carried over from earlier posts: the stream stays fixed. The changes that would most obviously move the floor, discussed below, all change the values for a given seed. trnrand is giving up the last factor of two to keep its streams stable.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The core split in _threefry_bulk32_body (trnrand/nki/dispatch.py on main):

n_prog = nl.num_programs() if nl.program_ndim() > 0 else 1
pid = nl.program_id(0) if n_prog > 1 else 0
if C % n_prog == 0:  # whole chunks per core: full-width instructions
    W = F
    c_lo = pid * (C // n_prog)
    c_hi = c_lo + C // n_prog
elif F % n_prog == 0:  # e.g. C = 1: split every chunk's columns
    W = F // n_prog
    c_lo = 0
    c_hi = C
else:
    n_prog = 1
    pid = 0
    W = F
    c_lo = 0
    c_hi = C
j0 = 0 if W == F else pid * W

The u24 → uniform step, one instruction per word:

nisa.tensor_scalar(
    u0, m0, op0=nl.multiply, operand0=inv24, op1=nl.maximum, operand1=clamp_eps
)

The fix for the largest single item in the host table is less clever (trnrand/distributions.py):

def _affine(out: torch.Tensor, scale: float, shift: float) -> torch.Tensor:
    if _compiling():
        return out * scale + shift
    if scale != 1.0:  # x * 1.0 == x exactly
        out.mul_(scale)
    return out.add_(shift)

Eager NKI draws come back as fresh host tensors, so nothing else holds a reference and the in-place version is safe. The arithmetic is the same two fp32 ops, so the values do not change. Nine milliseconds went to allocations in a Python expression that looks free.

docs.title: What didn't work
docs.text:
The Vector Engine cannot do the adds. If the adds could move to the Vector Engine, the shared-port problem would at least become a scheduling problem on one engine. A direct test of tensor_tensor(..., engine=vector) on uint32 operands gave wrong results in 99.7% of cases, because the Vector Engine computes the add in fp32. A 16-bit-limb add on the Vector Engine is exact but costs about 11 instructions, which is slower than one GpSimd add. The adds stay on GpSimd.

Rotate and xor cannot be fused. Fusing them would cut the Vector instruction count, which is the half of the critical path that GpSimd does not own. scalar_tensor_tensor does not accept bitvec ops, so the fusion cannot be expressed.

ScalarE cannot take the bitwork. ScalarE is 92% idle and would be the natural place to move rotate/xor off the shared port, but it has no bitvec ops.

The four-engine framing was right about which engine does what, and wrong about the throughput. Counter-based RNG does use GpSimd, the Vector Engine and ScalarE. What it did not get was their time in parallel. The full-words post's guess that Threefry is "more work than aten" was also wrong in a specific way: at v0.8.0 the kernel was about a fifth of the call, and that kernel was running on both cores.

Toolchain notes. NKI 0.7.0 on neuronx-cc 2.28.7631:

  • A gridless kernel at LNC=2 runs redundantly on both cores without any signal. The output was correct, so only the device profile showed it. A compiler note for gridless kernels compiled at LNC>1 would have caught it a window earlier.

Upstream ask. The trnrand comment on aws-neuron-sdk#1308 asked for documentation of which integer ops are exact on which engine. The result that Vector uint32 adds are computed in fp32 is one more row for that table. The SBUF port shared by GpSimd and the Vector Engine is a second gap: it decides whether a two-engine design can overlap at all. A short note in the NKI performance guide on which engine pairs contend for SBUF bandwidth would save the next library a profiling session. Neither of these has been filed as its own issue.

docs.title: 66 adds an LNC=2 source_to_mlir(..., lnc=2).verify() test for each split shape. Per aws-neuron-sdk#1443, verify() accepts some kernels that neuronx-cc rejects for hardware. So the test is a structural check, and the hardware suite remains the gate.
Numbers
docs.text:
trn2.3xlarge, public Neuron SDK 2.33.0 (torch-neuronx 2.14.3, NKI 0.7.0, neuronx-cc 2.28.7631), native neuron device. NEURON_RT_VISIBLE_CORES=2, host threads pinned with taskset -c 10,11, and OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 / torch.set_num_threads(2) for every column, including CPU randn. Warm medians of 30, two alternating rounds. The box was shared (load average about 7), so the ranges in the host columns mostly show contention.

n kernel, device-resident: v0.8.0 kernel: v0.9.0 normal() → host: v0.8.0 v0.9.0 aten randn (device) CPU randn 16,384 0.27–0.28 0.27–0.36 0.82–1.27 0.70–0.93 0.13–0.15 0.05–0.09 262,144 0.53–0.69 0.47–0.57 3.8–5.7 1.3–2.0 0.21–0.24 0.83–1.27 1,048,576 1.43 0.82–0.89 6.7–6.8 1.9–2.1 0.37–0.39 2.9–3.9 4,194,304 5.0–5.2 2.50–2.55 25.7–28.1 5.5–8.1 1.08–1.14 11.5–15.6

All times are in ms. "Kernel" is the nki_op launch with device inputs, synchronized. "normal() → host" is the public API, including the 16 MB device→host copy at 4M.

device profile, 4M, per core v0.8.0 v0.9.0 device time 4.56 ms (on both cores) 2.20 ms (split) GpSimd instructions 1,402 734 Vector instructions 4,295 2,225 GpSimd add time ~1.9 ms 1.43 ms validation (v0.9.0) result test_limb_variants_bit_identical, 8- vs 32-bit at n = 1, 16,385, 1,048,577, 4,194,305 (column split, odd C, two launches) bit-identical full neuron suite 90 passed, 1 xpassed simulator (-m nki_simulator) 132 passed CPU (-m "not neuron") 941 passed

The floor. A bit-identical Threefry4x32-20 needs about 62 GpSimd adds per (128, 512) chunk at about 2.9 µs each. At 4M that comes to about 1.4 ms per core. Add about 0.7 ms of Vector rotate/xor that cannot overlap the adds, and the total is roughly 2 ms of device time, about 2× aten's 1.1 ms. The measured 2.20 ms is close to that. There is little left to win without changing the stream.

Fit, stated plainly.

  • Where Trainium wins. Generating on the device and shipping the result to the host now beats CPU randn at 1M and 4M. trnrand also keeps its property of bit-identical streams across kernel widths, launch plans and cores.
  • Where the CPU wins. At 16k and 262k, the CPU is faster end to end. At 16k, both device paths are bound by launch overhead: the kernel takes 0.27 ms against aten's 0.14 ms.
  • Where aten wins. On the device, aten is about 2.3× faster at 4M at aligned shapes, and that gap is close to structural. aten presumably uses the hardware RNG (nisa.rand2/rng), which produces a different stream. Fewer Threefry rounds would also change the stream. More NeuronCores would cut the time without changing the stream, but that is a resource choice, not a kernel improvement. At shapes that are not multiples of 128, the comparison flips. aten randn has a cliff there (aws-neuron-sdk#1439, and the trnblas odd-shape post), while trnrand pads internally.

The architectural reason for the 2× is that Threefry is ALU-bound, integer-only work. Its two instruction classes run on two engines that share one SBUF port, and the engine with spare capacity has no bitwise instructions. The Tensor Engine, most of the silicon, is never touched. That matches the suite-wide finding on Trn2: hand-written kernels win where they avoid work that aten can't, not where they compete with it head to head.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• trnrand#60 is closed. The work in this post shipped in trnrand v0.9.0, which is tagged but not yet on PyPI.
  • Phase 5: trn2 PSUM sizing for larger batched tile generation (trnrand#21).
  • Benchmarks vs cuRAND (trnrand#3).
  • A hardware-RNG mode would be an opt-in, different-stream generator, like the existing key_mode="counter". It is an open design question, not yet an issue.
  • Suite context lives on the roadmap and the suite tracker.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: On Trainium, four engines do not add up to four times the throughput. Before splitting a workload across engines on the assumption that their work overlaps, profile which engines actually run concurrently. On Trn2, GpSimd and the Vector Engine share an SBUF port, so Threefry's integer adds and its rotate/xor run one after the other however the code is scheduled. Most of v0.9.0's gain came from things that were never about engines: a CPU affine, a host reorder, six copies, and a kernel running twice. What remains is about 2× aten, and that is the cost of keeping the stream bit-identical.

docs.title: trnsolver: Jacobi on hardware, six months after the argument
docs.text:
trnsolver's batched block-Jacobi eigh on one Trn2 core runs 1.5–2.2× faster than batched 2-thread CPU LAPACK for FP32 batches at n = 64 and 128 with B ≥ 64–256, and at n = 32 with B = 1024. Against a fairer CPU baseline, the batch split across the same threads, the margin shrinks to about 1.13× (see the correction below). Getting there meant first measuring the design the library had picked over Jacobi in April, batched Householder tridiagonalization, losing to the CPU by 6–17×. The April post argued that Trainium wants Jacobi, then the library deleted its Jacobi kernels two days later; this post is the hardware verdict on both decisions, for anyone with thousands of small symmetric eigenproblems, such as SCF inner loops.

Correction (2026-10-31)

The CPU column below is batched torch.linalg.eigh, which barely uses its second thread at these sizes. Splitting the batch across the same 2 threads is 1.6–5.8× faster (trnsolver#54). Against that baseline the single-core kernel at n = 128, B = 1024 is 310 vs 352 ms, 1.13× rather than 2×. Spreading the batch over all 4 cores of the chip brings it to 152 ms (0.43× of the split CPU on 2 threads), but against 8 CPU threads the best device result is at most 1.25× faster. The Jacobi-over-Householder verdict stands; the margin over a well-used CPU is small.

Code status

The one-sided Jacobi kernel (trnsolver#50) shipped in v0.17.0. The block kernel and the method="auto" region (#52) are in v0.18.0. The Householder device pipeline (#45, #47, #49) stays as draft PRs, kept for their measurements. Everything ran on a trn2.3xlarge with public Neuron SDK 2.33.0 (torch-neuronx 2.14.3, NKI 0.7.0, neuronx-cc 2.28.7631).

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
The previous trnsolver post ended with a concession: eigh on a neuron tensor ran in about 1 ms because aten's linalg_eigh executes on the host, and trnsolver's own NKI path was 100–1000× slower. The stated fix was on-device tridiagonalization, so that the NKI path stopped paying O(n) host syncs.

That fix landed: one launch that does the whole Householder reduction with A resident in SBUF (#45, rebuilt on the native dispatch path as #47). It is cuSOLVER's syevd plan: reduce, solve the tridiagonal, back-transform. At n = 128 the all-device path first measured 115.5 ms, against 1.5 ms for the aten cutover.

That 115.5 ms was wrong. Three other lanes were running heavy jobs on the box's 12 vCPUs, and the host LAPACK stages were competing with them for threads. With OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 the same path took 7.9 ms at n = 128 and 5.0 ms at n = 64. Since then, every timing job pins its host threads. The corrected gap was fixed overhead (launches, copies, a device apply_reflectors, host LAPACK), and still not the on-device reason to exist the previous post predicted. The honest framing: one small eigh is a latency benchmark, and the comparison that matters is a batch on the device against batched CPU LAPACK (#48).

docs.title: What the architecture suggests
docs.text:
A single n = 128 matrix fills one 128-partition tile once. A batch of small matrices can fill many tiles, but only if the algorithm gives every tile independent work to do at each step.

flowchart TB
    subgraph H["Householder tridiagonalization, per matrix"]
        direction TB
        H1["step k: matvec w = βAv"] --> H2["step k: rank-2 update<br/>A ← A − uvᵀ − vuᵀ"]
        H2 -->|"step k+1 needs the updated A<br/>(n−2 dependent steps)"| H1
    end
    subgraph J["One-sided Jacobi, per sweep"]
        direction TB
        J1["step r: n/2 disjoint column pairs,<br/>all independent"] --> J2["same work for every matrix<br/>in every tile"]
        J2 -->|"n−1 steps, fixed count;<br/>convergence checked between sweeps"| J1
    end

Householder is a dependency chain. Each of the n−2 steps is a BLAS-2 matvec plus a rank-2 update, and the next reflector needs the updated matrix. Running 16 matrices in lockstep gives the scheduler chains to overlap, but each is still small serial instructions, and the Tensor Engine sits mostly idle.

Jacobi is a fixed schedule of independent work. A sweep is n−1 steps, and each step rotates n/2 disjoint pairs. The trip count inside a sweep doesn't depend on the data. The only data-dependent decision, whether to run another sweep, happens between launches. That is the previous post's line, data deciding which values move versus how many times a loop runs, and Jacobi pushes the second kind out to sweep granularity: 6–8 sweeps for random matrices.

The batch is what fills the tile. In the compact layout each tile holds 128/n matrices, so n = 32 packs four per tile, and a launch holds up to 128 tiles: 512 matrices at n = 32.

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
Two kernels share a driver, jacobi_eigh_device.

One-sided (Hestenes) Jacobi, #50. The kernel rotates the columns of Z = A + σI, where σ is the Gershgorin bound, so ±λ pairs stay apart. The state X = [Zᵀ | Vᵀ] stays in SBUF for a whole sweep, and one launch is one sweep. Per step, the Tensor Engine applies the partner permutation as an exact matmul whose block-diagonal stationary operand every tile shares. The Vector Engine applies the rotations in the delta form X += (c−1)∘X − s∘M. Under LNC=2 each physical core of the pair takes half the tiles. Before the split both cores ran the same program redundantly; it gave close to 2×.

Block Jacobi, #52, for 33 ≤ n ≤ 128. The profile showed the #50 kernel was bound by the Vector Engine (table below). Its rows are 2n wide, and about 25 short column-math instructions run per step. The block kernel groups columns into blocks of 8, so each block pair forms a 16-column superblock. The Tensor Engine forms ZᵀZ, compacts each pair's 16 × 16 Gram block with a 0/1 matmul, and then applies all the pair rotations to [Zᵀ | Vᵀ] as one orthogonal matmul, with the circle-method block shuffle folded in. The Vector Engine runs Jacobi only on the 16 × 16 Gram blocks, on rows 32 wide. Here the Tensor Engine finally applies the rotations, which is the April post's "a rotation is a matmul" idea, but at block granularity.

The deliberate tradeoff is padding. The kernel's cost follows the padded size (32, 64 or 128), while aten's cost follows n. So at n = 80, B = 256 the kernel (77.9 ms) loses to the cutover (74.6 ms), and at n = 96 it wins. The method="auto" region encodes that, and the default cutover is unchanged outside it.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
From trnsolver/nki/jacobi.py, the block kernel's Tensor Engine half. gram builds each pair's Gram block and update applies the accumulated rotations as one matmul per tile:

        def gram(g):
            """Y[:, g] = [Gc | I]: the pairs' Gram blocks, rotations reset."""
            ps_t = nl.ndarray((ne, P), dtype=f32, buffer=nl.psum)
            nisa.nc_transpose(dst=ps_t, data=X[0:P, g, 0:ne], engine=nisa.engine.tensor)
            zm = nl.ndarray((ne, P), dtype=f32, buffer=nl.sbuf)
            nisa.activation(dst=zm, op=nl.copy, data=ps_t)
            ps_g = nl.ndarray((P, P), dtype=f32, buffer=nl.psum)
            nisa.nc_matmul(dst=ps_g, stationary=zm, moving=zm, accumulate=False)
            gm = nl.ndarray((P, P), dtype=f32, buffer=nl.sbuf)
            nisa.tensor_tensor(dst=gm, data1=ps_g, data2=mask, op=mul)
            ps_c = nl.ndarray((P, S), dtype=f32, buffer=nl.psum)
            nisa.nc_matmul(
                dst=ps_c, stationary=gm, moving=rid, is_moving_onezero=True, accumulate=False
            )
            nisa.activation(dst=Y[0:P, g, 0:S], op=nl.copy, data=ps_c)
            nisa.activation(dst=Y[0:P, g, S : 2 * S], op=nl.copy, data=rid)

            for g in range(g0, g1):
                ps_w = nl.ndarray((P, P), dtype=f32, buffer=nl.psum)
                nisa.nc_matmul(
                    dst=ps_w,
                    stationary=E[0:P, g, 0:P],
                    moving=pblk,
                    is_moving_onezero=True,
                    accumulate=False,
                )
                wsb = nl.ndarray((P, P), dtype=f32, buffer=nl.sbuf)
                nisa.activation(dst=wsb, op=nl.copy, data=ps_w)
                ps_x = nl.ndarray((P, 2 * ne), dtype=f32, buffer=nl.psum)
                nisa.nc_matmul(
                    dst=ps_x, stationary=wsb, moving=X[0:P, g, 0 : 2 * ne], accumulate=False
                )
                nisa.activation(dst=X[0:P, g, 0 : 2 * ne], op=nl.copy, data=ps_x)

The dispatch side, from trnsolver/eigen.py, is a table of measured (n_min, n_max, B_min) rows. TRNSOLVER_EIGH_JACOBI_AUTO overrides it:

_JACOBI_AUTO_REGION: tuple[tuple[int, int, int], ...] = (
    (1, 32, 512),
    (33, 64, 256),
    (65, 128, 1024),
    (96, 128, 256),
    (128, 128, 64),
)

group_plan pads the tail group with identity tiles to a power of two, "so each ne compiles at most log2(group) + 1 shapes whatever the batch size."

docs.title: What didn't work
docs.text:
The April plan, as first built. The April post's diagram had the per-round Jacobi kernel hitting the NEFF cache every round. On trn1 it didn't. trnsolver#9 recorded 67 compile workdirs after 39 minutes, because the driver called the kernel three times per round, each after different preceding XLA ops. #38 then weighed three candidates: full-sweep Jacobi in one kernel, Householder-QR, and block Jacobi. It picked Householder as "the most architecture-aligned" because rank-1 updates map onto PSUM accumulation, and v0.4.0 deleted rotate_pairs_kernel and the Brent–Luk driver. What shipped this month is #38's candidates A and C, the two it ranked below Householder. The redesign avoids #9's failure: one launch per sweep instead of three per round, the step loop inside the traced kernel, and padding that keeps launches on a handful of compiled shapes.

Batched Householder lost by 6–17×. #49 got the launch count down to 4 per chunk of 16 matrices: 256 launches instead of 5,120 at B = 1024. That made it 7–30× faster than per-matrix calls, and it still lost to CPU LAPACK by about 6× at n = 128 and 17× at n = 32. Device tridiagonalization alone cost 1594 ms at n = 128, B = 1024, about 1.6 ms per matrix. That stage is the dependency chain from the diagram.

"Rotation as matmul" was the slow mapping at the scalar level. Before #50, four formulations were measured per tile-step at n = 32. Dense-J two-sided Jacobi as matmuls took 3.2 µs, and the Vector Engine rotation took 0.6 µs, then 0.40 µs after the LNC=2 split. An FP32 nc_matmul costs 2 passes plus a LDWEIGHTS of the tile's own stationary, and a per-tile rotation matrix pays both on every tile. The permutation is one stationary shared by every tile, marked 0/1 since #52 (is_stationary_onezero, which the code credits with halving the FP32 passes).

Toolchain notes, NKI 0.7.0 / neuronx-cc 2.28.7631:

rule found what the kernel does instead source abs_max is NeuronCore-v4+ only |h| as max(-h, h) #50, jacobi.py hardware reciprocal was thought accurate to about 1e-3 (corrected: ~1.5e-6 in range; the real hazard is a silent clamp outside roughly |x| ∈ [2⁻⁴², 2⁴¹]) 1/x as rsqrt(x)², arguments clamped to the rsqrt table range [2⁻⁸⁷, 2⁹⁷]; no divide anywhere #50 each activation-table switch costs about 1.3 µs √x as x·rsqrt(x), so only the rsqrt table is loaded #50 accumulate=False matmuls into sub-bank column slices of one PSUM tile lose terms on hardware (the simulator computes them correctly) each matmul writes a whole 2 KiB bank (512 FP32 columns) or the bank-aligned tail jacobi.py; trnfft hit it first (trnfft#91, reported on aws-neuron-sdk#1443) the SBUF-only column-math chain on GpSimd failed at run time on Trn2 stays on the default engines #48

nki.simulate checks none of the ISA-version or partition rules, so tests/test_jacobi.py also runs source_to_mlir(...).verify() at lnc = 1 and 2. That gate isn't complete either: #1443 lists a tensor_tensor divide that passes verify() and then fails neuronx-cc ISA validation.

Two numerical findings also apply to the torch path. Rows p and q must use the same symmetrised a_pq, or clustered spectra stall at off ≈ 1e-4. And the delta form with c − 1 = −s²/(1+c) keeps FP32 orthogonality at about 1e-6, where plain JᵀX drifts to 3e-5 at n = 128.

The abs_max, reciprocal and table-switch rows are not filed upstream yet. The ask would be an accuracy column for each activation op and the ISA generation on each nisa op's docs page.

Fit. Trainium wins when the batch fills the tiles; then the block kernel keeps the Tensor, Vector and Scalar engines all at 57–74% busy, and DMA stays under 10%. It loses at B = 16 at every n, and at n = 32 below B = 256, because of fixed cost: launches plus about 6 ms of host preparation. A single small eigh still belongs on the host. The CPU baseline is 2 pinned threads on a shared box; a whole-socket LAPACK run would move the crossover and wasn't measured. Against training workloads, small eigenproblems are under-indexed: the 128 × 128 array helps only when many independent problems are stacked into it. An accurate reciprocal, or a divide in the (P, 1) column math, would shorten the chain of short instructions that still bounds the Vector Engine.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Fixed cost. The next levers in #52 are the per-tile load and store DMAs and the PSUM→SBUF copies on ACT, which decide the B = 16 rows. Tracked on #48.
  • Phase 4 — parallel Jacobi sweeps across NeuronCores. The batch is independent, so sharding it across logical NeuronCores should scale linearly; not yet measured.
  • Phase 5 — trn2 rotation-block tuning. Block size 8 won over 4 at n = 64 and over 16 at n = 128. n > 128 is multi-tile and untouched.
  • Phase 2 — iterative refinement, for chemistry that needs more than FP32's ~1e-6. Phase 3 — NEFF cache reuse.
  • Upstream: aws-neuron-sdk#1443, simulator and verifier gaps, including the PSUM slice hazard.

The suite-wide finding from this window: on Trn2, hand-written kernels win where they avoid work aten can't do, not on raw GEMM. See the migration tracker, the suite tracker and the roadmap.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: The April argument was right about the algorithm and wrong about the mechanism. Jacobi beats Householder on Trainium, by 3–21× at B = 1024 in #50, because a sweep is a fixed schedule of independent work, not a chain of n−2 dependent BLAS-2 steps. But per-rotation matmuls were the slowest of the four mappings measured. The Tensor Engine paid off when it moved data exactly and applied whole blocks of rotations at once, and when the batch filled its 128 partitions. When the batch is large it beats a 2-thread CPU by 1.5–2.2×. When the batch is small, the host still wins.

docs.title: trnsparse: the crossover density, with the sparsity pattern compiled in
docs.text: Before trnsparse#34, no sparse path in trnsparse beat plain dense aten on Trn2 (matmul, or unmasked SDPA), and about 60% of each BSR SpMM call went to padding and gathering on the device. The fix is to treat the block structure, which TorchNeuron already forces onto the host, as compile-time constants: the kernel unrolls exactly the stored 128×128 blocks with fixed DMA addresses and no gather, at the cost of one compile per distinct structure. The result is a measured crossover density by matrix size, which anyone choosing between BSR and dense on Trainium can read off a table.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
cuSPARSE's model is that the sparse matrix lives on the device. Row pointers, column indices and values are device arrays, and the kernel resolves the indirection at run time. A naive port to TorchNeuron fails at once, because torch.sparse_csr_tensor has no neuron implementation (aws-neuron-sdk#1442, trnsparse#30). The window-1 post concluded that this costs BSR "almost nothing", since the structure is a scheduling input and scheduling already happens on the host.

Window 2 showed the cost was real, just paid elsewhere. On main at 1fafcaf, the native path still behaved like a device-structure design: it built a padded (M_tiles, K_max) grid of blocks, gathered the matching slices of B on the device, and handed both to a kernel with fixed loop bounds. Two consequences:

  • Pad and gather took about 60% of every call. The Tensor Engine was not the bottleneck.
  • Every block row cost as much as the densest one. With a global-token attention mask, K_max equals the total number of block columns, so one dense row made the whole matrix dense. At seq 8192, forward plus backward took 127–195 ms.

The tile post said each block needs "no gather step", and the v0.6.0 post said "zero gather overhead". The tile post did note that padded rows "pay for the max". The claims were true of the format and false of the implementation. Each block was a Tensor Engine tile, but the code that lined the blocks up was the most expensive part of the call.

docs.title: What the architecture suggests
docs.text:
An NKI kernel is traced and compiled ahead of execution into a NEFF. Every Python value the trace knows becomes part of the instruction stream: loop trip counts, slice offsets, DMA sources and destinations. A GPU kernel reads a column index from memory and then issues a load. An NKI kernel can have the load address baked in, because it was known while the trace ran.

A BSR structure that lives on the host and changes rarely is exactly that kind of value. If row_ptrs and cols are tuples of Python ints at trace time, the kernel needs no gather, no padding to K_max, and no indirect DMA, which the tile post named as the blocker for row bucketing (#15). Each block row walks its own stored blocks, each B slice is a static DMA from a known offset, and PSUM accumulates across the row as before.

LNC=2 follows the same logic. On Trn2 a logical NeuronCore is two physical cores, and NKI traces the kernel once per core with program_id as a Python int. So deciding which core owns which output tile can also happen at trace time, from the same constants.

flowchart LR
    subgraph G["main (1fafcaf): gather path"]
        direction TB
        g1["host: BSR structure"] --> g2["device: pad to (M_tiles, K_max)<br/>gather B slices<br/>~60% of the call"]
        g2 --> g3["kernel: affine_range(K_max)<br/>every row pays the densest row"]
    end
    subgraph S["#34 / #36: static structure"]
        direction TB
        s1["host: row_ptrs, cols<br/>as int[] op arguments"] --> s2["trace: unroll stored blocks<br/>static DMA addresses<br/>split units across 2 cores"]
        s2 --> s3["NEFF per structure<br/>nc_matmul per block, PSUM accumulate"]
    end

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
PR #34 added three custom ops whose structure arguments are int[]. They reach the kernel as tuples, and torch-neuronx keys the compiled kernel on them:

  • trnsparse::bsr_spmm_static is now the default for bsr_spmm on the native path. It walks exactly the stored blocks and addresses B by block column.
  • trnsparse::attn_fwd_static: one launch, two passes, softmax statistics on chip. Pass 2 puts keys on partitions, so P^T is directly the stationary operand of P @ V. No per-block score round trip through HBM, no host reduction, no K/V gather.
  • trnsparse::attn_bwd_static computes dQ (row-first) and dK/dV (column-first) in one launch.

PR #36 splits output tiles between the two physical cores with a deterministic longest-processing-time greedy over stored-block counts: a global-token row gets a core to itself, and every output tile has one writer. The same PR adds bf16: the matmuls run in bf16 with fp32 PSUM accumulation, while scores, softmax statistics and exp stay in fp32.

The deliberate tradeoff is one compile per distinct structure. That takes 1–16 s, cached in-process and keyed by the constants. A test with two structures of identical shape confirmed the cache does not alias them. A fixed attention mask or basis-set block pattern pays once; a pattern that changes every step pays every time. Two guards bound the damage: above TRNSPARSE_STATIC_MAX_UNROLL (16,384 unrolled block matmuls by default) the dispatcher falls back to the gather path, and TRNSPARSE_STATIC_STRUCTURE=0 restores it outright.

Release status: #34 shipped in trnsparse v0.8.0 (tagged). The two-core split and bf16 from #36 are in v0.9.0.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The op wrapper, from trnsparse/nki/_native.py:

@nki_op("trnsparse::bsr_spmm_static", mutates_args={}, fake_fn=_fake_bsr_spmm_static)
def bsr_spmm_static(
    blocks: torch.Tensor, b: torch.Tensor, row_ptrs: list[int], cols: list[int]
) -> torch.Tensor:
    # Structure arrives as int lists and reaches the kernel as tuples, i.e.
    # compile-time constants (torch_neuronx keys the compiled kernel on them).
    return _k._bsr_spmm_static_kernel(blocks, b, tuple(row_ptrs), tuple(cols))

The inner loop of _bsr_spmm_static_kernel in trnsparse/nki/kernels.py. The loops are plain Python range over Python ints, so they unroll at trace time:

        for u in _assign_units(costs, n_prog, pid):
            m, nt = units[u]
            lo = row_ptrs[m]
            hi = row_ptrs[m + 1]
            r0 = m * _TILE_M
            n0 = nt * TILE_N
            if hi == lo:
                nl.store(
                    out[r0 : r0 + _TILE_M, n0 : n0 + TILE_N],
                    value=nl.zeros((_TILE_M, TILE_N), dtype=b.dtype),
                )
                continue
            psum = nl.zeros((_TILE_M, TILE_N), dtype=nl.float32, buffer=nl.psum)
            for idx in range(lo, hi):
                j = cols[idx]
                a_t = nl.load_transpose2d(blocks[idx, :, :])
                b_tile = nl.load(b[j * _TILE_K : (j + 1) * _TILE_K, n0 : n0 + TILE_N])
                nisa.nc_matmul(psum, a_t, b_tile, accumulate=True)
            _pp = nl.ndarray((_TILE_M, TILE_N), dtype=nl.float32)
            _pn = nl.ndarray((_TILE_M, TILE_N), dtype=nl.float32)
            nisa.activation(_pp, nl.relu, psum)
            nisa.activation(_pn, nl.relu, psum, scale=-1.0)
            c_sbuf = nl.copy(nl.subtract(_pp, _pn), dtype=b.dtype)
            nl.store(out[r0 : r0 + _TILE_M, n0 : n0 + TILE_N], value=c_sbuf)

j is an int, so b[j * _TILE_K : ...] is a fixed DMA. The last five lines are the PSUM evacuation, which comes up again in the bf16 results.

docs.title: What didn't work
docs.text:
bf16 is correct, and it narrows sparsity's advantage. Relative error is about 2e-3, which is bf16 output rounding. Against matched-precision dense aten, though, every crossover moves down. Dense matmul gets 1.6–3.3× faster in bf16. The sparse kernel gets 1.3–2.3× faster at 50% block density and less at low density. PR #36 attributes this to per-block cost being DMA and PSUM evacuation, not Tensor Engine work, so bf16's 4× PE rate barely shows. That reading comes from the shape of the numbers, not a profile. Three per-block costs are visible in the code:

  • load_transpose2d of fp32 A blocks is a software DMA transpose, because the hardware DMA transpose (hwdge) handles 2-byte types only. Pre-transposed blocks were 30% faster at 10% density and width 512, but they need a cache keyed on block identity, so they were left out.
  • The PSUM evacuation is two activations and a subtract.
  • Each block makes its own DMAs.

Two cores gave 1.1–1.6×, not 2×. The launch floor, about 0.22 ms for the kernel alone, is the same on one core or two, and calls below about 0.3 ms are bound by it. At low density the floor dominates, and the split has little left to halve.

The crossover moves between runs. PR #34's one-core crossovers and PR #36's one-core column disagree by up to 10 points (see the crossover table). Both ran on a shared trn2.3xlarge. #34 reported about ±0.1 ms of noise below 1 ms. #36 ran every configuration in two rounds and kept the lower warm median; the rounds disagreed by more than 30% in about 60 of roughly 400 cells, almost all below 1 ms. A crossover near the launch floor is good to a few points of density at best.

The reciprocal. The kernel docstring records that the hardware reciprocal alone is accurate to only about 1e-3. Correction: a later on-device repro found nl.reciprocal accurate to about 1.5e-6 relative in range; its real hazard is a silent clamp (it returns 1e7 or 0) outside roughly |x| ∈ [2⁻⁴², 2⁴¹], and nisa.reciprocal on the Vector Engine is correctly rounded across the full fp32 range. The forward therefore computes 1/denom as rsqrt², and the backward uses exact aten division.

CSR and screened SpMM still lose. CSR with host structure now scatters nnz triplets on the device below 10% density instead of copying a host-built dense matrix: 4–11× faster at ≤1% density, still far behind torch.sparse on two CPU threads. Screened SpMM is 1.5–2× faster than on main and still 2–3× slower than dense (A * mask) @ B on the device. It has no tile skipping, so screening sparsity saves it nothing.

Upstream. aws-neuron-sdk#1442 (sparse CSR on neuron) is open and acknowledged. BSR now routes around it, but .to("neuron") on a CSR tensor is still a hard failure rather than a fallback. #1443 (simulator and verify() parity) still applies, so every new kernel was gated on source_to_mlir(...).verify() plus a full NEFF compile (84 cases in tests/test_nki_compile.py). Not yet filed: a 4-byte hwdge transpose, or documentation that fp32 load_transpose2d takes a software path.

docs.title: Fit
docs.text:
BSR at 128×128 is the native sparse format on Trainium, and now there are numbers for where it pays. Below n = 1024, nothing sparse wins. One launch costs about 0.3 ms end to end, and dense aten does the whole product in 0.14 ms. At n = 8192 in fp32, BSR beats dense up to 26% block density at width 128 and up to 49% at width 512. In bf16 those limits fall to 12% and 20%. Dense work is what the Tensor Engine does fastest, so sparsity pays only when skipped blocks save more than the per-block DMA and evacuation cost. That matches the suite-wide finding on Trn2: hand-written kernels win where they avoid work aten can't, not on raw GEMM.

Element-level CSR is a poor fit. With no device CSR and no indirect gather in trnsparse's kernels, every CSR call either densifies or scatters, and a small CPU pool beats both at low density. Static structure is also a poor fit for patterns that change on the device, such as iterative pruning or graph rewiring, because each change means a host round trip and a compile. A future chip, or SDK, with cheap indirect DMA would remove the reason to compile structure in. Until then, compiling it in is what this hardware rewards.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• trnsparse#30: host-structure API. Next on the per-block overhead: pre-transposed fp32 blocks, a fused PSUM evacuation, and fewer, larger DMAs per block row.
  • Phase 3: #15: nnz-bucketing SpMM, streaming and the NEFF cache. The static-structure compile cost makes a persistent cache keyed on structure more interesting than before. #22 covers on-chip iterative solvers over BSR, where a fixed A amortizes one compile over many iterations.
  • Phase 4: #16: sharded sparse matrices across chips.
  • Phase 5: #17: trn2 DMA bandwidth for SpMM. After this window, that is where the remaining per-block cost lives.

Suite context: roadmap, suite tracker, trnsci.dev.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: On Trainium, a sparsity pattern that is known before the kernel runs is not data. It is part of the program. Compiling it in replaces gathers and padding with fixed DMAs, and the device then pays only for the blocks that are stored. That buys a 6.8–7.3× win over dense at 1% block density (n = 8192, width 512), and a crossover that climbs with matrix size, up to about 49% block density in fp32. Below n = 1024, or for element-level CSR, or when the pattern changes every step, dense aten or the CPU is the better tool, and the tables say so.

docs.title: trntensor: on Trn2 the planner earns its keep, the kernels don't
docs.text: On the native TorchNeuron path, trntensor's hand-written NKI kernels did not beat aten on the device at any size measured, so trntensor v0.18.0 now routes plain and fused contractions to aten by default. What the library does add on Trn2 sits one level up, in the host-side planner: contraction order, batching and precision modes. That planner had a bug that built a 4-index outer product, which cost 70 ms on a contraction that should take about 1 ms. Anyone writing contraction code for Trainium, or deciding whether a hand-written kernel is worth it, may find the measured split between "plan" and "kernel" more useful than any single speedup.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
trntensor's NKI kernels were written against NKI 0.3 on trn1, behind the PyTorch/XLA path. Their purpose rested on two posts. When the kernel boundary is the API argued that fused primitives such as mp2_energy and ao_to_mo_transform are the native Trainium shape for contraction. Dispatch granularity is the architecture argued that a fixed 0.67 ms XLA dispatch floor meant the kernel boundary belonged at the loop.

The move to TorchNeuron on Trn2 came in four stacked PRs. #43 fixed the kernels that NKI 0.7's verifier rejected. #44 made the precision bounds honest. #45 put reduce-parallel einsum on a real all-reduce (trntensor#30), which is the subject of the previous post. #46 registered all four kernels as trntensor:: custom ops through torch_neuronx.nki_op, without changing a kernel body.

docs.title: 46 also had to pick dispatch thresholds. It chose 1 G multiply-adds before host operands leave the host, and 128 M before NKI takes over from aten for device-resident operands. Its PR body labels both "provisional estimates, not measurements". The baseline changed too. The earlier posts measured the kernels against host torch. On TorchNeuron, aten runs eagerly on the neuron device, on the same Tensor Engine, so the real question is whether the kernel beats aten there. The XLA-era tables never asked it.
docs.text: The cuTENSOR analog splits the work: cuTENSOR executes a binary contraction, and something like opt_einsum picks the order. A port puts the effort into the executor. Trn2 suggests the order.

docs.title: What the architecture suggests
docs.text:
Once aten runs eagerly on the device, a hand-written kernel and aten draw on the same engines, SBUF and PSUM. A kernel can only win by changing the work: doing fewer operations, moving fewer bytes through HBM, or paying a lower launch cost. On launch cost the custom op starts behind. Its floor is about 0.24 ms, against about 0.13 ms for aten. On raw GEMM, trntensor's kernels, written for trn1, lose to whatever aten lowers to on Trn2, at every size.

That leaves two places where the library can change the work. One is inside a fused kernel. mp2_energy keeps each pair block in SBUF and PSUM and never writes the nocc²·nvir² amplitude tensor T to HBM. That advantage is real, but it only pays off once T stops fitting comfortably. The other is before any kernel runs: the order in which a 3+-operand einsum is contracted. That choice changes the operation count by orders of magnitude, and no executor can win it back. On Trn2 that host-side decision turned out to be the larger lever.

flowchart LR
  subgraph Bad["Before #49: greedy picks the cheapest-looking pair"]
    direction TB
    b1["mi , na<br/>no shared index"] --> b2[("mina<br/>nb²·no·nvir elements")]
    b2 --> b3["mina , mnP → iaP<br/>contract m and n together"]
  end
  subgraph Good["After #49: outer-product pairs ranked last"]
    direction TB
    g1["mi , mnP → inP<br/>contract m"] --> g2[("inP<br/>no·nb·naux elements")]
    g2 --> g3["na , inP → iaP<br/>contract n"]
  end

For DF-MP2's AO→MO transform at nb=256, no=32, naux=512, the left path took 70 ms and the right path 1.16 ms, on the same device with the same executor.

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
PR #49 replaced the estimates with measurements and accepted the verdict.

  • Three executors, not two. _route(flops, pinned) returns "host" (torch on the operands' own device), "aten" (move host operands to neuron, run aten, bring the result back) or "nki". The native defaults are 500 M multiply-adds for offload and never for NKI on the device.
  • Fused kernels only when asked. Under native "auto", mp2_energy and ao_to_mo_transform run as aten. set_backend("nki") or explicit thresholds still reach every kernel, and the XLA (Trn1) path is unchanged.
  • The planner ranks outer-product pairs last.
  • The aten references became real implementations. ao_to_mo_transform became two explicit binary einsums. mp2_energy became a vectorized form chunked over i, about 64 MiB of T per chunk, run on the operands' device.
  • Precision modes stay intact. kahan is still a host fp64 contraction. dd still raises on NKI hosts until trnblas#22 lands. When the aten route handles an sr matmul, the one-time NEURON_RT_STOCHASTIC_ROUNDING_EN warning from #43 still fires, because stochastic rounding is a process-wide runtime setting either way.

There were two deliberate tradeoffs. First, the kernels stay in the tree and stay tested: pytest -m neuron passes 29 with 3 skipped, and MLIR verify passes 27/27 across trn1, trn2 LNC=1 and trn2 LNC=2. Deleting them would also delete the one property aten can't provide, an MP2 energy that never holds T. Second, the offload threshold is 500 M, not the 40 M that autotune_dispatch.py recommended on the box. The autotune rule backs off to just above the last losing shape. The crossover also moves with the number of host threads, and the sweep used two. A default should survive a host with more cores; per-host calibration remains the override.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The router, from trntensor/nki/dispatch.py on main:

def _route(flops: int, pinned: bool) -> str:
    if not _on_native_path():
        return "nki" if flops >= _nki_flop_threshold(pinned) else "host"
    nki_ok = flops >= _MIN_NKI_FLOPS_NATIVE_PINNED
    if pinned:
        return "nki" if nki_ok else "host"
    if flops < _MIN_NKI_FLOPS_NATIVE:
        return "host"
    return "nki" if nki_ok else "aten"

With _MIN_NKI_FLOPS_NATIVE_PINNED = NKI_NEVER (2⁶³ − 1), nki_ok is never true on native unless the user sets a number. Thresholds now parse never and inf from environment variables and the autotune cache.

The planner fix, from the greedy path search in trntensor/plan.py, is a change to the cost key:

flops = 1
for idx in pair_union:
    flops *= size_map.get(idx, 1)
outer = not (set(inputs[i]) & set(inputs[j]))
cost = (outer, flops)

Before #49 the key was flops alone, the product of index sizes in the pair's union. That estimates the step's cost but ignores the size of what it leaves behind. For mi,na,mnP->iaP, the pair mi,na has union cost nb²·no·nvir and mi,mnP has nb²·no·naux. With nvir < naux the outer product looked cheaper, so the greedy search chose it, and every later step paid for the 4-index intermediate. The tuple key keeps "smallest step first" among pairs that share an index, and only falls back to an outer product when nothing else is left.

docs.title: What didn't work
docs.text:
The kernels. On device-resident operands, matmul and bmm lost to aten at every size from 128³ to 4096³ in fp32 and bf16, by 2.5–5× at the large end. PR #49's summary puts the fused AO→MO kernel at 6–20× slower than two aten einsums. The end-to-end ao_to_mo_transform before-and-after rows below show a wider gap than that, and the PR doesn't break down where the rest goes. The MP2 energy kernel was never faster. In the measured rows it ran 1.0–1.8× slower than the vectorized aten form, reaching parity only at nvir=128, where no padding is needed. The kernels have not been profiled or re-tuned for Trn2. They are the trn1 kernels, changed in #43 only as far as NKI 0.7's verifier required. The honest reading is "unoptimized for Trn2", not "can't win", but a dense GEMM kernel is not where a contraction library's effort should go.

The provisional thresholds. The hint was already on file. Window 1's spike, recorded in the body of trntensor#41, measured aten matmul beating matmul_kernel from N ≥ 512 (0.82 ms against 2.33 ms at N=2048). #46 still shipped a pinned threshold of 128 M, which sent device-resident matmuls from about 512³ upward to the slower kernel. The PR was candid that this was an estimate. Releasing the estimate as a default anyway was the mistake.

The planner bug. The greedy path search shipped in Phase 3 (trntensor#29) and passed its tests on small shapes, where an outer product of two thin matrices costs nothing worth noticing. At nb=256, trntensor's own einsum took 70.11 ms, slower than aten's torch.einsum on the device (57.88 ms), whose 3-operand einsum is similarly slow at that size. A library whose remaining claim to value is planning was losing to aten on planning. A threshold-calibration sweep surfaced it.

Smaller things the sweep caught.

  • autotune_dispatch.py reported 2·M·K·N, but dispatch compares M·K·N, so every recommended threshold was off by a factor of two.
  • multi_einsum could mix host and neuron operands in small contractions, which raised input tensor is on cpu device, expected neuron and failed three CPU-suite tests on the box.
  • The non-NKI mp2_energy path was a nocc² Python loop taking 131.4 ms where the vectorized form takes 3.14 ms.

What this changes in the earlier posts. The kernel-boundary post's architectural point still holds: a fused NKI program can keep T out of HBM, and cuTENSOR's plan model has no name for that. Its implied claim that fused kernels are faster does not hold on Trn2's native path at the sizes measured. Its tables compared against host torch, which flattered the kernels. The same post listed "3+ operand einsums fall back to torch.einsum, losing the optimal-order choice" as a gap. That gap turned out to be where the value is. The dispatch post's 0.67 ms floor was a property of the XLA path. On native, the floors are 0.13 ms for aten and 0.24 ms for the NKI custom op, so dispatch granularity now argues against custom ops at small sizes rather than for fusing them. Its batching idea survives: homogeneous multi_einsum batching still beats an aten loop at 256³ and 512³. It loses at 1024³, and on the MP2 J/K pair it is slower than aten.

Fit. Trn2's Tensor Engine is well suited to the GEMMs inside these contractions, and aten already reaches it well. The suite-wide pattern from this window applies here: on Trn2, hand-written kernels win where they avoid work aten can't, not on raw GEMM. trntensor's real work-avoidance happens on the host, in the plan. On-chip, the one candidate is mp2_energy's never-materialized T, and that only matters once the chunked aten form gets into trouble. The suite has seen that kind of trouble. trnblas found that an eager DF-MP2 loop slows 30–50× as device memory fills and then fails with "Failed to load model" (aws-neuron/aws-neuron-sdk#1447). Whether trntensor's fused kernel avoids that regime is unmeasured. One ask has not been filed yet: documentation of the per-launch cost of an nki_op custom op relative to an aten op, and of whether that 0.11 ms gap can be closed, would help every library deciding where a kernel boundary pays.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
trn2.3xlarge, Neuron SDK 2.33.0 (torch-neuronx 2.14.3, NKI 0.7.0, neuronx-cc 2.28.7631), native neuron device. The runs used one NeuronCore (NEURON_RT_VISIBLE_CORES=2) and two host threads pinned with taskset -c 6,7 and OMP_NUM_THREADS=2. Values are warm medians in ms. Device rows use device-resident operands and are timed to torch.neuron.synchronize(). The host was shared with other jobs, so expect about ±0.05 ms of noise near the launch floor and ±0.3 ms on the small MP2 rows. docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Shipped in v0.18.0: native dispatch (#46) and the measured routes and planner fix (#49). The tag is on GitHub but not yet on PyPI.
  • Phase 4: sharded contractions across chips (trntensor#30): multi-chip reduce-parallel, once a trn2.48xlarge or UltraServer is available.
  • Phase 5: trn2 fused multi-contraction paths (trntensor#31). After this window, the bar for a fused path is beating chunked aten on the device, not host torch. The T-never-in-HBM regime is the first place to look.
  • The XLA cross-kernel bug on trn1 (trntensor#39) is still open.
  • Sibling work: trnblas reached the same GEMM verdict and routed device GEMMs to aten. Its fused pair_energy_sym kernel is the suite's example of a kernel that wins by avoiding work.

Hardware-window record: trnsci#35. Live roadmap: trnsci.dev/roadmap/. Suite tracker: trnsci/trnsci#1.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: On Trn2's native path, aten already drives the Tensor Engine better than trntensor's hand-written GEMM and fused kernels, so the library now routes to it. What a contraction library can still contribute is the decision aten doesn't make well: which pair to contract first. One cost-key change turned a 70 ms outer-product path into a 1.16 ms one. No kernel could have recovered that. The earlier posts were right that the kernel boundary is a design surface. On this hardware, the most valuable boundary to design turned out to be the one between the plan and whatever executes it.

docs.title: trnblas
docs.text:
BLAS operations for AWS Trainium via NKI (Neuron Kernel Interface).

Trainium ships no BLAS library. trnblas provides Level 1–3 BLAS operations with NKI kernel acceleration on the Tensor Engine, targeting scientific computing workloads that are GEMM-dominated.

Part of the trnsci scientific computing suite (github.com/trnsci).

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
NVIDIA has cuBLAS with 152 optimized routines. Trainium has torch.matmul. That's fine for ML training but insufficient for scientific computing codes that need TRSM, SYRK, SYMM, and batched GEMM with specific transpose/scaling semantics.

trnblas closes this gap — same BLAS API surface, NKI-accelerated GEMM on Trainium, PyTorch fallback everywhere else.

docs.title: Primary use case
docs.text:
DF-MP2 quantum chemistry on large molecules (>3000 basis functions), where sustained GEMM throughput for tensor contractions dominates wall-time. See the Architecture page for the algorithm-to-BLAS mapping.

As of v0.4.0, trnblas's DF-MP2 is validated against PySCF to nanohartree precision on H2O, CH4, and NH3 at cc-pVDZ. Run the end-to-end example with:

pip install trnblas[pyscf]
python examples/df_mp2_pyscf.py --mol ch4 --basis cc-pvdz

docs.title: Related projects
docs.text:
• trnfft — FFT + complex ops for Trainium.
  • trnrand — Random number generation (Philox/Sobol) for Trainium.
  • trnsolver (planned) — Linear solvers and eigendecomposition.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
trnblas/
├── trnblas/
│   ├── __init__.py      # Re-exports all BLAS operations
│   ├── level1.py        # axpy, dot, nrm2, scal, asum, iamax
│   ├── level2.py        # gemv, symv, trmv, ger
│   ├── level3.py        # gemm, batched_gemm, symm, syrk, trsm, trmm
│   └── nki/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       └── dispatch.py  # auto/pytorch/nki dispatch + NKI GEMM kernel
├── tests/
├── examples/df_mp2.py
└── benchmarks/

docs.title: DF-MP2 → BLAS mapping
docs.text:
The DF-MP2 algorithm maps directly to trnblas Level 3 operations:

DF-MP2 Step Math trnblas Call Half-transform (iν|P) = C_occ^T @ (μν|P) gemm(1.0, C_occ, eri, transA=True) MO transform (ia|P) = C_vir^T @ (iν|P) gemm(1.0, C_vir, iv_P, transA=True) Cholesky J = L @ L^T torch.linalg.cholesky Metric solve L^T @ X = I trsm(1.0, L, I, uplo="lower", trans=True) Metric contract B = (ia|Q) @ J^{-1/2} gemm(1.0, ia_P, J_inv_half) Energy T_ab = B_i @ B_j^T gemm(1.0, B[i], B[j], transB=True)

docs.title: NKI GEMM strategy
docs.text:
The NKI GEMM kernel uses stationary tile reuse on the Tensor Engine:

  1. Load A tile (128×128) to SBUF as stationary operand.
  2. Stream B tiles through the systolic array as moving operand.
  3. Accumulate partial products in PSUM.
  4. One A load serves all B tiles → 2× fewer SBUF loads vs naive.

For DF-MP2, the MO coefficient matrix C is the natural stationary operand since it's reused across all auxiliary basis indices P.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• Level 3 NKI coverage is partial. gemm, batched_gemm, syrk, and trsm (left-side blocked) have NKI kernels. symm and trmm still dispatch straight to PyTorch. Neither is in the DF-MP2 hot path.
  • Batched-pair energy (v0.5.2–v0.5.4) solved the dispatch overhead. nki_batched_pair_energy (#43, #46) replaces the nocc²-loop dispatch with a single @nki.jit call (small shape) or chunked i-loop (medium/large). Warm: 3.6× faster than torch at small shape, 5.2× at medium shape.
  • No FP64. Trainium's Tensor Engine maxes out at FP32. Decision (2026-04-18): FP32 is sufficient — both gate cases are well below 1 µHartree. #10 closed "not needed"; #22 (double-double) deferred indefinitely. See Precision envelope below.
  • Level 1/2 are PyTorch-only. The Tensor Engine is wasted on vector ops; Level 3 is where NKI acceleration pays off. Not planned to change.

docs.title: Precision envelope
docs.text: Trainium's Tensor Engine is FP32-only. trnblas uses FP32 throughout. The question for chemistry workloads is when FP32 accumulation error becomes visible relative to a FP64 reference (PySCF).

docs.title: Measured |E_trnblas − E_pyscf| (v0.5.4, trn1.2xlarge, neuronxcc 2.24.5133)
docs.text:
All values from pytest -m "pyscf and slow" on hardware (2026-04-18, #20).

| Molecule | Basis | nocc | nvir | Pair-energy terms | |ΔE| Ha | |----------|---------|-----:|-----:|------------------:|----------:| | H₂O | sto-3g | 5 | 2 | 100 | < 1e-6 | | H₂O | cc-pVDZ | 5 | 19 | ~9000 | < 1e-5 | | CH₄ | cc-pVDZ | 5 | 29 | ~21000 | < 1e-5 | | NH₃ | cc-pVDZ | 5 | 21 | ~11000 | < 1e-5 | | glycine | sto-3g | 20 | 10 | ~160000 | 1.71e-08 | | glycine | cc-pVDZ | 20 | 75 | ~9000000 | 3.51e-07 | | (H₂O)₃ | sto-3g | 15 | 12 | ~324000 | 4.17e-08 | | H₂O | cc-pVTZ | 5 | 53 | ~70000 | 1.99e-07 |

All 8 cases pass their tolerances. The test_precision_envelope test class in tests/test_df_mp2_pyscf.py covers all rows.

docs.title: Decision gate for double-double (#10, #22)
docs.text:
Decision (2026-04-18): FP32 is sufficient. Both gate cases are well below the 1 µHartree threshold: glycine/cc-pVDZ = 3.51e-07 Ha and h2o/cc-pVTZ = 1.99e-07 Ha. #10 is closed as "not needed". #22 (double-double emulation) is deferred indefinitely.

For reference, the original gate: - |ΔE| < 1 µHartree at cc-pVTZ and glycine/cc-pVDZ → FP32 sufficient (this outcome) - |ΔE| > 10 µHartree → double-double emulation warranted

The FP32 precision floor for a single GEMM (M×K×N) is approximately sqrt(K) × machine_epsilon ≈ sqrt(K) × 6e-8. For DF-MP2, the dominant accumulation is over the auxiliary basis P (K = naux), so the per-element error in T = B_i @ B_j.T is O(sqrt(naux) × 6e-8). With naux = 1536 (medium shape) this is ~2.4e-6 per element, which can accumulate to ~µHartree in the energy sum for large nvir.

The pair-loop accumulation error grows as O(nocc² × nvir² × sqrt(naux) × ε). At glycine/cc-pVDZ (nocc=20, nvir=75, naux≈300), the theoretical FP32 floor is ~5e-5 Ha — which sets the tolerance in test_precision_envelope.

docs.title: AWS Setup for Neuron Tests
docs.text:
To run pytest -m neuron against real Trainium hardware, we use a local workflow:

  • Provision a Trainium EC2 instance with Terraform (stays stopped when not testing)
  • Run the test script locally from your machine, using AWS_PROFILE=aws
  • The script starts the instance, runs pytest via SSM, prints output, stops the instance

GitHub Actions does not touch AWS. All AWS interaction is human-initiated.

docs.title: 1. Provision the CI instance
docs.text:
Two separate Terraform roots, one per hardware family:

Hardware Terraform root Default region Instance Trainium1 infra/terraform/ us-east-1 trn1.2xlarge Trainium2 infra/terraform-trn2/ sa-east-1 trn2.3xlarge

trn2 availability (as of 2026-04-16):

Instance type Region AZs trn2.xlarge — not yet offered trn2.3xlarge sa-east-1 a, b, c trn2.48xlarge us-east-2 a, b, c

Trainium1 (trn1) — us-east-1: 

cd infra/terraform
AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform init
AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform apply \
  -var="vpc_id=vpc-xxxxxx" \
  -var="subnet_id=subnet-xxxxxx"

Trainium2 (trn2) — sa-east-1: 

cd infra/terraform-trn2
AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform init
AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform apply

The trn2 root is self-contained — it creates its own VPC, public subnet, internet gateway, and route table in sa-east-1. No vpc_id or subnet_id variables required.

If apply fails with InsufficientInstanceCapacity, the default AZ is sa-east-1a. Retry with a different AZ: 

AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform apply -var="az_suffix=b"   # or az_suffix=c

User-data takes ~5 minutes to install the Neuron SDK and clone trnblas.

Stop the instance once ready:

# trn1
cd infra/terraform
AWS_PROFILE=aws aws ec2 stop-instances \
  --instance-ids $(AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform output -raw instance_id) \
  --region us-east-1

# trn2
cd infra/terraform-trn2
AWS_PROFILE=aws aws ec2 stop-instances \
  --instance-ids $(AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform output -raw instance_id) \
  --region $(AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform output -raw aws_region)

docs.title: Running neuron tests
docs.text:
# trn1 (us-east-1, default)
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_neuron_tests.sh

# trn2 (sa-east-1, auto-detected from instance type)
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_neuron_tests.sh trn2

# Override region explicitly if needed
AWS_REGION=us-east-2 AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_neuron_tests.sh trn2

The script resolves the default region from the instance type argument: trn2* → sa-east-1, everything else → us-east-1. AWS_REGION overrides.

The script will:

  1. Look up the tagged instance (Name=trnblas-ci-trn1 by default, Name=trnblas-ci-trn2 for trn2)
  2. Start it if stopped; wait for SSM agent
  3. Send the pytest command over SSM
  4. Print stdout/stderr
  5. Stop the instance in a trap (even if pytest fails or you Ctrl-C)

It exits non-zero if any test fails.

docs.title: Running the DF-MP2 bench
docs.text:
Same instance, same SSM mechanism, runs examples/df_mp2.py --bench to capture per-step timing across small / medium / large synthetic shapes:

AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_df_mp2_bench.sh                 # all 3 shapes, torch energy
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_df_mp2_bench.sh --shape medium  # one shape
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_df_mp2_bench.sh --compare-all   # 3-way: torch vs fused-gemm vs batched-pair

Each shape runs cold then warm in the same Python process, so NEFF cache effects are visible in the reported numbers. --compare-all runs all three energy paths in one SSM session — the full Phase 3 table.
