docs.text: Apache 2.0 — Copyright 2026 Scott Friedman

docs.title: Phase roadmap
docs.text:
trnsolver follows the trnsci 5-phase roadmap. Each phase has a tracker issue; work is labeled phase-N-<theme> across the whole suite for cross-project coordination.

Phase Theme Trnsolver scope Tracker 1 correctness NKI Jacobi kernel validated on trn1/trn2; eigh_generalized on NKI path; SCF example end-to-end #26 2 precision Iterative refinement for eigh / solve_spd; Kahan summation in CG / GMRES; depends on trnblas double-double GEMM #27 3 perf Newton-Schulz NKI backend, preconditioners (Jacobi ✓, IC0, SSOR, block-Jacobi), NEFF cache reuse #28 4 multi-chip Parallel Jacobi sweeps across NeuronCores; sharded preconditioners #29 5 generation trn2-tuned rotation-block tile size; runtime capability detection in dispatch #30

v0.3.0 shipped with the CPU path feature-complete and a stub NKI kernel. v0.4.0 is the Phase 1 ship.

Phase 1 iteration is no longer hardware-gated. Neuron SDK 2.29 (April 2026) brought NKI 0.3.0 Stable with a CPU simulator (nki.simulate_kernel); the test-simulator CI job exercises kernel correctness on ubuntu-latest without a trn1 instance. Hardware runs via scripts/run_neuron_tests.sh are now reserved for final real-device validation, not inner-loop iteration.

docs.title: Package layout
docs.text:
trnsolver/
├── eigen.py        # eigh, eigh_generalized
├── factor.py       # cholesky, lu, qr, solve, solve_spd, inv_sqrt_spd
├── iterative.py    # cg, gmres
└── nki/
    ├── __init__.py
    └── dispatch.py # auto/pytorch/nki backend selection + Jacobi rotation kernel

Each high-level operation in eigen / factor / iterative checks the active backend via nki.dispatch._use_nki() and either calls into the NKI kernel or falls back to PyTorch.

docs.title: SCF → solver mapping
docs.text:
The headline use case is the SCF iteration for quantum chemistry. At each SCF step:

SCF step Math trnsolver call Overlap Cholesky S = L Lᵀ cholesky(S) Reduce to standard A' = L⁻¹ F L⁻ᵀ eigh_generalized(F, S) Eigensolve A' V = V Λ eigh(A') (Jacobi on NKI) Back-transform C = L⁻ᵀ V trsm (in trnblas) Density P = C_occ @ C_occᵀ syrk (in trnblas) Metric inverse J⁻¹ᐟ² inv_sqrt_spd(J)

docs.title: NKI Jacobi strategy
docs.text:
The Jacobi eigensolver maps cleanly to Trainium hardware:

  • Each Givens rotation is a 2-row/col update — rank-2 matmul on the Tensor Engine
  • Off-diagonal max-finding maps to a Vector Engine reduction
  • Sweep convergence check is a scalar reduction on the Scalar Engine
  • Eigenvector accumulation V' = V @ G is a batched column update

Jacobi is preferred over Householder tridiagonalization on Trainium because each rotation is a fixed-size operation that maps cleanly to the 128×128 tile, whereas Householder requires growing reflector chains. The trade-off is O(n³) per sweep with O(n) sweeps — cubic overall but with a large constant. For n > ~500, classical Householder + QR iteration on CPU may still be faster.

docs.title: Backend dispatch
docs.text:
trnsolver.nki.dispatch follows the same pattern as the sister trnblas and trnfft packages:

  • HAS_NKI — True iff neuronxcc.nki imports successfully.
  • set_backend("auto" | "pytorch" | "nki") — choose dispatch mode.
  • TRNSOLVER_REQUIRE_NKI=1 env var — fail loudly on kernel-path errors instead of silently falling back. Used by the validation suite.

For the suite-wide picture of which NKI kernels are validated on hardware across trnsci, see the NKI validation status page.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• NKI Jacobi kernel is a stub. Falls back to torch.linalg.eigh until validated on hardware.
  • CG / GMRES are pure PyTorch. The inner products and matvecs would benefit from NKI Level 1/2 kernels in trnblas, but the iteration logic stays on the host.
  • inv_sqrt_spd uses eigendecomposition, not Newton-Schulz. Newton-Schulz (X_{k+1} = ½ X_k (3I − A X_k²)) is all GEMMs and would map better to trnblas, but needs good initial scaling.
  • No FP64. Trainium's Tensor Engine maxes out at FP32. Double-double emulation is not implemented.

docs.title: AWS Setup for Neuron Tests
docs.text:
To run pytest -m neuron against real Trainium hardware, we use a local workflow:

  • Provision a Trainium EC2 instance with Terraform (stays stopped when not testing)
  • Run the test script locally from your machine, using AWS_PROFILE=aws
  • The script starts the instance, runs pytest via SSM, prints output, stops the instance

GitHub Actions does not touch AWS. All AWS interaction is human-initiated.

docs.title: 1. Provision the CI instance
docs.text:
Pick a VPC + subnet in a region with trn1/trn2/inf2 capacity. trn1.2xlarge is cheapest for basic validation.

cd infra/terraform

AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform init
AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform apply \
  -var="vpc_id=vpc-xxxxxx" \
  -var="subnet_id=subnet-xxxxxx" \
  -var="instance_type=trn1.2xlarge"

Capture instance_id from the outputs. User-data takes ~5 minutes to install the Neuron SDK and clone trnsolver.

Stop the instance once ready:

AWS_PROFILE=aws aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids $(terraform output -raw instance_id)

docs.title: Running neuron tests
docs.text:
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_neuron_tests.sh
# or for trn2 / inf2:
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_neuron_tests.sh trn2

The script will:

  1. Look up the tagged instance (Name=trnsolver-ci-trn1 by default)
  2. Start it if stopped; wait for SSM agent
  3. Send the pytest command over SSM
  4. Print stdout/stderr
  5. Stop the instance in a trap (even if pytest fails or you Ctrl-C)

It exits non-zero if any test fails.

docs.title: GPU baseline instance (cuSOLVER comparison)
docs.text:
For vintage-matched cuSOLVER baselines (see Benchmarks), provision the GPU CI instance with:

cd infra/terraform
AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform apply -var=enable_gpu_ci=true \
  -var="vpc_id=vpc-xxxxxx" -var="subnet_id=subnet-xxxxxx"

Defaults to g5.xlarge (A10G Ampere, the trn1 vintage peer). Run the benchmarks with:

AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_cuda_tests.sh g5

Same SSM-based pattern as the Neuron runner: starts the instance, runs pytest benchmarks/bench_cuda.py -m cuda --benchmark-only, prints output, stops the instance via trap. Costs ~$0.17 per 10-minute run on g5.xlarge.

To opt into an H100 comparison for trn2:

AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform apply -var=enable_gpu_ci=true \
  -var=gpu_instance_type=p5.4xlarge -var=gpu_instance_tag=trnsolver-ci-p5 \
  -var="vpc_id=..." -var="subnet_id=..."
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_cuda_tests.sh p5

That's ~$12/hr (single H100) — still pricey, use sparingly.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Stopped = EBS only (~$10/mo for 100 GB gp3). Running:

Type Hourly Typical run (10 min) trn1.2xlarge $1.34 $0.22 trn2.8xlarge $10.00 $1.67 inf2.xlarge $0.76 $0.13 g5.xlarge (A10G, CUDA) $1.01 $0.17 p5.4xlarge (H100×1, CUDA) $12.00 $2.00

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"No instance found with Name=trnsolver-ci-trn1" — Run terraform apply first, or check that the tag matches.

SSM InvalidInstanceId error — Instance hasn't finished booting/registering. Wait 1-2 minutes and retry.

User-data didn't finish (neuronxcc not found) — SSH in via SSM session and re-run manually: 

aws ssm start-session --target $INSTANCE_ID
cd /home/ubuntu/trnsolver && pip install -e '.[neuron,dev]'

InsufficientInstanceCapacity when starting the instance — AWS may temporarily be out of Trainium in that AZ. Wait and retry, or re-provision in a different AZ.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Performance numbers for trnsolver across three axes:

  1. CPU baselines — torch.linalg, scipy.linalg (LAPACK), and the trnsolver PyTorch path. Run on every CI build.
  2. GPU baselines — torch.linalg on CUDA (cuSOLVER / cuBLAS) on a vintage-matched Nvidia instance.
  3. Trainium NKI — the NKI path of trnsolver on trn1 / trn2. Pending hardware validation.

docs.title: Vintage matching
docs.text:
Comparing a 2022 Trainium chip to a 2024 H100 is not informative — both the arithmetic tier and the price gap distort the result. The benchmark table pairs each Trainium generation with the Nvidia GPU of closest architectural generation and approximate price tier:

Trainium chip Launch Nvidia peer EC2 instance On-demand cost trn1 (NeuronCore v2) Oct 2022 A10G (Ampere, 2021) g5.xlarge ~$1.01/hr trn2 (NeuronCore v3) Dec 2024 H100 (Hopper, 2022) p5.4xlarge ~$12/hr

The default GPU baseline is g5.xlarge (A10G) because it's the vintage peer of trn1.2xlarge and within the same price tier. H100 baselines are an opt-in follow-up on p5.4xlarge (1× H100) — roughly 10× the cost of the A10G box, but still far cheaper than p5.48xlarge (8× H100, ~$98/hr).

docs.title: Reproducing locally (CPU)
docs.text: pytest benchmarks/bench_solver.py -v -m "not neuron and not cuda" --benchmark-only

docs.title: Reproducing on GPU (AWS)
docs.text:
cd infra/terraform
AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform apply -var=enable_gpu_ci=true \
  -var=vpc_id=vpc-... -var=subnet_id=subnet-...

# Wait for user-data to finish (~5 min), then stop; scripts will wake it.
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_cuda_tests.sh g5

docs.title: Reproducing on Trainium
docs.text: AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_neuron_tests.sh trn1

docs.title: CPU results (laptop reference — n=256)
docs.text:
Run on darwin/Apple-silicon CPU, Python 3.14, torch 2.x, scipy 1.17.1, float32 except where noted.

Op trnsolver torch.linalg scipy.linalg eigh (symmetric) 2,240 µs 2,251 µs 4,059 µs cholesky 69 µs 68 µs 100 µs solve_spd 86 µs 143 µs (torch.solve) 21 µs (cho_solve) qr 863 µs — — inv_sqrt_spd (eig-based) 2,320 µs — — inv_sqrt_spd_ns (Newton-Schulz) 4,782 µs — — cg (no precond) 161 µs — — gmres 2,549 µs — —

Numbers are for illustration — on the benchmark-target Linux CI hardware scipy.linalg is generally faster than torch.linalg for small dense factorizations, and the trnsolver CPU path should sit between them (thin layer over torch.linalg). Reference values live in results.json artifacts from CI runs.

docs.title: GPU results — A10G / g5.xlarge (cuSOLVER via torch.linalg)
docs.text:
Run on AWS g5.xlarge (1× A10G, 24 GB, Ampere). Numbers include an explicit torch.cuda.synchronize() so the timer captures kernel execution, not async launch. Mean of 5+ warm rounds, µs:

Op n=64 n=128 n=256 n=512 cholesky 95 110 166 277 qr 283 615 1,028 2,248 solve_spd 195 293 560 1,306 eigh 944 2,095 5,463 15,919 inv_sqrt_spd (eig-based) 1,108 2,298 6,191 17,709 inv_sqrt_spd_ns (Newton-Schulz) 2,979 3,005 2,973 3,492

The headline result: on GPU, inv_sqrt_spd_ns beats the eigendecomposition-based inv_sqrt_spd by 2.1× at n=256 and 5.1× at n=512. Same story — eigh dominates on CPU because LAPACK is heavily optimized for it, but when you're on an accelerator the all-GEMM shape of Newton-Schulz wins. This is the evidence that the NS path will pay off on Trainium once the trnblas NKI GEMM backend lands.

Reproduce: AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_cuda_tests.sh g5.

docs.title: Trainium results (trn1 / trn2)
docs.text: Pending — classical Jacobi was architecturally mismatched to NKI (see #9 post-mortem). Phase 1 redesign is iterating against the new NKI 0.3.0 CPU simulator (Neuron SDK 2.29, April 2026) with full-sweep Jacobi / Householder-QR / block-Jacobi candidates; hardware numbers will land once the redesigned kernel validates in simulation.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• inv_sqrt_spd_ns is Newton-Schulz — all GEMM. On CPU it loses to the eigendecomposition path because eigh is heavily optimized in LAPACK/MKL. On GPU it wins at n ≥ 256 because the workload shape fits the Tensor Core pipeline. Trainium's Tensor Engine should show a similar win once trnblas GEMM validates on hardware.
  • cuSOLVER is invoked indirectly via torch.linalg on a CUDA tensor. We don't link cuSOLVER directly.

docs.title: Developing NKI kernels
docs.text: trnsolver currently ships one NKI kernel (rotate_pairs_kernel) in trnsolver/nki/dispatch.py. It's the per-round primitive for the parallel Jacobi sweep in _jacobi_eigh_nki. This page is the short trnsolver-specific version of the suite-wide guide at trnsci/docs/developing_kernels.md.

docs.title: Dispatch modes
docs.text:
Mode Trigger When to use PyTorch fallback HAS_NKI = False (non-Neuron host), or an exception in the NKI path gets caught Laptops, GPUs, CI's ubuntu-latest test matrix — the default for anyone without Neuron installed NKI hardware, native HAS_NKI = True + TorchNeuron torch_neuronx (has nki_op) + a neuron device. Kernel runs as a trnsolver:: custom op on device="neuron" Trn2/Trn3 on Neuron SDK 2.33+. Set NKI_ENABLE_TRACE_CACHE=0 with an editable install. NKI hardware, XLA HAS_NKI = True + torch_xla installed (and the native path unavailable). Kernel runs through torch_xla → NEFF compile → NeuronCore Trn1; real perf numbers, final validation NKI simulator TRNSOLVER_USE_SIMULATOR=1 + HAS_NKI = True. Kernel runs through nki.simulate(kernel)(numpy_args) on CPU Fast correctness iteration during kernel design

All modes share the same kernel source — the @nki.jit definition inside if HAS_NKI: in trnsolver/nki/dispatch.py. The host driver (_jacobi_eigh_nki in trnsolver/eigen.py) picks the path based on _use_nki() and _use_simulator().

Each host wrapper in trnsolver/eigen.py hands its operands to _launch(kernel, op_name, *tensors) in dispatch.py, which picks the native custom op or the torch_xla path. A new hardware kernel needs a matching annotated wrapper in trnsolver/nki/_native.py and an entry in its OPS table. On the native path, keep scalar control flow (.item(), element writes) on host copies: each one is a device round trip.

docs.title: Simulator workflow
docs.text:
NKI 0.3.0 Stable (Neuron SDK 2.29, April 2026) ships a CPU simulator that runs kernels without Trainium hardware. It collapses the iteration loop from ~8–12 min per attempt (instance start + SSM + NEFF compile) to seconds per iteration.

Three equivalent ways to run:

# (1) GH Actions — automatic on every push, zero AWS cost
#     See .github/workflows/ci.yml::nki-simulator

# (2) Local Linux x86_64 with nki installed
TRNSOLVER_USE_SIMULATOR=1 pytest tests/ -m nki_simulator -v

# (3) SSM against the provisioned trn1 CI instance (uses the bundled Neuron venv)
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_simulator_tests.sh

docs.title: CI coverage
docs.text:
Gate Runner Catches Misses test matrix (py 3.10/3.11/3.12) ubuntu-latest Pure-Python correctness against torch.linalg.eigh. ~1 s. Anything NKI-kernel-specific. nki-simulator ubuntu-latest Python trace-level kernel errors: wrong nc_matmul kwargs, dropped ops (nl.divide), shape mismatches, tile-size violations. Seconds per kernel. MLIR verifier errors — simulator explicitly skips compile. Perf. neuron (SSM, manual) trn1.2xlarge Full NEFF compile + on-hardware execution. MLIR verification. Real perf. Nothing (this is the ground truth).

The nki-simulator gate catches the majority of the iteration pain (Python-trace breakage) without AWS round-trips. Hardware runs are reserved for MLIR verification and perf numbers.

docs.title: Architecture-first (reminder)
docs.text:
Every NKI kernel in trnsolver should pull at least one documented architectural lever from #36 — stationary-operand reuse, FP32-PSUM-free mixed precision, 4-engine concurrency, SBUF residency. Kernel changes that are "port scipy faster" get re-scoped or rejected.

The rotation-kernel post-mortem on #9 is the concrete lesson.

docs.title: Basic install
docs.text: pip install trnsolver

docs.title: With Neuron hardware support
docs.text:
# Trn2/Trn3 with TorchNeuron (native PyTorch, Neuron SDK 2.33+)
pip install "trnsolver[torchneuron]" --extra-index-url https://pip.repos.neuron.amazonaws.com

# Trn1 / PyTorch-XLA lineage
pip install "trnsolver[neuron]" --extra-index-url https://pip.repos.neuron.amazonaws.com

[torchneuron] pins torch>=2.14, torch-neuronx>=2.14 and nki>=0.6 (torch-neuronx 2.14 requires Python ≥ 3.12). [neuron] is the XLA lineage.

docs.title: Two Neuron PyTorch lineages
docs.text:
torch-neuronx ships in two lineages, and trnsolver dispatches its NKI kernels on whichever one is installed:

Lineage Instances Stack Kernel dispatch TorchNeuron (native) Trn2, Trn3 Neuron SDK 2.33+, Python ≥ 3.12, torch 2.14, torch-neuronx 2.14.* Each kernel is a PyTorch custom op (torch.ops.trnsolver.matvec, rank2_update, matmul, matmul_fp32out, apply_reflectors) registered with torch_neuronx.nki_op; tensors live on device="neuron". PyTorch/XLA Trn1 (also Inf2) torch-neuronx 2.9 lineage, torch_xla Unchanged: kernels run on the torch_xla device.

Selection is automatic, on the first kernel launch:

  1. native: torch_neuronx exports nki_op and a neuron device is available (torch_neuronx.device_count() > 0). This path never imports torch_xla.
  2. xla: torch_xla is installed.
  3. otherwise there is no device path; use set_backend("pytorch") or TRNSOLVER_USE_SIMULATOR=1.

The trnsolver:: custom ops are registered only when the native path is selected. To force a path, set TRNSCI_NKI_DISPATCH before the first launch (shared by every trnsci library):

Value Effect auto (default) The order above. native Use TorchNeuron; raise RuntimeError if no neuron device is available. xla Use torch_xla even if TorchNeuron is present; raise RuntimeError if torch_xla is missing. cpu No device path.

TRNSCI_XLA_DEPRECATION=1 makes the XLA path emit one DeprecationWarning. It is off by default.

docs.title: Editable installs and the NKI kernel cache
docs.text:
TorchNeuron enables the NKI trace cache by default (NKI_ENABLE_TRACE_CACHE=1). The cache only versions source that belongs to an installed wheel (a site-packages tree with .dist-info), so an editable install can get a stale kernel after you edit dispatch.py. When developing with pip install -e, turn it off before starting Python:

export NKI_ENABLE_TRACE_CACHE=0

See the TorchNeuron environment variables reference.

docs.title: Deep Learning AMI (XLA lineage)
docs.text:
On a Trainium/Inferentia instance, install into the AMI's pre-built Neuron venv (which already contains neuronxcc, since it's not on public PyPI):

source /opt/aws_neuronx_venv_pytorch_2_9/bin/activate
pip install trnsolver[dev]

The trnsolver[neuron] extra is only useful when building a custom Neuron environment from scratch.

docs.title: Development install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/trnsci/trnsolver.git
cd trnsolver
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest tests/ -v

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python >= 3.10
  • PyTorch >= 2.1
  • NumPy >= 1.24
  • neuronxcc >= 2.15 (optional, for Trainium hardware)
  • torch-neuronx >= 2.1 (optional, for Trainium hardware)

docs.title: Hardware compatibility
docs.text:
The NKI Jacobi rotation kernel is scaffolded but not yet validated on hardware — trnsolver.eigh falls back to torch.linalg.eigh whenever the NKI path isn't selected. CPU/PyTorch correctness is preserved across all platforms.

For a pre-built CI instance, see AWS Setup and the Terraform module in infra/terraform/.

docs.title: Symmetric eigendecomposition
docs.text:
import torch
import trnsolver

A = torch.randn(64, 64)
A = A @ A.T  # symmetric

eigenvalues, eigenvectors = trnsolver.eigh(A)

# Reconstruction check
recon = eigenvectors @ torch.diag(eigenvalues) @ eigenvectors.T
assert torch.allclose(A, recon, atol=1e-5)

docs.title: Generalized eigenproblem
docs.text:
The SCF problem FC = SCε is a generalized symmetric eigenvalue problem. eigh_generalized reduces it to standard form via Cholesky of the overlap matrix S:

F = build_fock_matrix(...)  # symmetric
S = build_overlap_matrix(...)  # SPD

eigenvalues, eigenvectors = trnsolver.eigh_generalized(F, S)

docs.title: Factorizations
docs.text:
L = trnsolver.cholesky(A_spd)  # A = LL^T
P, L, U = trnsolver.lu(A)  # PA = LU
Q, R = trnsolver.qr(A)  # A = QR

docs.title: Direct solvers
docs.text:
x = trnsolver.solve(A, b)  # LU-based
x = trnsolver.solve_spd(A, b)  # Cholesky — faster for SPD A
A_inv_sqrt = trnsolver.inv_sqrt_spd(A)  # density-fitting metric inverse

docs.title: Iterative solvers
docs.text:
x, iters, residual = trnsolver.cg(A_spd, b, tol=1e-8)
x, iters, residual = trnsolver.gmres(A, b, tol=1e-6)

docs.title: Backend selection
docs.text:
trnsolver.set_backend("auto")  # NKI if available, else PyTorch (default)
trnsolver.set_backend("pytorch")  # force PyTorch fallback
trnsolver.set_backend("nki")  # require NKI; raises if unavailable

Run the SCF demo end-to-end:

python examples/scf_eigen.py --demo

docs.title: eigh(A, tol=1e-10, *, method=None)
docs.text:
Symmetric eigendecomposition A = V Λ Vᵀ for real symmetric A. Returns (eigenvalues, eigenvectors) with eigenvalues in ascending order.

method=None reads TRNSOLVER_EIGH_METHOD (default auto).

  • auto: on the native neuron device, n < TRNSOLVER_EIGH_NKI_MIN_N (default 512) uses torch.linalg.eigh; otherwise the NKI path (Householder tridiagonalization, host QR iteration). Off-device, torch.linalg.eigh.
  • jacobi (#48): batched Jacobi for (n, n) or (..., n, n) input. On the native neuron device (FP32, n ≤ 128) it runs the SBUF-resident one-sided Jacobi kernel: one launch per sweep, each holding up to 128 tiles of 128 / n matrices (512 at n = 32) in SBUF. Elsewhere it runs a torch implementation (two-sided Jacobi as batched matmuls). Uses the lower triangle, like torch.linalg.eigh. For 33 ≤ n ≤ 128 the kernel is block Jacobi: per step the Tensor Engine forms each matrix's Gram matrix and applies one orthogonal matmul per block pair, and the Vector Engine only rotates the 16 × 16 pair Gram blocks.
  • Multi-core (opt-in): TRNSOLVER_EIGH_CORES=<k>|auto splits a Jacobi batch over logical NeuronCores, one host thread per core (#48). With TRNSOLVER_EIGH_POOL=proc as well, a host batch goes to persistent worker processes instead, one per core (TRNSOLVER_EIGH_POOL_CORES, else NEURON_RT_VISIBLE_CORES), through shared memory (#29). The pool is the faster split (Trn2, n = 128, B = 4096, 8 host CPUs: 324 ms on 4 cores against 531 ms with threads and 655 ms for 8-thread batch-parallel LAPACK), but a NeuronCore belongs to one process: the calling process must not use those cores itself, so device-resident input keeps the thread split. Workers start on the first call (about 10 s, plus any kernel compile) and stay up; call trnsolver.nki.eigh_pool.shutdown() to free the cores. Scripts that use the pool need an if __name__ == "__main__": guard (the workers are spawned). TRNSOLVER_JACOBI_SWEEPS_PER_LAUNCH=<k> runs the scalar kernel's (n ≤ 32) first sweeps k per launch: 5–14% faster on one core (Trn2).
  • auto also runs the Jacobi kernel for FP32 batches on the native neuron device inside a measured region (n ≤ 32 with B ≥ 512, 33 ≤ n ≤ 64 with B ≥ 256, 65 ≤ n ≤ 128 with B ≥ 1024, plus B ≥ 256 for n ≥ 96 and B ≥ 64 at n = 128), where it beats the aten cutover. TRNSOLVER_EIGH_JACOBI_AUTO overrides the region.
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = trnsolver.eigh(A)
w, V = trnsolver.eigh(A_batch.to("neuron"), method="jacobi")  # (B, n), (B, n, n)

docs.title: eigh_generalized(A, B)
docs.text:
Generalized symmetric eigenproblem A x = λ B x with B SPD — the form that arises in the SCF iteration as F C = S C ε.

Reduces to standard form via Cholesky of B:

  1. B = L Lᵀ
  2. A' = L⁻¹ A L⁻ᵀ
  3. eigh(A') → (Λ, V')
  4. Back-transform V = L⁻ᵀ V'
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = trnsolver.eigh_generalized(F, S)

docs.title: Backend notes
docs.text: Householder tridiagonalization is n − 2 dependent BLAS-2 steps and leaves the Tensor Engine idle (#48). A parallel-ordered Jacobi step rotates n/2 disjoint pairs at once, so a batch of matrices advances in lockstep with no long dependency chain. In the kernel the Tensor Engine applies the step's partner permutation (an exact matmul shared by every tile) and the Vector Engine applies the rotations. For measurements against batched CPU LAPACK see #48.

docs.title: cholesky(A, upper=False)
docs.text:
A = L Lᵀ (or Uᵀ U with upper=True) for SPD A. Returns L (or U).

L = trnsolver.cholesky(A_spd)

docs.title: lu(A)
docs.text: Pivoted LU decomposition. Returns (P, L, U) with P A = L U.

docs.title: qr(A)
docs.text: A = Q R with Q orthogonal and R upper-triangular.

docs.title: solve(A, B)
docs.text: Solves A X = B via LU.

docs.title: solve_spd(A, B)
docs.text: Solves A X = B via Cholesky — faster than solve when A is SPD.

docs.title: inv_spd(A)
docs.text: Returns A⁻¹ for SPD A via Cholesky.

docs.title: inv_sqrt_spd(A)
docs.text:
Returns A⁻¹ᐟ² for SPD A via eigendecomposition: A⁻¹ᐟ² = V Λ⁻¹ᐟ² Vᵀ. Robust default for general SPD, including ill-conditioned metrics.

M = trnsolver.inv_sqrt_spd(metric)

docs.title: inv_sqrt_spd_ns(A, *, max_iters=20, tol=1e-7)
docs.text:
Returns (X, iters, residual) where X ≈ A⁻¹ᐟ², computed via the coupled Newton-Schulz iteration T = ½(3I − ZY); Y ← YT; Z ← TZ starting from a Frobenius-norm-scaled Y₀. All operations are GEMMs, which maps cleanly to the Trainium Tensor Engine via trnblas.gemm once that backend validates.

Choose this over inv_sqrt_spd when the NKI backend is active and A is well-conditioned (condition number ≲ 10⁶). For ill-conditioned SPD, stick with the eigendecomposition path.

M, iters, res = trnsolver.inv_sqrt_spd_ns(metric, tol=1e-8)

docs.title: Iterative Solvers
docs.text: Both solvers operate on the host (PyTorch). The matvec / inner-product hot path would benefit from NKI Level 1/2 kernels in trnblas, but the iteration loop itself stays on CPU.

docs.title: cg(A, b, x0=None, tol=1e-6, maxiter=1000, M=None)
docs.text:
Conjugate Gradient for SPD A. A may be a tensor or a callable A(x) → A @ x.

  • x0 — initial guess; defaults to zeros
  • tol — relative residual tolerance
  • maxiter — iteration cap
  • M — optional preconditioner (tensor or callable applying M⁻¹)

Returns (x, iters, residual).

x, iters, residual = trnsolver.cg(A_spd, b, tol=1e-8)

docs.title: gmres(A, b, x0=None, tol=1e-6, maxiter=200, restart=30)
docs.text:
GMRES for general (non-symmetric) systems. Same calling convention as cg. restart controls the Krylov subspace size before restart.

x, iters, residual = trnsolver.gmres(A, b, tol=1e-6)

docs.title: jacobi_preconditioner(A)
docs.text:
Build a diagonal (Jacobi) preconditioner callable M(r) = r / diag(A) for use as the M= argument of cg. Cheap and effective when A is diagonally dominant or has widely varying diagonal scales.

M = trnsolver.jacobi_preconditioner(A)
x, iters, res = trnsolver.cg(A, b, M=M, tol=1e-8)

Raises ValueError if any diagonal entry is within 1e-15 of zero. More-capable preconditioners (IC0, SSOR, block-Jacobi) are tracked in #16.

docs.title: NKI Backend
docs.text: Backend selection mirrors the sister trnblas and trnfft packages.

docs.title: set_backend(backend)
docs.text:
trnsolver.set_backend("auto")  # NKI if available, else PyTorch (default)
trnsolver.set_backend("pytorch")  # force PyTorch fallback
trnsolver.set_backend("nki")  # require NKI; raises if unavailable

docs.title: get_backend()
docs.text: Returns the current backend string.

docs.title: HAS_NKI
docs.text: Module-level boolean — True iff the nki package (NKI 0.3.0 Stable, Neuron SDK 2.29+) imported successfully.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Effect TRNSOLVER_REQUIRE_NKI=1 Kernel-path failures re-raise instead of silently falling back to PyTorch. Used by the validation suite to catch silent kernel breakage. TRNSOLVER_EIGH_NKI_MIN_N=<n> On the native neuron device, eigh uses torch.linalg.eigh for matrices with fewer than n rows and the NKI path otherwise. Default 512; 0 always uses NKI. Ignored when TRNSOLVER_REQUIRE_NKI=1. (#42) TRNSOLVER_EIGH_METHOD=auto\|jacobi eigh method when method= is not passed. jacobi selects the batched Jacobi solver (#48). Default auto. TRNSOLVER_JACOBI_GROUP=<g> Jacobi kernel: tiles per launch (rounded down to a power of two). Default 128 (n ≤ 32: scalar kernel; 33 ≤ n ≤ 128: block kernel), split across the two physical cores of a logical NeuronCore. TRNSOLVER_JACOBI_CHAINS=<c> Jacobi kernel: independent dependency chains per step. Default 8 for n ≤ 32, 2 for the block kernel. TRNSOLVER_JACOBI_BLOCK=0 Run the scalar Jacobi kernel for 33 ≤ n ≤ 128 instead of the block kernel (#48). TRNSOLVER_EIGH_JACOBI_AUTO=off\|<rows> Region where method="auto" runs the Jacobi kernel (FP32 batches on neuron). off, or rows n_min-n_max:B_min, e.g. 1-32:512,33-64:256. Default: the measured table in eigen._JACOBI_AUTO_REGION. TRNSCI_NKI_DISPATCH=auto\|native\|xla\|cpu Suite-wide. Forces the native or XLA dispatch path; auto (default) detects. Forcing an unavailable path raises. TRNSCI_XLA_DEPRECATION=1 The XLA path emits one DeprecationWarning. Off by default. NKI_ENABLE_TRACE_CACHE=0 TorchNeuron (not trnsolver) setting. Turns off the cross-process NKI kernel cache, which cannot version editable installs. TRNSOLVER_USE_SIMULATOR=1 Route kernel dispatch through nki.simulate(kernel)(numpy_args) on CPU instead of torch_xla. No hardware needed. See Developing kernels.

docs.title: Dispatch path
docs.text:
On Neuron hardware, kernels run on one of two torch-neuronx lineages, detected on the first kernel launch:

  • Native (TorchNeuron, Trn2/Trn3): each kernel is a PyTorch custom op on device="neuron", also callable directly and inside torch.compile(backend="neuron"): torch.ops.trnsolver.matvec, rank2_update, matmul, matmul_fp32out, apply_reflectors, jacobi_sweeps, jacobi_block. The ops are registered only once this path is selected.
  • XLA (Trn1): kernels run on the torch_xla device, as before.

set_backend is unaffected: it still chooses NKI vs PyTorch. See Installation.

docs.title: Jacobi rotation kernel
docs.text:
trnsolver.nki.dispatch.rotate_pairs_kernel is the primary NKI acceleration target. Each sweep round:

  • Loads the n/2 pairs of rows (even / odd at strided positions 2i, 2i+1) and rotates them by per-row (c, -s; s, c)
  • The host driver calls the kernel three times per round (D rows, D cols, V cols) under a Brent-Luk permutation
  • Compile graph is stable per (half, n, dtype) — NKI caches after the first invocation

See Architecture and #9 for the design rationale.

docs.title: trnsparse
docs.text:
Sparse matrix operations for AWS Trainium via NKI.

A cuSPARSE-equivalent for Trainium: CSR/COO formats, SpMV, SpMM, and integral screening for sparse scientific computing.

Primary use case: Schwarz-screened Fock builds for large-basis quantum chemistry. At >3000 basis functions, >99% of shell quartets screen to zero. Storing and operating on the integral tensor in dense format wastes both memory and compute. trnsparse makes the sparsity explicit.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install trnsparse
pip install trnsparse[neuron]   # on Neuron hardware

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
import torch
import trnsparse

dense = torch.randn(1024, 1024)
dense[dense.abs() < 0.5] = 0.0

A = trnsparse.CSRMatrix.from_dense(dense)
x = torch.randn(1024)
y = trnsparse.spmv(A, x)

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Alpha. CSR/COO formats, SpMV/SpMM, and Schwarz screening are functional via PyTorch fallback. NKI gather-matmul-scatter SpMM kernel is scaffolded; on-hardware validation is the next milestone.

Part of the trnsci scientific computing suite.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
• CSRMatrix(indptr, indices, data, shape) — compressed sparse row
  • .from_dense(dense, threshold=0) — construct by thresholding a dense tensor
  • .to_dense() — materialize back to a dense torch.Tensor
  • .transpose() — transpose to CSR (via CSC)
  • .nnz, .shape, .dtype, .device
  • COOMatrix(rows, cols, vals, shape) — coordinate format
  • .to_csr() / CSRMatrix.to_coo() — roundtrip conversions

docs.title: Ops
docs.text:
• spmv(A, x) — sparse matrix × dense vector
  • spmv_symmetric(A, x) — for symmetric A; skips duplicate work
  • spmm(A, B) — sparse matrix × dense matrix (gather-matmul-scatter on NKI)
  • sparse_add(A, B, alpha=1.0, beta=1.0) — α A + β B
  • sparse_scale(A, s) — scalar multiply
  • transpose(A) — transpose of CSR / COO

docs.title: Screening
docs.text:
• schwarz_bounds(shell_pair_integrals) — Cauchy-Schwarz bounds $Q_{pq} = \sqrt{(pq|pq)}$
  • screen_quartets(Q, threshold) — keep only quartets with $Q_{pq}Q_{rs} > \text{threshold}$
  • density_screen(Q, P, threshold) — density-weighted screening
  • sparsity_stats(mask) — density, nnz, per-row nnz distribution

docs.title: Dispatch
docs.text:
• set_backend("auto" | "pytorch" | "nki") — select compute backend
  • get_backend() — current backend
  • HAS_NKI — module-level flag set at import time

On Neuron hardware the NKI backend runs on one of two torch-neuronx lineages, detected on the first kernel launch (force with TRNSCI_NKI_DISPATCH=native|xla|cpu):

  • Native (TorchNeuron, Trn2/Trn3) — each kernel is a custom op on device="neuron": torch.ops.trnsparse.spmm_dense, bsr_spmm, screened_spmm, attn_stats, attn_out, attn_bwd_dq, attn_bwd_dkdv, and the composite bsr_attn / bsr_attn_bwd. Backwards are attached with torch.library.register_autograd; spmm also traces under torch.compile(backend="neuron", fullgraph=True). The ops are registered only once this path is selected.
  • XLA (Trn1) — kernels run on the torch_xla device, as before.

Placement on the native path: sparse structure (CSR row_ptrs / col_indices / values, BSR block_row_ptrs / block_col_indices) stays on the host; dense operands and BSR blocks may be on neuron; results are on the dense operand's device. See Installation.

docs.title: Multi-core (trnsparse.multicore, native path)
docs.text:
A Trn2 chip at LNC=2 has four logical NeuronCores, which TorchNeuron exposes as neuron:0 … neuron:3 (NEURON_RT_VISIBLE_CORES=0-3). Each static kernel already splits its work across the two physical cores of one logical core; these classes split it across logical cores.

  • logical_cores(n=None): the visible logical cores as devices.
  • partition_block_rows(row_ptrs, n_parts): block rows split into groups balanced by stored blocks (the same greedy as the in-kernel split).
  • ShardedBSR(A, devices=None, pretransposed=True): A split by block rows, with each core's blocks resident on that core.
  • .replicate(B) copies B to every core.
  • .spmm(B_replicas) returns one output per core, issuing one kernel launch per core without waiting.
  • .gather(outs) assembles C on the host.
  • pretransposed=True runs the pre-transposed kernel (no in-kernel transpose, fewer DMAs, and B tiles shared by groups of up to 8 block rows). Gradients reach each core's B replica and block copy.
  • ShardedAttention(mask, devices=None): a single-head block-sparse attention forward, split by query block rows. Use .shard_rows(Q), .replicate_kv(K, V), .forward(Qts, KVs) and .gather(outs). It is forward only. For several heads, put whole heads on different cores and call block_sparse_attention_tiled there; that path has autograd.

TorchNeuron does not copy tensors between logical cores. A neuron:0 tensor's .to("neuron:1") comes back still on core 0, and copy_ across cores raises. So per-core operands are built on the host and copied once, and results return through the host. The kernel ops run on the logical core of their operands, and operands on two different cores are an error.

docs.title: Why BSR is Trainium-native
docs.text:
Trainium's Tensor Engine is a 128×128 systolic array. nisa.nc_matmul moves a 128-partition stationary tile against a moving operand of up to 128 × 512, all on-chip. The natural "unit of sparse work" on this architecture is therefore not a single nonzero — it's a 128×128 block.

BSR (block-sparse row) at block_size=128 stores a matrix as a list of these blocks plus a block-level CSR pattern. Every stored block is already in the shape the systolic array wants: one nc_matmul per block, no gather step, no padding-within-tile waste. The architectural match is exact.

Contrast with CSR, which stores individual nonzero elements. The v0.2.0 NKI path for CSR materializes the matrix into a dense (M, K) tile before the matmul (see the SpMM path below) — necessary for correctness, but it pays the full M × K cost whether the matrix is sparse or not. BSR skips this because blocks are already dense.

Consequence for the library's shape: CSR remains the construction and interop format (scipy compatibility, PyTorch's torch.sparse_csr_tensor interop). BSR is the compute format for the NKI path. For matrices with real block structure — Fock/ERI tensors after Schwarz screening, FEM stiffness matrices, graph adjacencies, block-sparse attention masks — BSR is strictly preferred. For truly unstructured sparse (random CSR), the PyTorch fallback is already within 2× of scipy; NKI adds nothing.

See Benchmarks for numbers that validate this framing.

trnsparse/
├── trnsparse/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── formats.py       # CSRMatrix, COOMatrix, BSRMatrix, from_dense
│   ├── ops.py           # spmv, spmm, bsr_spmm, screened_spmm, ...
│   ├── screening.py     # schwarz_bounds, screen_quartets, density_screen
│   ├── iterative.py     # cg_bsr, power_iteration_bsr, jacobi_preconditioner_bsr
│   └── nki/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── kernels.py   # _bsr_spmm_kernel, _screened_spmm_kernel
│       └── dispatch.py  # torch.autograd.Function wrappers + routing
├── tests/
├── examples/
│   ├── sparse_fock.py             # Schwarz-screened Fock (3 paths + trnblas)
│   ├── pyscf_bridge.py            # Real AO integrals via PySCF
│   └── block_sparse_attention.py  # Block-sparse attention via bsr_spmm

docs.title: NKI dispatch hierarchy
docs.text: CSR and COO are interop and PyTorch-fallback formats. BSR is the NKI compute format. nki/dispatch.py exposes HAS_NKI, set_backend("auto"|"pytorch"|"nki"), get_backend(), and the NKI entry points.

docs.title: spmm(csr, B) — PyTorch fallback
docs.text: Routes through torch.sparse_csr_tensor operations. Benchmarked within 2× of scipy at typical shapes; the NKI per-op overhead doesn't pay off for CSR SpMM until the matrix is large enough that the v0.2.0 CSR kernel (densify-then-GEMM) would dominate anyway. SpMV also stays on this path.

docs.title: bsr_spmm(bsr, B) — NKI, _bsr_spmm_kernel
docs.text: One nisa.nc_matmul per nonzero block. Host-side preamble pads each block-row to the same K_max so the kernel's affine_range bounds are fixed. torch.autograd.Function-wrapped (_BSRSpMMFunction); gradcheck passes at atol=1e-4 on hardware.

docs.title: screened_spmm(A, diag, B, threshold) — NKI, fused
docs.text: Fuses Schwarz bound (outer-product pair bound), threshold mask, and matmul into one dispatch. Saves ~30–50% vs the unfused schwarz_bounds → screen_quartets → from_dense → spmm flow on Fock-build-sized inputs.

docs.title: Block-sparse attention
docs.text: bsr_spmm applied to the post-softmax attention weight matrix. No new kernel — a BSRMatrix with a local-window or dilated block pattern IS an attention mask. See sparse_attention.md.

docs.title: Static structure on the native path (Trn2/Trn3)
docs.text:
TorchNeuron has no device sparse CSR, so the structure stays on the host (#30). The native path turns that into an advantage: bsr_spmm and block-sparse attention pass block_row_ptrs / block_col_indices to the kernel as compile-time constants (trnsparse::bsr_spmm_static, attn_fwd_static, attn_bwd_static). The trace unrolls exactly the stored blocks with static DMA addresses: no (M_tiles, K_max) padding (one dense global-token row no longer makes every row cost K_max blocks), no gathered copies of B / K / V, and the attention softmax statistics stay on chip. The cost is one compile per distinct structure (seconds), which a reused pattern amortizes. TRNSPARSE_STATIC_STRUCTURE=0 restores the gather path. Measured crossovers against dense aten: docs/benchmarks.md.

Under LNC=2 (the Trn2 default) NKI traces each kernel once per physical core, with program_id 0 and 1 as Python ints. The static kernels split their output tiles between the two traces, balanced by stored blocks:

  • SpMM: block rows and 512-column tiles.
  • Attention forward: block rows.
  • Attention backward: one pool of dQ block rows and dK/dV block columns.

Each output tile has exactly one writer. TRNSPARSE_CORE_SPLIT=0 turns the split off, for A/B measurements.

The static kernels take fp32 or bf16 operands. When every operand is bf16, the matmuls run in bf16 and accumulate in fp32 PSUM. Scores, softmax statistics and score-space arithmetic stay fp32; only P and dS are rounded to bf16 for their matmuls. Outputs come back in bf16, and the attention statistics (row_max, row_denom) are always fp32. Mixed fp32/bf16 operands run in fp32.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
• CSR: row pointer + column indices + values. Preferred for construction, interop with scipy/PyTorch, and SpMV.
  • COO: three parallel 1-D tensors. Preferred for construction and permutation.
  • BSR (block_size=128): stacked 128×128 blocks + block-level CSR pattern. Every block maps to one nc_matmul; zero gather overhead.

All three support from_dense, to_dense, and interconversion.

docs.title: Autograd wrapping
docs.text: Every NKI kernel lives inside a torch.autograd.Function (satisfies trnsci/trnsci#3). Backward passes run at the PyTorch level via block-gradient projection. Block-selection is non-differentiable by construction; grad_out is routed into exactly the stored blocks. gradcheck at atol=1e-4 is part of the hardware test matrix for all three NKI kernels.

docs.title: Fused screened SpMM (v0.4.0)
docs.text:
screened_spmm(A, diag_integrals, B, threshold) fuses the chemistry-screened SpMM pipeline — Schwarz bound from the diagonal integrals, pair-bound threshold mask, masked matmul — into a single NKI kernel. The unfused equivalent does four host passes (sqrt, outer product, threshold, mask-apply) plus a separate from_dense + spmm call; the fused kernel collapses all of that into one dispatch.

Mask semantics: mask[i,j] = sqrt(|diag[i]|) * sqrt(|diag[j]|) > sqrt(threshold), matching schwarz_bounds + screen_quartets composed. No gradient flows back to diag_integrals or threshold — the mask is treated as a discrete gate; grad_A *= mask and grad_B = (A * mask).T @ grad_C.

Restricted to square A (M == K) with 1-D diag_integrals in v0.4.0 — the common Fock-build case. Rectangular / asymmetric-bounds extension is a follow-up if asked for.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Row-bucketing CSR (#15) — parked. Requires NKI indirect-DMA gather (not exposed as of NKI 0.3.0). The CSR PyTorch fallback is within 2× of scipy; that's the current story.
  • Fused tile-level attention scores (#25) — v0.4.4 ships the NKI kernel pair (_attn_stats_kernel + _attn_out_kernel). block_sparse_attention_tiled routes through NKI on the nki backend; the PyTorch two-pass reference remains on the pytorch backend. head_dim ≤ 128 in v0.4.4 (nc_matmul partition limit); head_dim=256 requires K-tiling.
  • Fused iterative solvers (#22) — CG blocked on nl.affine_range iteration-carried scalar state. v0.4.3 ships chebyshev_bsr and richardson_bsr: fixed-K solvers with pre-computed coefficients (no inner products in the loop) that have the correct structure for eventual NKI fusion. The "A SBUF-resident across all iterations" win remains gated on affine_range vector-carry support.
  • Multi-chip sharded BSR (#16) — gated on suite-level multi-chip collectives.
  • SpMV stays PyTorch. Single output column on the Tensor Engine doesn't amortize compile + dispatch overhead.

docs.title: AWS Setup for Neuron Tests
docs.text:
To run pytest -m neuron against real Trainium hardware, we use a local workflow:

  • Provision a Trainium EC2 instance with Terraform (stays stopped when not testing)
  • Run the test script locally from your machine, using AWS_PROFILE=aws
  • The script starts the instance, runs pytest via SSM, prints output, stops the instance

GitHub Actions does not touch AWS. All AWS interaction is human-initiated.

docs.title: 1. Provision the CI instance
docs.text:
Pick a VPC + subnet in a region with trn1/trn2/inf2 capacity. trn1.2xlarge is cheapest for basic validation.

cd infra/terraform

AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform init
AWS_PROFILE=aws terraform apply \
  -var="vpc_id=vpc-xxxxxx" \
  -var="subnet_id=subnet-xxxxxx" \
  -var="instance_type=trn1.2xlarge"

Capture instance_id from the outputs. User-data takes ~5 minutes to install the Neuron SDK and clone trnsparse.

Stop the instance once ready:

AWS_PROFILE=aws aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids $(terraform output -raw instance_id)

docs.title: Running neuron tests
docs.text:
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_neuron_tests.sh
# or for trn2 / inf2:
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_neuron_tests.sh trn2

The script will:

  1. Look up the tagged instance (Name=trnsparse-ci-trn1 by default)
  2. Start it if stopped; wait for SSM agent
  3. Send the pytest command over SSM
  4. Print stdout/stderr
  5. Stop the instance in a trap (even if pytest fails or you Ctrl-C)

It exits non-zero if any test fails.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Stopped = EBS only (~$10/mo for 100 GB gp3). Running:

Type Hourly Typical run (10 min) trn1.2xlarge $1.34 $0.22 trn2.8xlarge $10.00 $1.67 inf2.xlarge $0.76 $0.13

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"No instance found with Name=trnsparse-ci-trn1" — Run terraform apply first, or check that the tag matches.

SSM InvalidInstanceId error — Instance hasn't finished booting/registering. Wait 1-2 minutes and retry.

User-data didn't finish (neuronxcc not found) — SSH in via SSM session and re-run manually: 

aws ssm start-session --target $INSTANCE_ID
cd /home/ubuntu/trnsparse && pip install -e '.[neuron,dev]'

InsufficientInstanceCapacity when starting the instance — AWS may temporarily be out of Trainium in that AZ. Wait and retry, or re-provision in a different AZ.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Performance results for trnsparse.spmm across four backends on the same numeric inputs:

  • scipy — scipy.sparse.csr_matrix @ B (compiled C reference)
  • torch.sparse — torch.sparse_csr_tensor @ B
  • trnsparse (pytorch) — v0.1.3 vectorized fallback that lowers to torch.sparse
  • trnsparse (nki) — v0.2.0 NKI dispatch: materialize CSR dense, run tiled GEMM on the Tensor Engine via @nki.jit, return dense

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
• Instance: trn1.2xlarge (single NeuronCore v2)
  • AMI: Deep Learning AMI Neuron PyTorch 2.9 · Ubuntu 24.04
  • Neuron SDK: 2.24 · neuronxcc 2.24

docs.title: What to read into this
docs.text:
v0.2.0 ships NKI for correctness, not speed. At every data point the NKI path is slower than both CPU backends. Two reasons, both structural:

  1. No sparsity exploitation yet. v0.2.0's NKI kernel materializes the CSR into a dense (M, K) tile before the matmul. At density 0.001 on a 1024 × 1024 matrix, this means 1000× more work than scipy does. Real sparse speedups come from row-bucketing + gather-matmul-scatter, which lands in v0.3.0 (#15).
  2. Kernel-launch overhead dominates. The NKI times are roughly constant at ~1.3-2.5 ms across densities — the NEFF dispatch + HBM round-trip amortizes over large workloads, not these small ones. trn2 (v0.2.x Phase 5, #17) and NEFF-cache reuse (part of Phase 3) close this gap for steady-state workloads.

What v0.2.0 does deliver:

  • set_backend("nki") now actually runs SpMM on the Tensor Engine.
  • Forward + backward (via torch.autograd.Function) both validated on hardware; torch.autograd.gradcheck passes at atol=1e-4.
  • The full Neuron toolchain — compile, NEFF cache, XLA dispatch, PyTorch integration — is exercised end-to-end, which is what Phase 1 is for.

docs.title: Reproducing
docs.text:
# CPU only (scipy + torch.sparse + trnsparse pytorch)
pytest benchmarks/bench_spmm.py --benchmark-only

# On trn1, add NKI column:
AWS_PROFILE=aws ./scripts/run_benchmarks.sh trn1

Results above were generated at commit cee2e34 on trn1.2xlarge.

docs.title: Results (BSR SpMM, v0.3.0)
docs.text:
BSRMatrix stores a matrix as stacked (block_size, block_size) dense blocks plus a block-level CSR pattern. At block_size=128 each nonzero block is exactly a Tensor-Engine tile — no gather overhead.

Sizes are (m_blocks × 128, n_blocks × 128). block_density is the fraction of (m_blocks, n_blocks) blocks actually stored. Lower is better; dense is torch.matmul(A_dense, B) on the trn1.2xlarge CPU as a ceiling.

m_blocks n_blocks block_density N bsr PyTorch (ms) bsr NKI (ms) dense CPU (ms) 4 4 0.10 128 0.11 1.85 0.12 4 4 0.25 128 0.18 1.87 0.12 4 4 0.50 128 0.43 2.05 0.13 4 8 0.50 256 1.01 3.00 0.49 8 4 0.50 256 1.05 3.11 0.47

docs.title: Reading the BSR table
docs.text:
Three observations, all consistent with the architectural framing:

  1. bsr PyTorch scales linearly with block density (0.11 → 0.43 ms as density goes 0.10 → 0.50, ~4× more work done). It's the straightforward "iterate stored blocks, do A_block @ B_slice" reference. This is what the NKI path has to beat.
  2. bsr NKI is roughly constant at 1.8-3.1 ms across configurations. Kernel dispatch + compilation + HBM round-trips dominate at these small sizes, not the matmul work itself. This mirrors the v0.2.0 CSR finding — Trainium rewards amortizing the kernel launch.
  3. Dense CPU is the ceiling to beat — scipy / torch.sparse / BSR PyTorch are all within 2-4× of it on the trn1.2xlarge's Xeon. NKI needs workloads where the matmul work is large enough to swamp dispatch, or where the kernel launch can be amortized across many operations.

docs.title: Where NKI wins — shipped v0.4.x
docs.text:
Not in raw "one-shot SpMM at N=128 vs CPU." The BSR table above measures kernel dispatch overhead. The architectural wins come from fusing multiple host passes into one dispatch:

  • screened_spmm (v0.4.0, #19) ✅ shipped: fuses Schwarz bound + threshold + mask + matmul into one NKI dispatch. On Fock-build-sized inputs: ~30–50% faster than the unfused 4-step path (schwarz_bounds → screen_quartets → from_dense → spmm) because it eliminates 3 HBM round-trips and the host-side CSR build.
  • Block-sparse attention (v0.4.2, #21) ✅ shipped: bsr_spmm handles attn_weights @ V for local-window / dilated / global-token masks. At seq_len=8192, window=2: 4.9% block density means 95% of nc_matmul calls are skipped. Current example still materializes the full score matrix (follow-up: #25).
  • #22 — on-chip iterative solvers: CG/power-iteration with A SBUF-resident across all iterations (replaces #20). v0.3.2 ships the Python-loop plumbing; fused kernel gated on NKI scalar-carry capability.

See docs/architecture.md for why BSR is the Trainium-native format.

BSR results from commit 411a3a7.

docs.title: Trn2 native path (TorchNeuron), static-structure kernels
docs.text:
Setup. trn2.3xlarge (LNC=2; one logical NeuronCore, NEURON_RT_VISIBLE_CORES=3), Neuron SDK 2.33 venv: torch 2.14.0, torch-neuronx 2.14.3, nki 0.7.0, neuronx-cc 2.28. fp32 throughout. Structure on the host, dense data (blocks, operands) already on device="neuron". Warm median of 10–30 calls with torch.neuron.synchronize() after each; the first call (compile) is excluded. CPU columns: same box, 2 threads (taskset -c 8,9, OMP_NUM_THREADS=2). The box ran other jobs on other NeuronCores, so sub-millisecond numbers carry ~±0.1 ms noise. "main" = 1fafcaf (gather path); "PR" = static-structure kernels. Script: benchmarks/bench_native_trn2.py.

Crossover vs dense aten matmul on the device (BSR 128×128, linear interpolation between measured densities):

n width 128 width 512 1024 never (0.3 ms launch floor vs 0.14 ms dense) never 4096 ~2% ~16% 8192 ~14% ~34%

docs.title: Reading the Trn2 tables
docs.text:
• BSR SpMM pays off at scale and moderate sparsity. At n = 8192 the static kernel beats dense aten up to ~14% block density (width 128) and ~34% (width 512); at 1% it is 2.7–6.8× faster. Its cost is linear in stored blocks (~1.9 µs per 128×128×512 block vs ~0.66 µs per block for dense aten), so the crossover moves up with n and with width. At n = 1024 nothing sparse wins: one launch costs ~0.3 ms and dense aten is 0.14 ms. Against CPU (dense or torch.sparse) the device wins everywhere above n = 1024.
  • The gather path was the bottleneck, not the Tensor Engine. On main, device-side pad + gather took 60% of every call and the K_max padding made each row cost as much as the densest row. With the structure as kernel constants both are gone: 3–6× faster end to end at 8192.
  • Attention forward never beats unmasked dense SDPA (a fused kernel at 0.77 ms for seq 8192), but it is what to compare against when the mask is real: masked SDPA costs 5.0–5.2 ms at 8192 and the static kernel 1.4–3.5 ms. Forward + backward beats unmasked dense SDPA at seq 8192 for local and global masks (3.5–4.2 ms vs 6.3–6.6 ms), not for 25% dilated (11 ms) and not at seq ≤ 4096.
  • Global-token masks were the pathological case for the gather path (K_max = all blocks): seq 8192 fwd+bwd went from 127–195 ms to ~4 ms.
  • Screened SpMM is 1.5–2× faster than on main but still 2–3× slower than dense aten (A * mask) @ B on the device: the fused kernel does not pay on Trn2 in fp32. It has no tile skipping, so it never benefits from screening sparsity.
  • CSR SpMM (host structure) is now 4–11× faster at ≤ 1% density (device scatter of nnz triplets instead of a full dense H2D copy), but stays far behind torch.sparse on CPU at low density and behind dense aten when A is already dense on the device. On Trainium, use BSR.

docs.title: Trn2: across the logical NeuronCores of one chip (#30)
docs.text:
Setup. - Hardware: trn2.3xlarge at LNC=2, all four logical NeuronCores visible to one process (NEURON_RT_VISIBLE_CORES=0-3), with the whole chip reserved for these runs. - Software: Neuron SDK 2.33 venv with torch 2.14.0, torch-neuronx 2.14.3, nki 0.7.0 and neuronx-cc 2.28. fp32 throughout. - Host: taskset -c 8,9, OMP_NUM_THREADS=2. - Script: benchmarks/bench_multicore_trn2.py. - Operands are built on the host and copied once to every core that uses them. The time covers issuing one launch per core from one Python thread and synchronizing every core used; host gathers are excluded. - Dense baselines are split too: "dense kc" is aten A @ B with A's rows split over k cores and B on each. SDPA "4c" splits the query rows (one head) or the heads (four heads) the same way. - "API 1c" is the public one-core bsr_spmm, the path from #36, now with keyed ops. "plain" is ShardedBSR(..., pretransposed=False), the #36 kernel. "pre-T" is the new pre-transposed, row-grouped kernel. - Rounds: BSR and single-head attention show the lower of two rounds' warm medians (15 calls each). The four-head runs are one round. Sub-millisecond cells carry about ±0.1–0.2 ms of noise. The crossovers interpolate linearly between the measured densities.

Crossover density vs dense aten (BSR 128×128):

n width API 1c vs dense 1c (#36 path) pre-T 1c vs dense 1c best of pre-T 1/2/4c vs dense 1c pre-T 4c vs dense 4c best sparse (any cores) vs best dense (any cores) 8192 128 ~33% ~82% ~96% ~20% ~62% 8192 512 ~65% >100% >100% ~69% ~69% 16384 128 ~69% ~97% >100% ~74% ~77% 16384 512 ~69% ~98% >100% ~50% ~50%

Block-sparse attention, four heads, whole heads per core (fp32, ms)
One process per core (BSR, n = 8192, width 512, pre-T, ms)
docs.text:
benchmarks/bench_multiproc_trn2.py: each process owns one core and its share of the block rows, and all processes are pinned to the same two host CPUs.

processes barrier dense (rows split) 1% 5% 10% 25% 50% 1 0.02 2.31 0.28 0.32 0.41 0.70 1.20 2 0.05 1.54 0.44 0.39 0.36 0.69 0.89 4 0.11 1.66 0.84 1.02 0.78 1.10 1.12

docs.title: Reading the multi-core tables
docs.text:
• The per-block fix moved the crossover more than extra cores did.
  • On one core, the pre-transposed, row-grouped kernel is 1.1–2.2× faster than the #36 kernel at 25–50% density.
  • It beats dense aten on that same core up to ~82–98% block density, and still beats it at 100% for n = 8192, width 512. In #36 the crossover was ~26–49% on two physical cores.
  • Where the time goes: B-tile loads, shared across up to 8 block rows of a group, and the in-kernel transpose, now gone.
  • Four logical cores pay only for large work per call.
  • Speedup from one core to four (pre-T): 1.4–2.3× at n = 16384 and 25–100% density, 1.2–1.6× at n = 8192 and width 512 above 25%.
  • It is a slowdown (0.45–0.8×) below ~0.6 ms of single-core work.
  • Why the speedup stops there:
  • One Python thread issues the launches, at about 0.1 ms each (0.4–0.7 ms for four).
  • Concurrent kernels on different logical cores also slow each other. At n = 16384, width 512, 50% density, one shard takes 1.15–1.3 ms alone and 1.9–2.9 ms with all four running. Dense aten slabs barely contend (2.5 ms alone, 3.1 ms for four).
  • Two cores reach most of the four-core gain.
  • One process per core does not help with two host CPUs: four processes are no faster than one.
  • Against dense split the same way, the crossover drops. Dense aten scales better across cores (3.7× from one to four at n = 16384, width 512), so the four-core crossovers are ~50–74% at n = 16384 and ~69% at n = 8192, width 512. At n = 8192, width 128 both sides sit on the launch floor (0.5–0.7 ms), so splitting is pointless there.
  • Attention, one head:
  • The forward on one core now beats unmasked dense SDPA at seq 16384 for local and global masks: 0.85–1.6 ms vs 2.0–2.2 ms.
  • At seq 8192 it ties: 0.55–0.89 ms vs 0.72–0.77 ms.
  • Splitting query rows over cores pays only for the 25% dilated mask at seq 16384: 5.2–5.7 → 2.9–3.0 ms, but that is still slower than dense SDPA at 1.8–2.2 ms.
  • Masked SDPA (32–33 ms at 16384 on one core, 6.6–11 ms on four) loses to every sparse configuration.
  • Attention, four heads (fwd+bwd):
  • With whole heads per core, sparse beats dense SDPA split the same way at seq 16384 for local and global masks: 10.5–14 ms vs 26–28 ms.
  • At seq 8192 the margin is narrower: 7.6–9.6 vs 10.5–12.5 ms.
  • The 25% dilated mask loses at both lengths.
  • Core scaling is 1.1–2.1×, held back by about 10–20 host-issued aten ops per head on the public path.

docs.title: Trn2: fused SBUF-resident CG (cg_bsr_fused, #22)
docs.text:
trn2.3xlarge, Neuron SDK 2.33.0, native TorchNeuron, one logical NeuronCore (LNC=2: two physical cores) unless noted. Host threads pinned to 2 CPUs (taskset, OMP_NUM_THREADS=2) for every column, CPU baselines included. Wall time from the host call to the solution on the host, warm median of 3, tolerance 1e-5 on ||r|| / ||b||. Reproduce with benchmarks/bench_cg_fused_trn2.py --tiles T --density d.

Matrices: the synthetic block-screened overlap matrix of normalised s-type Gaussians on a synthetic molecular cluster, one 128-function fragment per block row, with blocks between distant fragments dropped to hit the block density and a level shift setting κ exactly. A is built in fp64. The device and the fp32 columns get its fp32 rounding. "true res" is ||b − A x|| / ||b|| with the fp64 A, and "err" is against an fp64 direct solve.

Columns: fused = cg_bsr_fused (one launch). host_bsr = CG over the keyed pre-transposed BSR SpMM op with device tensors, synced every 8 steps. cg_bsr = the shipped Python loop (one .item() per dot). dense_aten = CG with torch.mv on a dense fp32 A on the device, synced every 8 steps. scipy = scipy.sparse.linalg.cg on fp64 BSR. torch fp64/fp32 = the cg_bsr_fused host path (block bmm). "resident" = blocks held in SBUF (summed over the two physical cores); the rest stream from HBM inside the launch. "µs/iter" = (fused − fused with max_iter=0) / iterations.

docs.title: Plain CG (ms to tol 1e-5, warm median)
Block-Jacobi PCG (ms to tol 1e-5, warm median)
LNC=2 row split vs whole solve on one physical core (fused, plain CG, µs/iter)
Several right-hand sides (ms per right-hand side, warm median)
Reading the CG tables
docs.text:
• The win is removing the host from the iteration loop. The fused solve is 3.5–11x faster than the best 2-thread CPU solver at every size and density here. It is 5–58x faster than the same CG driven from the host over the already fast BSR SpMM op: that loop costs about 1–1.5 ms per iteration in launches and syncs, against 15–250 µs on the device.
  • A matvec costs about 0.5 µs per stored block per physical core, whether the block is resident or streamed. That is the TensorE load of a 128x128 fp32 stationary block for one moving column (a microbenchmark gives 497 ns per matmul at 1 column, 524 ns at 64, 985 ns at 512; bf16 is 100 ns). The DMA queues keep up streaming 64 KiB blocks from HBM at that rate (about 128 GB/s), so at n = 8192 with 1024 blocks, the 384 non-resident blocks did not cost extra time per block. SBUF residency stops fitting at 320 fp32 blocks per physical core (640 per logical core with the split), but past that point nothing falls off a cliff. Residency matters only when the per-block compute gets cheaper than the DMA (bf16, or many more moving columns).
  • The LNC=2 row split is 1.7–2.1x per iteration over running the whole solve on one physical core. LNC=1 matches the unsplit LNC=2 kernel.
  • Several right-hand sides are nearly free. R columns share each stationary load: 128 right-hand sides take 12.7 ms against 6.0 ms for one (n = 4096), i.e. 0.10 ms per solve. The best CPU per-solve time here is 2.6 ms (block bmm, R = 64), so that is about 26x.
  • Checking convergence on the device every 1–8 steps costs little. The device-side while test adds about 3 µs per check.
  • Precision is fp32. The recursive residual reaches tol. The true residual against the fp64 A lands at 0.5–2x tol for κ = 1e3, and the error against fp64 is 1e-6 to 1e-5. At κ = 1e5 the error grows to 1e-4 to 3e-4 (fp32 rounding of A times κ), where the fp64 CPU solvers do not have that floor. fp32 CG also takes about 5–25% more iterations than fp64 CG.

docs.title: Independent solves, one process per logical core (whole chip)
docs.text:
n = 4096, 256 blocks, plain CG, 40 solves per process, every process pinned to the same 2 host CPUs (driver script posted on #22). The rate is solves / the slowest process's solve-loop time.

logical cores solves/s scaling per solve (ms) 1 148 1.00x 6.8 2 333 2.25x 6.0 4 356 2.41x 11.2

For reference, the same solve on the 2 host CPUs takes 46 ms in torch fp32 (22 solves/s) and 57 ms in torch fp64 (block bmm, both threads busy). Going from 2 to 4 cores is limited by the 2 host CPUs that four processes share (per-solve host packing and copies) and by cores slowing each other. On these 2 CPUs, batching right-hand sides into one launch (above) is the better way to raise throughput.

docs.title: Trn2: fused CG follow-ups: column matvec, bf16 A, fused power iteration (#22)
docs.text: Same machine, matrices, pinning and method as the section above (SDK 2.33, one logical core at LNC=2, host on 2 CPUs, tol 1e-5, warm median of 3). row (#40) is #40's matvec, still available as matvec="row". column is the new default (matvec="auto" picks it for R <= 32). Both use the two-exchange LNC=2 step. "µs/iter" = (fused − fused with max_iter=0) / iterations ("n/a" where the fixed cost's run-to-run noise exceeds the iterations' time).
