docs.title: Backend selection
docs.text:
trntensor.set_backend("auto")  # default
trntensor.set_backend("pytorch")  # force PyTorch fallback
trntensor.set_backend("nki")  # force NKI (requires Neuron hardware)

docs.title: Tutorial: DF-MP2 with trntensor
docs.text:
Density-fitted second-order Møller–Plesset perturbation theory (DF-MP2) is a widely-used post-Hartree–Fock method in quantum chemistry. It's also a textbook-perfect workload for a tensor library — the whole calculation is a stack of einsum contractions over occupied, virtual, and auxiliary indices. This tutorial walks through implementing DF-MP2 with trntensor and shows how the contraction planner routes each step.

Full runnable code lives at examples/df_mp2_einsum.py.

docs.title: The calculation in 100 words
docs.text:
DF-MP2 compresses the 4-index two-electron integral tensor (ia|jb) into a 3-index tensor B_ia^P via the resolution of the identity. The correlation energy is

$$ E_\text{MP2} = \sum_{ijab} \frac{T_{ijab}\,(2T_{ijab} - T_{ijba})}{\varepsilon_i + \varepsilon_j - \varepsilon_a - \varepsilon_b} $$

where $T_{ijab} = \sum_P B_{ia}^P B_{jb}^P$. Each $(i,j)$ pair needs a matmul; the energy denominator is an element-wise division. Natural territory for an einsum library.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
import torch
import trntensor

nocc, nvir, naux = 5, 19, 72
torch.manual_seed(42)
B = torch.randn(nocc, nvir, naux) * 0.1
eps_occ = -torch.sort(torch.rand(nocc))[0] - 0.5
eps_vir = torch.sort(torch.rand(nvir))[0] + 0.1

docs.title: Inspecting the plan
docs.text:
Before running, ask the planner what it's going to do:

plan = trntensor.plan_contraction("ap,bp->ab", B[0], B[1])
print(plan.strategy, plan.backend, plan.estimated_flops)
# matmul pytorch 116736

strategy="matmul" means the planner has reduced the einsum to a single matmul. backend="pytorch" means this specific call will go through torch.matmul — the contraction is too small (116 K FLOPs) for the NKI dispatch overhead to pay off. See benchmarks for the threshold.

For a large matmul, the planner routes the same code path through NKI automatically:

plan = trntensor.plan_contraction("ij,jk->ik", torch.randn(2048, 2048), torch.randn(2048, 2048))
print(plan.backend)
# nki   (on Trainium; "pytorch" elsewhere)

docs.title: The pair-energy loop
docs.text:
def df_mp2_energy(B, eps_occ, eps_vir):
    nocc = B.shape[0]
    e_mp2 = 0.0
    for i in range(nocc):
        for j in range(nocc):
            T = trntensor.einsum("ap,bp->ab", B[i], B[j])
            denom = eps_occ[i] + eps_occ[j] - eps_vir.unsqueeze(1) - eps_vir.unsqueeze(0)
            e_mp2 += (T * (2 * T - T.T) / denom).sum().item()
    return e_mp2

Each iteration is:

  1. einsum("ap,bp->ab", B[i], B[j]) — contracts over the auxiliary index p. With B[i] of shape (nvir, naux), this is exactly a matmul B[i] @ B[j].T. The planner picks strategy="matmul" with transB=True.
  2. Denominator tensor built via broadcasting.
  3. Antisymmetrized numerator divided element-wise and summed.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
>>> e = df_mp2_energy(B, eps_occ, eps_vir)
>>> e
-50.5432928801

On a trn1.2xlarge, 25 pair contractions complete in ~3 s end-to-end. The contractions themselves are dispatch-bound at this size, so they route to the PyTorch path; the NKI kernels would only kick in if nocc×nvir were in the thousands.

docs.title: What happens on Trainium vs CPU
docs.text:
Nothing changes in the code. When neuronxcc is installed and the operands are large enough, trntensor.einsum routes through the NKI matmul_kernel transparently. When they aren't, it falls back to torch.matmul. The plan.backend field tells you which path a given call will take, so a profiling loop like

for i in range(nocc):
    for j in range(nocc):
        p = trntensor.plan_contraction("ap,bp->ab", B[i], B[j])
        print(i, j, p.backend, p.estimated_flops)

will reveal exactly where NKI is or isn't being used.

docs.title: Fusing the whole calculation
docs.text:
The Python loop above does 25 einsum calls, 25 elementwise passes, and 25 host reductions — each landing in HBM between steps. On Trainium, trntensor can compile the entire DF-MP2 energy into one NKI program:

E = trntensor.mp2_energy(B, eps_occ, eps_vir)

Inside that single call:

  1. T_ab = Σ_P B[i,a,P] B[j,b,P] accumulates in PSUM via nc_matmul
  2. The spin-adapted numerator (2T − T^T) and the denominator Δ_ab = ε_i + ε_j − ε_a − ε_b are built on the Vector Engine from SBUF-resident ε tiles
  3. (T·(2T − T^T) / Δ).sum() folds into a scalar accumulator in SBUF
  4. One HBM partial per (i, j) pair; host sums to the final scalar

No intermediate T tensor is ever materialized to HBM. See API: quantum and Architecture for the full description.

docs.title: Starting from AO integrals
docs.text:
If you have AO-basis density-fitted integrals rather than pre-transformed MO coefficients, use ao_to_mo_transform to get B:

import trntensor

# eri: (nbasis, nbasis, naux) density-fitted AO ERIs
# C_occ: (nbasis, nocc) occupied MO coefficients
# C_vir: (nbasis, nvir) virtual MO coefficients
B = trntensor.ao_to_mo_transform(eri, C_occ, C_vir)
E = trntensor.mp2_energy(B, eps_occ, eps_vir)

ao_to_mo_transform is another fused NKI kernel — one dispatch, C matrices SBUF-resident across all P. See api/quantum.md.

docs.title: Keeping tensors on the accelerator
docs.text:
In the above the Python runtime sees B as an intermediate tensor and could try to move it back to the CPU between the two calls — paying for a large HBM → host transfer just to send it right back to the device for mp2_energy. trntensor.to_xla and trntensor.from_xla let you opt into explicit residency:

eri_xla = trntensor.to_xla(eri)
C_occ_xla = trntensor.to_xla(C_occ)
C_vir_xla = trntensor.to_xla(C_vir)
eps_occ_xla = trntensor.to_xla(eps_occ)
eps_vir_xla = trntensor.to_xla(eps_vir)

B_xla = trntensor.ao_to_mo_transform(eri_xla, C_occ_xla, C_vir_xla)
E_xla = trntensor.mp2_energy(B_xla, eps_occ_xla, eps_vir_xla)
E = trntensor.from_xla(E_xla)

When every operand passed to a trntensor call is already on XLA, the dispatch layer skips the host↔device transfer and returns the result on XLA. Only the final from_xla(E) pays the round-trip, and it's pulling a 0-D scalar.

docs.title: Current limitations
docs.text:
• The energy denominator is a separate element-wise op. A fused kernel that folds the division into the PSUM accumulation — E = Σ T²/Δ in one kernel — is tracked in #13. Landing it collapses the pair-energy loop into a single tensor-engine invocation per (i,j).
  • For typical chemistry sizes (tens of occupied, tens of virtuals, ~100 auxiliary), the per-pair contraction is well below the NKI dispatch threshold. NKI wins start at GEMMs of ~2048² and above. See #33 for overhead reduction work.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
trntensor's public API is organized into four modules:

  • einsum — einsum, multi_einsum
  • plan — plan_contraction, ContractionPlan, estimate_flops
  • decompose — cp_decompose, tucker_decompose, and reconstructors
  • quantum — fused chemistry primitives (mp2_energy)
  • nki — backend dispatch (set_backend, get_backend, HAS_NKI)

docs.title: Decompositions
docs.text: CP (CANDECOMP/PARAFAC), Tucker (HOSVD), and Tensor Train (TT-SVD) decompositions for compressing high-order tensors. Used in quantum chemistry for tensor hypercontraction (THC), low-rank factorization of DF-coefficient tensors, and DMRG-style high-dimensional compression.

docs.title: cp_decompose(tensor, rank, *, max_iter=100, tol=1e-6, nonneg=False, factors=None) -> (factors, weights)
docs.text:
Decompose a tensor as T ≈ Σ_r w_r · a_r ⊗ b_r ⊗ c_r ⊗ ... via alternating least squares (ALS).

  • factors: list of factor matrices, one per mode with shape (I_k, R)
  • weights: (R,) tensor of component weights
Argument Default Description tensor — Input tensor of any order rank — Number of CP components max_iter 100 Maximum ALS iterations tol 1e-6 Relative reconstruction-error convergence threshold nonneg False Enforce non-negative factors via multiplicative updates factors None Warm-start factor matrices; list of (I_k, R) tensors, one per mode — skips random initialization 
# Standard CP decomposition
factors, weights = trntensor.cp_decompose(T, rank=8)
T_approx = trntensor.cp_reconstruct(factors, weights)

# Non-negative CP (e.g. for density-matrix elements that must stay ≥ 0)
factors_nn, weights_nn = trntensor.cp_decompose(T, rank=8, nonneg=True)

# Warm-start from a previous run (e.g. after increasing rank by one)
factors_new, weights_new = trntensor.cp_decompose(
    T, rank=9, factors=prev_factors + [torch.randn(I, 1)]
)

# nonneg and warm-start compose
factors_ws, weights_ws = trntensor.cp_decompose(T, rank=8, nonneg=True, factors=seed_factors)

docs.title: cp_reconstruct(factors, weights) -> torch.Tensor
docs.text: Reconstruct the full tensor from CP factors and weights.

docs.title: tucker_decompose(tensor, ranks) -> (core, factors)
docs.text:
Higher-order SVD: T ≈ G ×_1 U_1 ×_2 U_2 .... Each factor matrix U_k is orthonormal by construction.

core, factors = trntensor.tucker_decompose(T, ranks=(4, 4, 4))
T_approx = trntensor.tucker_reconstruct(core, factors)

docs.title: tucker_reconstruct(core, factors) -> torch.Tensor
docs.text: Reconstruct from a Tucker core and factor matrices.

docs.title: tt_decompose(tensor, max_rank) -> list[torch.Tensor]
docs.text:
Decompose a d-dimensional tensor into a chain of d cores via TT-SVD (Oseledets 2011). Bond dimensions are capped at max_rank.

Each core has shape (r_{k-1}, n_k, r_k) where: - r_0 = r_d = 1 (boundary ranks) - n_k is the size of mode k - r_k ≤ max_rank

T[i_1, i_2, ..., i_d] ≈ G_1[1, i_1, :] · G_2[:, i_2, :] · ... · G_d[:, i_d, 1]

Returns a list of d core tensors.

cores = trntensor.tt_decompose(T, max_rank=16)
# cores[k].shape == (r_{k-1}, n_k, r_k)

T_approx = trntensor.tt_reconstruct(cores)

Use case — DMRG-style compression. For a 6-mode tensor with modes of size 20 each, full storage is 20^6 ≈ 64M floats. At max_rank=10 the TT representation needs 6 · 10 · 20 · 10 = 12k floats — a 5000× reduction, at the cost of some truncation error.

docs.title: tt_reconstruct(cores) -> torch.Tensor
docs.text:
Contract the TT core chain back to the full tensor by successive tensordot over the bond dimensions.

T_approx = trntensor.tt_reconstruct(cores)
# T_approx.shape == (n_1, n_2, ..., n_d)

docs.title: einsum
docs.text: Einstein summation with contraction planning. Mirrors the subscript notation used by torch.einsum and numpy.einsum, with additional control over scaling, accumulation precision, and mixed-precision compute.

docs.title: einsum(subscripts, *operands, *, alpha, beta, out, dtype, precision) -> torch.Tensor
docs.text:
Execute a single contraction.

einsum(
    subscripts: str,
    *operands: torch.Tensor,
    alpha: float = 1.0,
    beta: float = 0.0,
    out: torch.Tensor | None = None,
    dtype: str | torch.dtype | None = None,
    precision: str = "fast",
) -> torch.Tensor

The planner selects matmul, bmm, path, or torch.einsum based on the subscript pattern and operand shapes. When a NKI backend is active and the pattern maps to a 2-index matmul, the kernel in trntensor.nki._kernels.matmul_kernel is used.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Default Description subscripts — Einstein summation string, e.g. "ij,jk->ik" *operands — Input tensors alpha 1.0 Scalar multiplier on the contraction result beta 0.0 Scalar multiplier on out before accumulation out None Accumulation tensor; result is α·contract + β·out dtype None Cast all operands to this dtype before contracting; result is returned in this dtype. Accepts torch.dtype or strings: "bf16", "bfloat16", "fp16", "float16", "f32", "float32" precision "fast" Accumulation precision: "fast", "kahan", "sr", or "dd" (see below)

docs.title: Basic examples
docs.text:
import trntensor

# Matrix multiply
C = trntensor.einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B)

# Batched matmul
C = trntensor.einsum("bij,bjk->bik", A, B)

# DF-MP2 pair contraction
T_ab = trntensor.einsum("ap,bp->ab", B_i, B_j)

# 4-index AO→MO transform step
Inu = trntensor.einsum("mi,mnP->inP", C, eri)

docs.title: alpha / beta scaling
docs.text:
Matches cuTENSOR's GEMM-style interface: alpha·contract(A, B) + beta·C.

# Scaled GEMM: 2·A@B + 0.5·C
result = trntensor.einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B, alpha=2.0, beta=0.5, out=C)

# In-place accumulation (beta=1, alpha=1): result += A@B
trntensor.einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B, beta=1.0, out=acc)

docs.title: dtype — mixed-precision compute
docs.text:
Cast operands to a lower dtype to hit the NKI bf16 matmul path without changing the model's weight dtype. The result is returned in the requested dtype.

# Route through NKI bf16 kernel even if weights are fp32
result_bf16 = trntensor.einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B, dtype="bf16")

# Use torch.dtype directly
result = trntensor.einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B, dtype=torch.float16)

docs.title: precision — accumulation precision
docs.text:
Value Behavior "fast" Native operand dtype; NKI kernels accumulate in fp32 via PSUM "kahan" Contracts in fp64 and rounds once back to the operand dtype; bypasses NKI dispatch. Operands on a device without native fp64 (the Neuron device, XLA) are contracted on the host and the result moved back. Error ≤ K·2⁻⁵³ + u_out, so the result is as accurate as its dtype allows (~1 ulp), not ~16 digits, unless the operands are float64 "sr" Stochastic rounding at the PSUM→SBUF downcast (BF16/FP16); mean-zero √K·u error instead of K·u. On Trainium requires NEURON_RT_STOCHASTIC_ROUNDING_EN=1 at process start (see below) "dd" Double-double accumulation via trnblas Phase 2 — raises NotImplementedError until trnblas#22 lands 
# High-precision DF-MP2 energy accumulation
E_corr = trntensor.einsum("ijab,ijab->", T, T2, precision="kahan")

docs.title: Error bounds and the output-dtype floor
docs.text:
Every mode's promise is a componentwise bound on max |C − C_exact| / (|A||B|), with u the operand unit roundoff and u_out the unit roundoff of the result dtype (the result is returned in the operand dtype, so u_out = u):

Mode Bound "fast" K·u + u_out "sr" √K·u + u_out (expected value) "dd" K·u² + u_out "kahan" K·2⁻⁵³ + u_out

trntensor.forward_error_bound(mode, dtype, K) returns these values. The u_out term is the final rounding of the result and is a floor no accumulation mode can beat: about 3.9e-3 for bf16 results and 6.0e-8 for fp32. target_forward_error= uses these bounds to pick the cheapest mode. When the target is below the floor (e.g. 1e-4 on bf16 inputs, 1e-8 on fp32 inputs), einsum / multi_einsum emit a one-time RuntimeWarning and still run the most accurate mode, "kahan". To actually meet such a target, pass float32 or float64 operands (or dtype=), or loosen the target. A target below K·2⁻⁵³ raises ValueError.

docs.title: Stochastic rounding on Trainium is a runtime setting
docs.text:
On NKI 0.7+ (Neuron SDK 2.33) the kernel cannot pick its own rounding mode; the Neuron Runtime picks one for the whole process at init from NEURON_RT_STOCHASTIC_ROUNDING_EN (AWS: rounding modes).

NEURON_RT_STOCHASTIC_ROUNDING_EN precision="sr" precision="fast" unset or 0 round-to-nearest-even + one-time RuntimeWarning round-to-nearest-even 1 stochastic also stochastic
  • Set the variable before the process starts (or at least before the first Neuron device access). Setting it later from Python has no effect on rounding.
  • With it set, every FP32→BF16/FP16 downcast in the process rounds stochastically, including "fast" contractions and other libraries' kernels. Results are not bitwise reproducible run to run.
  • Without it, "sr" still computes but gives round-to-nearest results, so the √K·u bound does not apply. This also covers target_forward_error= when it selects "sr".
  • The CPU fallback (no Neuron hardware) emulates SR in software and is not affected by the variable.
NEURON_RT_STOCHASTIC_ROUNDING_EN=1 python my_bf16_job.py

docs.title: multi_einsum(*contractions) -> list[torch.Tensor]
docs.text:
Execute several contractions in one call. Each contraction is a tuple of (subscripts, *operands). Results are returned in input order.

When NKI dispatch is active, operand tensors that appear in more than one contraction (by object identity) are pre-pinned to the XLA device once before executing the loop, eliminating redundant host↔device transfers.

results = trntensor.multi_einsum(
    ("ap,bp->ab", B_i, B_j),  # Coulomb term
    ("ap,bp->ab", B_i, B_k),  # exchange term — B_i pinned once
)

docs.title: Plan cache helpers
docs.text:
These are documented on the Planning page but are also relevant to einsum performance:

  • trntensor.clear_plan_cache() — discard all cached plans
  • trntensor.plan_cache_info() — return {"size": N} cache statistics

docs.title: NKI dispatch
docs.text: Backend selection between the PyTorch fallback and the NKI-accelerated path on Trainium. Kernels live in trntensor.nki._kernels; the public-facing dispatch is in trntensor.nki.dispatch.

docs.title: set_backend(backend: str)
docs.text:
• "auto" — use NKI if nki is importable, else PyTorch
  • "pytorch" — always use torch.matmul / torch.einsum
  • "nki" — require NKI; raises RuntimeError on non-Neuron hosts

docs.title: get_backend() -> str
docs.text: Return the current backend selection.

docs.title: HAS_NKI: bool
docs.text: Module-level flag set at import time. True when nki (0.3.0+) is importable, otherwise False.

docs.title: Dispatch path
docs.text:
On Neuron hardware, kernels run on one of two torch-neuronx lineages, detected on the first kernel launch (never at import):

  • Native (TorchNeuron, Trn2/Trn3, Neuron SDK 2.33+) — chosen when torch_neuronx exports nki_op and a neuron device is available (torch_neuronx.device_count() > 0). Each kernel is a PyTorch custom op on device="neuron", also callable directly and inside torch.compile(backend="neuron"): torch.ops.trntensor.matmul, batched_matmul, mp2_energy, ao_to_mo_transform. The ops are registered only once this path is selected, and this path never imports torch_xla.
  • XLA (Trn1) — chosen when torch_xla is installed and the native path is unavailable. Kernels run on the torch_xla device, unchanged.
  • Otherwise there is no device path: the host wrappers fall back to torch (or raise under TRNTENSOR_REQUIRE_NKI=1), as before.

set_backend is unaffected: it still chooses NKI vs PyTorch. Set the suite-wide TRNSCI_NKI_DISPATCH=native or xla to force a path; forcing an unavailable path raises RuntimeError.

The reduce-parallel all-reduce kernel (trntensor.nki.collectives) is native-only already; it keeps its torch_neuronx.wrap_nki launch because its ReplicaGroup argument is a compile-time constant that a custom-op schema cannot carry.

Precision modes follow the same launch: precision="sr" passes use_sr=True to the matmul / batched_matmul op (stochastic rounding still needs NEURON_RT_STOCHASTIC_ROUNDING_EN=1 at process start and warns once otherwise); precision="kahan" contracts in true fp64 on the host (Trainium has no fp64 datapath) on both paths; precision="dd" still raises on NKI hosts pending trnblas#22.

docs.title: to_device(tensor) -> Tensor / from_device(tensor) -> Tensor
docs.text:
Pin an operand on the Trainium device of the active dispatch path — neuron on TorchNeuron, the XLA device on Trn1 — so repeated trntensor calls skip the host↔device transfer that otherwise dominates dispatch overhead.

import trntensor

# One-time transfer onto the accelerator.
eri_d = trntensor.to_device(eri)
C_occ_d = trntensor.to_device(C_occ)
C_vir_d = trntensor.to_device(C_vir)
eps_occ_d = trntensor.to_device(eps_occ)
eps_vir_d = trntensor.to_device(eps_vir)

# Full DF-MP2 pipeline — B_d never leaves the device.
B_d = trntensor.ao_to_mo_transform(eri_d, C_occ_d, C_vir_d)
E_d = trntensor.mp2_energy(B_d, eps_occ_d, eps_vir_d)

# Pull the scalar back when we actually need it in Python.
E = trntensor.from_device(E_d)
  • to_device: no-op when the tensor is already on a Neuron device. Raises RuntimeError on hosts without the NKI runtime.
  • from_device: no-op when the tensor is already on CPU.

When every operand is already on the device, dispatch skips the per-call transfer, uses the lower "pinned" FLOP threshold, and returns the result on the device — the caller controls when to pull back.

docs.title: to_xla(tensor) -> Tensor / from_xla(tensor) -> Tensor
docs.text: The original names, kept for compatibility. On Trn1 they behave exactly as before. On TorchNeuron there is no XLA device, so to_xla places the tensor on neuron instead (residency works the same way) and from_xla moves it back to CPU.

docs.title: Migrating from to_xla / from_xla
docs.text:
Replace to_xla with to_device and from_xla with from_device. Same behaviour on Trn1; on Trn2/Trn3 the new names say what they do. Checks such as t.device.type == "xla" become t.device.type in ("xla", "neuron").

to_xla / from_xla stay available. When the suite-wide TRNSCI_XLA_DEPRECATION=1 is set (off by default; trnsci turns it on at TorchNeuron GA), each emits a one-time DeprecationWarning pointing at the new names, and selecting the XLA dispatch path emits: "the PyTorch/XLA path is deprecated on Trn2/Trn3; use TorchNeuron (native). Trn1/Inf2 remain supported in maintenance mode."

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Effect TRNTENSOR_REQUIRE_NKI=1 Re-raise kernel exceptions instead of falling back to PyTorch. Useful in the validation loop to surface silent kernel breakage. TRNTENSOR_MIN_NKI_FLOPS=<int> XLA path: override the FLOP threshold (M·K·N) below which dispatch skips NKI and uses torch.matmul / torch.bmm directly. Default: 2_000_000_000. Set to 0 to force NKI for kernel validation. TRNTENSOR_MIN_NKI_FLOPS_PINNED=<int> XLA path, operands already on the device. Default: 1_000_000_000. TRNTENSOR_MIN_NKI_FLOPS_NATIVE=<int> Native (TorchNeuron) path, operands on CPU: M·K·N at which the work leaves the host for the neuron device. Below it, torch.matmul / torch.bmm run on the host. Above it, the operands are offloaded. The offload runs aten unless the pinned threshold below selects NKI. Default: 500_000_000 (measured on Trn2, see below). TRNTENSOR_MIN_NKI_FLOPS_NATIVE_PINNED=<int>\|never Native path: M·K·N at which the NKI kernel replaces aten on the device. Below it, device-resident operands run torch.matmul / torch.bmm (aten) on neuron. Default: never, because on Trn2 aten beat the NKI kernels at every measured size. TRNSCI_NKI_DISPATCH=auto\|native\|xla Suite-wide. Force the native or XLA dispatch path; auto (default) detects. Forcing an unavailable path raises. TRNSCI_XLA_DEPRECATION=1 Suite-wide, off by default. Emit the one-time XLA-path and to_xla / from_xla deprecation warnings. NKI_ENABLE_TRACE_CACHE=0 TorchNeuron setting (not trntensor's). Turns off the cross-process NKI kernel cache, which cannot version editable installs and may serve a stale kernel after a source edit. Set it with pip install -e; the test suite sets it by default. TRNTENSOR_MP2_ENERGY=auto\|rows\|aten\|legacy Native path: force the mp2_energy executor (rows = the Trn2 row kernel, legacy = the original kernel, deprecated there). TRNTENSOR_AO_TO_MO=auto\|trn2\|aten\|legacy Native path: force the ao_to_mo_transform executor (trn2 = the Trn2 kernel, or ao_to_mo_trn2_packed_kernel for a packed 2-D eri; legacy = the original kernel, deprecated there; aten and legacy unpack a packed eri first). TRNTENSOR_HOST_ROUTE=auto\|host\|device Native path, "auto" backend, all operands on the host: where the work runs (#56). auto (default) uploads it once it reaches the measured thresholds below; host keeps it on the host; device always uploads. Covers mp2_energy, ao_to_mo_transform, einsum / multi_einsum (matmul, bmm, generic and multi-operand plans). Only float32 / bfloat16 / float16 operands are uploaded. set_backend("pytorch") and set_backend("nki") ignore it. TRNTENSOR_PINNED_OUTPUT=0 Native path: download results with plain .to("cpu") instead of into memory from the caching host allocator (torch.empty(..., pin_memory=True), results of 1 MiB and up; #56). TRNTENSOR_FORCE_BACKEND=pytorch\|nki\|auto Override the backend selection at runtime without calling set_backend(). Used by benchmarks to sweep both paths on the same machine. TRNTENSOR_USE_SIMULATOR=1 Route kernel dispatch through nki.simulate(kernel)(numpy_args) on CPU instead of XLA → NEFF → hardware. Catches Python-trace-level errors without AWS round-trips. MLIR verifier errors remain hardware-only.

docs.title: Native thresholds: measured on Trn2
docs.text:
These were measured on a trn2.3xlarge (Neuron SDK 2.33, NKI 0.7.0), using one NeuronCore and two host threads, with scripts/bench_native_einsum.py and scripts/autotune_dispatch.py (#41):

  • Pinned operands: NKI never beats aten. On device-resident operands, aten torch.matmul / torch.bmm beat the trntensor NKI matmul and batched-matmul kernels at every size from 128³ to 4096³, in both fp32 and bf16. Examples:
  • 4096³ bf16: 1.38 ms with aten, 6.82 ms with NKI.
  • 1024³ fp32: 0.20 ms with aten, 0.55 ms with NKI.

The eager launch floor is about 0.13 ms for an aten op and about 0.24 ms for an NKI custom op. - Host operands: offload to aten from about 0.5 G multiply-adds. Offloading to aten (upload, run on device, download) beats offloading through the NKI kernel at every size. It also beats host torch: - fp32: from about 134 M multiply-adds (512³) when the host has two threads. - bf16: from about 0.5 to 1 G multiply-adds.

The default of 500 M sits between these. A host with more threads moves the crossover up. Re-measure on your host with scripts/autotune_dispatch.py.

docs.title: Host operands: upload or stay (#56)
docs.text:
With every operand on the host, native "auto" uploads the work, runs it on the device by the device-resident policy, and downloads the result into memory from the caching host allocator, once the work reaches:

entry point work offload from (2 host threads) mp2_energy nocc²·nvir²·naux 1.5e8 ao_to_mo_transform, full eri nocc·nbasis²·naux 2e8 ao_to_mo_transform, packed eri nocc·nbasis²·naux 3e7 einsum, generic or multi-operand plan contraction multiply-adds (a path: the sum of its steps) 5e8, and at least 0.5 multiply-adds per byte moved einsum matmul / bmm M·K·N TRNTENSOR_MIN_NKI_FLOPS_NATIVE (5e8, above)
  • The first four scale with torch.get_num_threads() / 2, as trnblas#65 does: the host side is compute-bound and the thresholds were measured with 2 threads. The matmul threshold keeps its own override and is not scaled.
  • Einsums with little reuse stay on the host at any size: under 0.5 multiply-adds per byte moved, such as elementwise (0.08) and outer (0.25) products. They measured 1.4-2.9x faster uploaded, but only because 2 host threads stream memory slower than the link. Host bandwidth grows with threads and the link's does not, and these patterns fill device memory.
  • float64 and complex operands stay on the host, matmul included. The device computes in at most fp32.
  • If the upload or the device call fails (for example, a full device), the call runs on the host. TRNTENSOR_REQUIRE_NKI=1 raises instead.
  • The first call of each shape on the device pays its compile. These tables are warm.

Measured on Trn2 (SDK 2.33, one logical core at LNC=2, fp32, warm medians, host in to host out). Host threads were pinned to 2 CPUs on two physical cores:

"Host" is the host route on two physical cores; the column after it is the same on one physical core (both hyperthreads). "Device" is upload + the device-resident auto route + download. Bold is what auto now picks.

mp2_energy, ms:

nocc/nvir/naux work host host, 1 core device 8/56/192 3.9e7 1.4 1.7 3.1 8/80/256 1.1e8 3.8 4.9 4.2 8/96/256 1.5e8 5.1 6.8 4.1 16/112/384 1.2e9 26.0 39.0 3.7 16/240/768 1.1e10 173 253 6.5 32/224/1024 5.3e10 646 1128 16.4 48/336/1152 3.0e11 3697 6457 47.4 64/448/1536 1.3e12 15849 28157 135

ao_to_mo_transform, ms (full eri / packed eri):

nbasis/naux/nocc work host host, 1 core device 64/192/8 6.3e6 1.0 / 1.3 1.1 / 1.7 5.7 / 6.7 128/384/16 1.0e8 4.7 / 6.7 7.4 / 11.0 7.5 / 5.3 128/512/16 1.3e8 6.2 / – 10.1 / 21.7 8.9 / 4.1 160/480/20 2.5e8 9.4 / – 16.3 / 32.9 7.1 / 5.1 256/512/8 2.7e8 16.0 / 54.2 26.5 / 71.0 13.6 / 13.0 256/1024/32 2.2e9 66.6 / 138 111 / 198 25.7 / 15.7 384/1152/48 8.2e9 211 / 397 355 / 571 62.2 / 37.9 512/1536/64 2.6e10 574 / 979 959 / 1473 137 / 79.9

einsum with host operands, ms:

contraction work MACs per byte host host, 1 core device mi,mnP->inP 128/16/384 1.0e8 3.6 3.2 5.5 4.4 mi,mnP->inP 256/32/768 1.6e9 7.1 30.5 52.4 19.7 mi,mnP->inP 512/4/1536 1.6e9 1.0 – 252 123 iap,jbp->ijab 16/112/384 1.2e9 67 7.5 13.3 3.8 iaP,PQ->iaQ 64/448/1536 6.8e10 187 386 707 31.9 abc,cd->abd 256 4.3e9 32 46.9 62.7 11.7 mi,na,mnP->iaP 256/32/224/768 (path) 3.0e9 13.5 – 90.1 19.0 ij,ij->ij 8192² 6.7e7 0.08 – 85.8 60.3 ab,cd->abcd 160 6.6e8 0.25 – 580 199 ij,jk->ik 640³ 2.6e8 53 2.3 3.7 2.6 ij,jk->ik 768³ 4.5e8 66 3.4 5.6 2.7 ij,jk->ik 1024³ 1.1e9 85 6.5 12.1 3.2
  • Results match the host route to 5e-7 relative (fp32 summation order).
  • On one physical core the host is about 1.7x slower, so the device wins earlier: from 3e7 for the full eri, and below 1.3e8 for matmul. The thresholds were set on the faster host, so they are on the host's side.
  • The device floor varied between runs, 1.2 to 2.6 ms for a small matmul.

Kernel status on the native path after #51:

  • matmul / bmm: retired in favour of aten. A Trn2 rewrite used both physical cores through the program_id split, Tensor Engine transposes of A and B-tile reuse across four stationaries. It was 1.2–4.3× faster than the original kernel and still slower than aten at every size: 4096³ fp32 took 4.10 ms against 3.80 ms, and 4096³ bf16 1.61 ms against 1.43 ms. It was not kept. set_backend("nki") still runs the original kernels on the native path, with a one-time FutureWarning. A later release will route them to aten.
  • AO→MO: kept, rewritten for Trn2 (ao_to_mo_trn2_kernel). It is 1.3–1.6× faster than the two aten einsums at nbasis 256–768, and native "auto" uses it there for device-resident eri. Below nbasis ≈ 256 "auto" keeps aten.
  • MP2 energy: kept, rewritten for Trn2 (mp2_energy_row_kernel). It is 1.25–1.9× faster than aten once each row launch carries at least 3 GFLOP, and native "auto" uses it there.

The original AO→MO and MP2 kernels remain the XLA-path (Trn1) kernels. See Quantum-chemistry primitives for the tables.

docs.title: Kernels (internal)
docs.text:
• matmul_kernel(a, b) — 2-index matmul with stationary-A tile reuse. Tile constants: TILE_M=128, TILE_K=128, TILE_N=512.
  • batched_matmul_kernel(a, b) — per-batch-slice matmul. Batch dim iterated via nl.affine_range; each slice reuses the stationary-A tile layout.

The DF-MP2 pair pattern einsum("ap,bp->ab") is served by matmul_kernel through the planner's transB=True route — no dedicated kernel needed. Fused energy-denominator kernel is tracked in #13.

docs.title: Planning
docs.text: The planner analyzes einsum subscripts to select a concrete execution strategy, estimate cost, and cache the decision so repeated calls are cheap.

docs.title: plan_contraction(subscripts, *operands, *, precision="fast") -> ContractionPlan
docs.text:
Inspect the dispatch decision without executing.

plan = trntensor.plan_contraction("ij,jk->ik", A, B)
plan.strategy  # "matmul" | "bmm" | "torch" | "path"
plan.contraction_indices  # list of indices being summed over
plan.batch_indices  # list of batch indices
plan.output_indices  # list of output indices in order
plan.transA, plan.transB  # whether to pre-transpose before matmul
plan.contraction_path  # [(i,j), ...] for "path" strategy
plan.precision  # "fast" | "kahan" | "dd" | "sr"

Results are cached by (subscripts, operand shapes, precision). Repeated calls with the same subscript, shapes, and precision skip replanning entirely. Call clear_plan_cache() to invalidate (e.g. after a backend change).

docs.title: precision values
docs.text:
Value Effect on planning "fast" Default; NKI kernels eligible for matmul/bmm strategies "kahan" Signals fp64 promotion at execution time; plan is still computed but einsum will use torch.einsum in fp64 regardless of strategy "dd" Raises NotImplementedError at execution time (trnblas#22 pending) "sr" Stochastic rounding at the PSUM→SBUF downcast for matmul/bmm strategies. On Trainium requires NEURON_RT_STOCHASTIC_ROUNDING_EN=1 at process start, otherwise one-time RuntimeWarning and round-to-nearest; see einsum 
plan_fast = trntensor.plan_contraction("ij,jk->ik", A, B, precision="fast")
plan_kahan = trntensor.plan_contraction("ij,jk->ik", A, B, precision="kahan")
# Two distinct cache entries — plan_fast is not plan_kahan

docs.title: ContractionPlan
docs.text:
Dataclass returned by plan_contraction. All fields are read-only after the planner returns.

Field Type Description subscripts str Original subscript string strategy str "matmul" | "bmm" | "torch" | "path" backend str "nki" or "pytorch" transA bool Pre-transpose first operand (matmul only) transB bool Pre-transpose second operand (matmul only) contraction_indices list[str] Indices summed over batch_indices list[str] Shared batch indices output_indices list[str] Output index order estimated_flops int Multiply-add estimate contraction_path list[tuple[int,int]] Greedy pair order for "path" strategy (opt_einsum convention) precision str "fast" | "kahan" | "dd" | "sr"

docs.title: Strategy selection
docs.text:
• "matmul" — 2-operand, 2D tensors, single contracted index → torch.matmul (or NKI kernel when backend is "nki")
  • "bmm" — 2-operand, 3D tensors, single contracted index + single batch index → torch.bmm (or NKI batched kernel)
  • "torch" — 2-operand fallback for patterns that don't fit matmul/bmm → torch.einsum
  • "path" — 3+ operands → greedy binary contraction ordering; each binary step is dispatched through the full backend-selection stack so large sub-contractions still reach NKI

docs.title: estimate_flops(subscripts, *operands) -> int
docs.text:
Estimate multiply-add operations for a contraction as the product of all distinct index sizes.

trntensor.estimate_flops("ij,jk->ik", A, B)  # M*K*N
trntensor.estimate_flops("iap,jbp->ijab", B, B)  # nocc² * nvir² * naux

docs.title: clear_plan_cache() -> None
docs.text:
Discard all cached contraction plans. Call after changing the active backend or when memory is a concern.

trntensor.set_backend("nki")
trntensor.clear_plan_cache()  # flush plans that may have chosen "pytorch"

docs.title: plan_cache_info() -> dict[str, int]
docs.text:
Return cache statistics. Currently returns {"size": N} where N is the number of cached plans.

info = trntensor.plan_cache_info()
print(f"cached plans: {info['size']}")

docs.title: Quantum-chemistry primitives
docs.text: Domain-specific fused kernels where the whole computation — contraction, elementwise shaping, reduction — lives in a single NKI program. The architectural core of trntensor (see Architecture).

docs.title: trntensor.mp2_energy(B, eps_occ, eps_vir) -> scalar
docs.text:
Density-fitted second-order Møller–Plesset correlation energy.

E_MP2 = Σ_{i,j,a,b} T_{i,j,a,b} (2 T_{i,j,a,b} - T_{i,j,b,a}) / Δ_{i,j,a,b}

T_{i,j,a,b}  = Σ_P  B[i, a, P] B[j, b, P]
Δ_{i,j,a,b}  = ε_i + ε_j - ε_a - ε_b

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
• B: (nocc, nvir, naux) tensor — density-fitted ERI coefficients
  • eps_occ: (nocc,) tensor — occupied orbital energies
  • eps_vir: (nvir,) tensor — virtual orbital energies

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: A 0-D tensor containing the correlation energy.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import torch
import trntensor

nocc, nvir, naux = 5, 19, 72
B = torch.randn(nocc, nvir, naux) * 0.1
eps_occ = -torch.sort(torch.rand(nocc))[0] - 0.5
eps_vir = torch.sort(torch.rand(nvir))[0] + 0.1

E = trntensor.mp2_energy(B, eps_occ, eps_vir)
print(f"E_MP2 = {E.item():.6f}")

docs.title: Backend behaviour
docs.text:
• CPU, and small problems on native TorchNeuron: aten ops on the operands' device. T[i, j, a, b] is contracted with torch.einsum in chunks over i, which bounds peak memory to about 64 MiB of T at a time. The T-weighted sum is vectorized.
  • Native TorchNeuron (Trn2/Trn3): the row kernel. mp2_energy_row_kernel is launched once per occupied row i. It covers j = i + d (mod nocc) for d = 0..nocc/2 and uses the pair symmetry e_ij = e_ji. Per pair, one GEMM fills T = B[i] B[j]ᵀ in SBUF, and the Tᵀ blocks come from Tensor Engine transposes. T never reaches device memory. At LNC=2 each physical core takes half of the j window. The design follows trnblas pair_energy_sym (trnblas#55, #58).
  • "auto" uses the row kernel when B is on the device and each row launch carries at least 3 GFLOP, counted on the padded sizes as 2·(nocc//2+1)·nvir²·naux. Below that, the ~nocc custom-op launch floors lose to aten.
  • set_backend("nki") uses it whenever its SBUF working set fits.
  • TRNTENSOR_MP2_ENERGY=auto|rows|aten|legacy overrides the choice. legacy is the original single-launch kernel, which is deprecated on the native path.

Measured on Trn2 (fp32, one LNC=2 core, device-resident, warm, #51):

nocc, nvir, naux aten row kernel 16, 128, 512 1.5 ms 5.1 ms 32, 256, 768 12.1 ms 11.6 ms 32, 320, 1024 24.9 ms 19.8 ms 48, 384, 1152 75.7 ms 39.2 ms 64, 448, 1536 240 ms 120 ms 96, 672, 2304 1.30 s 0.69 s

Holding 12 or 18 GB of the core's 24 GB on the device did not slow either path. The aten path's 64 MiB T chunks stay clear of the slowdown in aws-neuron-sdk#1447. The row kernel's input staging is about 1.5× the padded B, so near a full device it needs more memory than aten does. "auto" therefore keeps aten when this process's live device allocations plus that staging would leave less than 3 GiB free. A shape whose kernel launch fails anyway falls back to aten and is remembered for the rest of the process. - Host B on native TorchNeuron (#56). Under "auto", a host B with nocc²·nvir²·naux of at least 1.5e8 multiply-adds (scaled by torch.get_num_threads() / 2) is uploaded with the orbital energies, the device route above runs, and the energy comes back as a host scalar. Smaller problems stay on the host. On Trn2 with 2 host threads this took 646 ms -> 16 ms at 32/224/1024 and 15.8 s -> 135 ms at 64/448/1536. See host operands for the table and TRNTENSOR_HOST_ROUTE. - PyTorch/XLA path (Trn1): the original single-launch mp2_energy_kernel. It accumulates T in PSUM, builds Δ on the Vector Engine, and writes one partial per (i, j) pair.

docs.title: trntensor.ao_to_mo_transform(eri, C_occ, C_vir) -> Tensor
docs.text:
Fused 4-index AO→MO integral transform. The canonical quantum-chemistry primitive.

B[i, a, P] = Σ_{μ, ν} C_occ[μ, i] · C_vir[ν, a] · eri[μ, ν, P]

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
• eri — density-fitted three-centre integrals in the AO basis, one of:
  • (nbasis, nbasis, naux): the full square;
  • (npair, naux), npair = nbasis(nbasis+1)/2: the packed lower triangle, row μ(μ+1)/2 + ν for ν ≤ μ (see Packed integrals);
  • (naux, npair): PySCF's _cderi, as is. When naux == npair the shape is ambiguous and is read as (npair, naux); pass cderi.T then.
  • C_occ: (nbasis, nocc) tensor — occupied molecular orbital coefficients
  • C_vir: (nbasis, nvir) tensor — virtual molecular orbital coefficients

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: A (nocc, nvir, naux) tensor of transformed DF coefficients B_ia^P.

docs.title: Example — full DF-MP2 pipeline
docs.text:
import trntensor

B = trntensor.ao_to_mo_transform(eri, C_occ, C_vir)
E = trntensor.mp2_energy(B, eps_occ, eps_vir)

docs.title: Packed integrals
docs.text:
Real three-centre integrals are symmetric in μ↔ν, and drivers store only the lower triangle (PySCF _cderi, trnblas.parallel.pack_tril). Pass it packed (#54):

B = trntensor.ao_to_mo_transform(cderi, C_occ_d, C_vir_d)  # cderi: host (naux, npair)
  • trntensor.pack_tril(eri) and trntensor.unpack_tril(eri_packed, nbasis) convert between the layouts (one index_select each, exact).
  • A host eri with device C_occ is uploaded to C_occ's device, in the layout given. The result stays on the device.
  • On the native path, "auto" sends packed device integrals to ao_to_mo_trn2_packed_kernel under the same conditions as the full kernel. Its stage 1 fetches each (128 μ, NUB ν, TP aux) block from the packed rows with one batched indirect DMA. The full square never exists in device memory. Its result is bit-identical to the full kernel's.
  • The aten and legacy routes unpack on the tensor's device first.

Why: on Trn2 the host link carries about 13.8 GB/s for the whole chip, so the upload of eri was DF-MP2's largest stage. Packed, it is half the bytes.

Upload of eri alone (Trn2, one logical core; host threads pinned to 2 CPUs):

nbasis/naux full packed packed, from pinned host memory 384/1152 49.2 ms 25.1 ms 24.9 ms 512/1536 115.7 ms 58.5 ms 58.4 ms

Pinned host memory and copy_ into a preallocated device tensor upload no faster: H2D already runs at the link rate from ordinary host memory. Packing a full host tensor costs more than it saves: 180 ms on 2 host threads at 512/1536, against a 57 ms saving. Neither does uploading the triangle row by row (281 ms). So a 3-D host eri is uploaded as is. Packing pays only when the integrals already arrive packed.

Kernel alone, device-resident, warm (fp32; padded nvir included):

nbasis/naux/nocc LNC=2 full LNC=2 packed LNC=1 full LNC=1 packed device unpack_tril 256/768/32 1.09 ms 0.91 ms 1.86 ms 1.93 ms — 384/1152/48 5.38 ms 5.81 ms 5.72 ms 5.95 ms 3.1 ms 512/1536/64 6.28 ms 6.27 ms 12.87 ms 12.75 ms 5.5 ms

docs.title: Backend behaviour
docs.text:
• CPU: two explicit aten steps on the operands' device: einsum("mi,mnP->inP") then einsum("na,inP->iaP").
  • Native TorchNeuron (Trn2/Trn3): ao_to_mo_trn2_kernel. Both stages are plain GEMMs with the contraction index on the partition axis, so there are no DMA transposes.
  • Stage 1: X[i, ν, P] = Σ_μ C_occ[μ, i] eri[μ, ν, P].
  • Stage 2: B[i, a, P] = Σ_ν C_vir[ν, a] X[i, ν, P].
  • The auxiliary index is split across both physical cores at LNC=2.
  • "auto" uses the kernel for device-resident eri with nocc ≤ 128 when its SBUF working set fits and the stage-1 work nocc·nbasis²·naux is at least 5e8 multiply-adds (about nbasis ≥ 256). Smaller problems lose to the launch floor and the padding copies; otherwise it runs the two aten steps. TRNTENSOR_AO_TO_MO=auto|trn2|aten|legacy overrides the choice.

Measured on Trn2 (fp32, one LNC=2 core, device-resident, warm, #51):

nbasis, nocc, naux two aten einsums Trn2 kernel (op) ao_to_mo_transform, "auto" original kernel 64, 8, 128 0.41 ms — 0.41 ms (aten) 6.0 ms (#49) 128, 16, 256 0.49 ms 0.43 ms 0.49 ms (aten) 16.1 ms 256, 32, 512 1.23 ms 1.11 ms 0.92 ms 112 ms (#49) 512, 32, 1024 7.30 ms 4.56 ms 4.72 ms — 768, 48, 1536 18.3 ms 11.8 ms 12.0 ms —

The op column takes tile-multiple inputs (the raw kernel). The "auto" column includes the padding of nvir to 128 and is the shipped route. At nbasis 64 and 128 it measured 0.79 and 0.57 ms with the kernel forced, which is why "auto" keeps aten there.

  • Host inputs on native TorchNeuron (#56). Under "auto", with eri, C_occ and C_vir all on the host, the inputs are uploaded (eri in the layout given), the device route above runs, and the result is downloaded, once nocc·nbasis²·naux reaches 2e8 for a full eri or 3e7 for a packed one (both scaled by torch.get_num_threads() / 2). A packed host eri otherwise pays a host unpack, so its threshold is lower. On Trn2 with 2 host threads at 512/1536/64 this took 574 -> 137 ms full and 979 -> 80 ms packed. PySCF's (naux, npair) layout went from 5.2 s to 83 ms on one physical core. See host operands for the table and TRNTENSOR_HOST_ROUTE.
  • PyTorch/XLA path (Trn1): the original kernel. It loops over P, with the (i, ν) intermediate round-tripping through kernel-scratch HBM. On the native path it is deprecated.

docs.title: Current limitations
docs.text:
• Both NKI kernels need nocc ≤ 128; larger nocc runs the aten steps (native) or raises NotImplementedError (XLA).
  • The (nocc, nbasis, naux) intermediate goes through kernel-scratch HBM between the two stages, as it does between the two aten einsums. Stage 1 leaves i on the partition axis, and stage 2 needs ν there.

docs.title: matmul dispatch overhead findings (#33)
docs.text: Date: 2026-04-17 Tracker: #33 Method: scripts/run_neuron_profile.sh --dispatch-timing on trn1.2xlarge Hardware: trn1.2xlarge, Neuron runtime 2.31.24, compiler 2.24.5133

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The per-call overhead in nki_matmul is ~0.67 ms fixed XLA dispatch latency regardless of tensor size. Host↔device transfer scales with tensor size on top of this.

  • Without residency: NKI barely beats CPU at 1024² (2.94 ms vs 2.94 ms); 2.1× at 1536². Crossover: ~2 GFLOPs (current _MIN_NKI_FLOPS default is correct).
  • With residency (to_xla pre-applied): Eliminates host→device transfer. NKI wins at 1024² (1.60 ms vs 2.90 ms = 1.8×); 5.65× at 2048². Crossover: ~900 MFLOPs (new _MIN_NKI_FLOPS_PINNED default set to 1 GFLOPs).

docs.title: Step-by-step timing (trn1.2xlarge)
docs.text:
Size FLOPs PT ms to_xla ms kern ms to_cpu ms nki_tot ms winner 128 4M 0.025 0.080 0.680 0.082 0.038† PyTorch 256 34M 0.109 0.105 0.670 0.128 0.070† PyTorch 512 268M 0.393 0.295 0.672 0.322 0.419† PyTorch 768 906M 1.274 0.703 0.673 0.779 1.270† PyTorch 1024 2.1G 2.938 1.502 0.684 0.970 2.935 NKI (1.0×) 1536 7.2G 9.441 3.998 0.879 1.859 4.514 NKI (2.1×) 2048 17G 23.547 7.282 1.003 2.960 17.934 NKI (1.3×)

† Sizes below _MIN_NKI_FLOPS (2 GFLOPs) fall through to torch.matmul via the dispatch gate; nki_tot is measuring the fallback path, not NKI execution.

The individual step measurements (to_xla, kern, to_cpu) always invoke the NKI path directly, bypassing the gate, and are accurate.

docs.title: 1. ~0.67 ms is fixed XLA dispatch latency
docs.text:
The kern ms column is nearly constant at 128–1024 (0.67–0.68 ms). This is the cost of submitting the XLA lazy graph for the NKI kernel — not the kernel execution time itself. XLA defers execution until a synchronization point (.to(cpu)). The "kern" timing only measures submission; actual execution is included in to_cpu.

This ~0.67 ms is a fundamental floor for any individual NKI kernel dispatch. It cannot be reduced by kernel tuning; it can only be amortized by batching multiple operations into one XLA graph compile.

docs.title: 2. Residency changes the economics
docs.text: Without residency, to_xla is the dominant cost at large sizes (7.3 ms at 2048²). With residency, that cost is paid once per session. The pre-pinned crossover (~900 MFLOPs vs ~2 GFLOPs) means users who call to_xla() before a loop of matmuls get NKI benefit at roughly half the matrix size.

docs.title: 3. Current threshold was correct; pinned threshold is new
docs.text: The 2 GFLOPs default was approximately right. The new _MIN_NKI_FLOPS_PINNED = 1 GFLOPs captures the pre-pinned benefit with a conservative margin above the ~900 MFLOPs crossover.

docs.title: 4. 2048² only 1.3× faster unpinned — transfer dominates
docs.text: At 2048², to_xla alone takes 7.3 ms. The kernel result is only 2.96 ms to retrieve. The NKI win (17.9 ms vs 23.5 ms) is entirely because the kernel itself runs in ~1 ms while torch.matmul spends 23 ms on CPU. The transfer overhead is significant. Users with 2048² workloads should pre-pin.

docs.title: What this means for #33
docs.text:
The four items in the #33 description:

Approach Finding Lower _MIN_NKI_FLOPS Done for pinned path (1 GFLOPs); 2 GFLOPs remains correct for unpinned Keep tensors on XLA across calls Already implemented (to_xla/from_xla); pinned threshold now lower to exploit it Batch dispatches into one XLA graph Not yet — would amortize the 0.67 ms fixed cost; relevant for multi_einsum loops torch_xla.compile on einsum body Unexplored; would require graph-mode tracing

The batching approach (fusing multiple matmul dispatches into one XLA graph) is the next lever. For DF-MP2's O(N²) pair loop — for i in range(nocc): for j in range(nocc): T = B[i] @ B[j].T — each iteration pays 0.67 ms. At nocc=64, that's 64² × 0.67 ms ≈ 2.7 s of pure overhead. A batched dispatch would pay 0.67 ms once. This is the Phase 3 architectural target.

docs.title: Recommended next steps
docs.text:
1. Close #33 partially — thresholds calibrated, findings documented. The fundamental dispatch overhead is understood and bounded.

  2. Phase 3 batching investigation — prototype fusing the nocc×nocc pair loop into one torch_xla.compile call or a single multi_einsum dispatch with an explicit graph.

  3. Run scripts/run_neuron_profile.sh --kernel matmul to get Tensor Engine utilization for the kernel itself (separate from dispatch overhead). Expected: TE-dominant (contrast with trnblas _mp2_energy_kernel which was VE-dominant at 96.45%).

  4. Provision trntensor-ci-trn1 — run terraform apply in infra/terraform/ to get a dedicated instance. Current approach borrows trnblas-ci-trn1.

docs.title: matmul_kernel engine utilization profile
docs.text: Date: 2026-04-17 Tracker: #33 Hardware: trn1.2xlarge, Neuron SDK 2.29.18.0, NKI 0.3.0 Method: sustained workload timing + neuron-monitor (see Profiling approach note)

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: matmul_kernel at 1024² is Tensor Engine-dominant (by design — GEMM maps directly to TE tiles). The ~0.67 ms fixed overhead per dispatch is entirely in the XLA graph submission path, not in kernel execution. At 1024², the kernel itself executes in ~0.68 ms; the remaining ~0.9 ms of the 1.6 ms pre-pinned total is device→host transfer.

docs.title: Sustained throughput (trn1.2xlarge, 1024² fp32)
docs.text:
Measurement: run 3793 iterations of einsum("ij,jk->ik", A, B) in 15 s on a warmed-up (post-compile) instance.

Metric Value Iterations 3793 in 15 s Throughput 252 iters/s Wall-clock / iter ~3.97 ms FLOPs per iter (1024²) 2.15 GFLOPs Effective throughput 541 GFLOPS trn1 peak bf16 TE 190 TFLOPS (2 NeuronCores) trn1 peak fp32 TE 47.5 TFLOPS (2 NeuronCores) Estimated TE utilization (fp32) ~1.1%

The low utilization reflects the dispatch-dominated regime: each iteration pays ~0.67 ms of XLA submission overhead that the TE is idle during. The kernel itself runs in ~0.68 ms (from the dispatch timing sweep).

docs.title: Per-step breakdown at 1024² (from dispatch timing findings)
docs.text: Step Time host→XLA transfer 1.50 ms Kernel submission 0.68 ms device→host transfer 0.97 ms Total (unpinned) 2.94 ms Kernel only (pre-pinned) 0.68 ms device→host (pre-pinned) 0.92 ms Total (pre-pinned) 1.60 ms

docs.title: At 2048² (pre-pinned)
docs.text:
Step Time Kernel 0.97 ms device→host 3.14 ms Total pre-pinned 4.12 ms PyTorch baseline 23.27 ms Speedup 5.65×

At 2048², the kernel execution (0.97 ms) is fast. The dominant cost is device→host transfer (3.14 ms), not the TE. For workloads where results are immediately fed into another NKI kernel (no from_xla needed), this cost disappears — that is the Phase 3 batching motivation.

docs.title: Profiling approach note
docs.text:
Neuron Profiler 2.0 trace capture (neuron-profile capture -n model.neff) requires a standalone .neff file. In NKI 0.3.0 / Neuron SDK 2.29, trntensor kernels go through the torch_xla → XLA lazy graph → Neuron XLA backend path. The NEFF is compiled in-memory and is not written to /var/tmp/neuron-compile-cache/ (the location used by earlier neuronxcc.nki.* direct-compile workflows like trnblas). The NEURON_PROFILE and NEURONX_DUMP_TO environment variables did not produce on-disk artifacts in the tested configuration.

Alternative for TE/VE breakdown: compile matmul_kernel via nki.jit with an explicit output path (NKI 0.3.0 nki.compiler API), then run neuron-profile capture -n <path>/model.neff. This avoids the torch_xla compilation path and produces a NEFF that the profiler can consume. Planned for a follow-up run once the trntensor-ci-trn1 instance is provisioned (currently using trnblas-ci-trn1 as a stop-gap).

docs.title: 1. Kernel execution at 1024² is ~0.68 ms
docs.text:
From the dispatch timing sweep (unpinned step isolation): the matmul_kernel submission step itself is nearly constant at 0.67–0.68 ms for 128²–1024². At 1536²–2048² it rises to 0.88–1.0 ms as the kernel has more work per tile.

This ~0.68 ms is the XLA graph submission latency: it includes: - Python dispatch through torch_xla lazy tensor - XLA lazy graph compilation or cache lookup - NEFF dispatch to the Neuron Runtime - Waiting for the first partial result (before to_cpu completes)

docs.title: 2. Transfer costs dominate at moderate sizes
docs.text:
At 1024² (unpinned): to_xla = 1.50 ms, to_cpu = 0.97 ms, kernel = 0.68 ms. Transfer accounts for 77% of the total 3.14 ms.

Pre-pinning eliminates to_xla; Phase 3 batching eliminates redundant to_cpu between loop iterations.

docs.title: 3. Homogeneous batching impact (Phase 3, v0.5.0)
docs.text:
For the DF-MP2 pair loop with nocc=64, pre-Phase 3: - 64² = 4096 dispatches × 0.67 ms overhead = 2.75 s pure overhead

Post-Phase 3 (all same-shape "ap,bp->ab" contractions): - 1 batched nki_batched_matmul dispatch = 0.67 ms overhead - Stack + unstack cost: ~0.1 ms - ~4000× reduction in dispatch overhead for this loop

Kernel work for 4096 contractions of shape (nvir=512, naux=512): - FLOPs: 4096 × 2 × 512² = 2.15 TFLOPs - At 190 TFLOPS trn1 bf16 peak: theoretical minimum ~11 ms - At 47.5 TFLOPS fp32 peak: ~45 ms - Actual: one batched dispatch submits all of this in one NEFF

docs.title: 4. Kern and to_cpu already partially overlap (#35 closed)
docs.text:
The kern ms column in the dispatch timing tables measures XLA graph submission latency — Python dispatch, lazy graph compilation/cache lookup, and NEFF handoff to the Neuron Runtime — not the raw Tensor Engine execution time. When measured as nki_tot (end-to-end NKI path wall-clock), the sum of steps slightly exceeds the total:

Size to_xla kern to_cpu Sum nki_tot Gap 1024² (unpinned) 1.502 ms 0.684 ms 0.970 ms 3.156 ms 2.935 ms −0.22 ms

The gap confirms kern and to_cpu already partially pipeline: the Neuron Runtime begins DMA while the host is still processing the XLA submission handoff.

No additional async pipelining is available at the dispatch level. The xm.mark_step() call in _to_xla is a necessary correctness barrier: without it, the XLA lazy evaluator fuses consecutive NKI kernels into a single graph that triggers trn2-only shared-memory instructions failing trn1 verification (#39). The sync is not a performance regression — removing it would improve latency only until the compiler bug is fixed, and would produce wrong results on trn1 in the meantime.

docs.title: Recommended next steps
docs.text:
1. Provision trntensor-ci-trn1 (cd infra/terraform && terraform apply) for a dedicated instance not shared with trnblas tests.

  2. Formal TE utilization profile via nki.compiler compile path: compile matmul_kernel to a NEFF without torch_xla, use neuron-profile capture -n model.neff to get the TE/VE/DMA breakdown. Add the summary-text table here.

  3. 2048² batched matmul profile — at large shapes the kernel should be TE-dominant (unlike the dispatch-dominated 1024² case). Profile to confirm.

docs.title: Cross-project integration: DF-MP2
docs.text:
The canonical integration demo is examples/quantum_chemistry/df_mp2_synthetic.py. It computes a density-fitted MP2 correlation energy on a small synthetic system, with each stage handled by a different library in the suite:

Stage Library API used Random occupied / virtual coefficients (demo only) trnrand normal() Cholesky of the DF metric $J$ trnsolver cholesky() Half-transform $\mu\nu P \to ia P$ via GEMM trnblas gemm(), batched_gemm() Pair energy contraction $B_{iaP} B_{jbP}$ trntensor einsum("ap,bp->ab", ...) FLOPs estimate trntensor estimate_flops()

The same pattern could substitute trnsparse for the DF tensor when shell screening is enabled (not shown in the minimal demo — see trnsparse/examples/sparse_fock.py).

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
python examples/quantum_chemistry/df_mp2_synthetic.py --demo

Output reports per-stage wall time and a FLOPs estimate from the contraction planner.

docs.title: Why this example
docs.text: DF-MP2 is the natural proving ground for the suite: it exercises dense GEMM (trnblas), small linear algebra (trnsolver), and tensor contractions with an FLOPs budget (trntensor). On Trainium, this is the path toward NKI-backed post-Hartree-Fock correlation methods.

docs.title: Workflow: quantum chemistry
docs.text:
A significant share of the motivation for trnblas, trnsolver, trnsparse, and trntensor comes from post-Hartree-Fock correlation methods in computational quantum chemistry — specifically density-fitted MP2 (DF-MP2), DF-CCSD, and related approaches on molecules with several thousand basis functions.

These calculations are GEMM-dominated: most of the wall time is spent in dense matrix multiplications inside tensor contractions. On conventional CPU clusters, a single DF-MP2 energy evaluation on a large-basis system can run for many hours. Accelerator hardware helps, but only if the library stack exists to express the workload.

docs.title: The DF-MP2 shape
docs.text:
A canonical DF-MP2 pipeline, reduced to its linear-algebra skeleton:

  1. DF metric Cholesky — factor the auxiliary-basis metric J = L L^T.
  2. Half-transform the three-center integrals from AO to MO basis: (μν|P) → (ia|P) via two GEMMs.
  3. Contract with J⁻¹ᐟ² to form the DF coefficient tensor B_{iaP}.
  4. Pair-energy contraction: for each pair of occupied orbitals (i, j), compute T_{ab} = B_{ia}^P B_{jb}^P, then sum with the orbital-energy denominator.
  5. (For >3000 basis functions) Integral screening — the vast majority of shell quartets contribute below threshold and can be dropped via Schwarz inequality bounds.

Every step lives in a different trnsci library:

Step Library API 1. Cholesky trnsolver cholesky 2. Half-transform trnblas gemm, batched_gemm 3. Metric contraction trnblas trsm, batched_gemm 4. Pair energies trntensor mp2_energy, estimate_flops 5. Screening trnsparse schwarz_bounds, screen_quartets

This is the single workload that motivates four of the six libraries. Getting DF-MP2 to run end-to-end on Trainium is the suite's proving ground.

docs.title: Why Trainium
docs.text: The DF-MP2 hot path is dense-GEMM-heavy — exactly what the Trainium Tensor Engine's systolic array is optimized for. The regular shapes (AO, MO, and auxiliary basis dimensions are fixed per calculation) are friendly to the Neuron compiler. And the cost economics of Trainium relative to comparable NVIDIA instances meaningfully change the wall-clock budget for exploratory chemistry — which is the scientific case.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A minimal synthetic version of the DF-MP2 pipeline is in examples/quantum_chemistry/. It constructs a synthetic (AO × AO × aux) three-center integral tensor with random MO coefficients, runs each stage through its respective library, reports per-stage timing, and prints a FLOPs estimate from the contraction planner. The energy is not physically meaningful — this is a plumbing demo. A real calculation would feed AO integrals and converged SCF MO coefficients from a driver such as PySCF.

See also examples/quantum_chemistry/pyscf_bridge_sketch.md for notes on wiring a real chemistry driver to the trnsci stack.

docs.title: Related CUDA samples
docs.text:
• cuBLAS/Level-3/gemm — the canonical dense GEMM sample; the DF-MP2 half-transform is several applications of this primitive.
  • cuSOLVER/potrf — Cholesky of an SPD matrix; directly corresponds to the DF metric factorization.
  • cuTENSOR/contraction — general tensor contraction; the pair-energy step is a natural cutensorContract call, and maps onto trntensor.einsum.

docs.title: Workflow: speech enhancement
docs.text:
One of the workloads that motivates trnfft is speech enhancement — taking a noisy waveform and recovering a cleaner version of the underlying speech. The standard pipeline is:

  1. STFT the noisy waveform to a complex spectrogram.
  2. Estimate a complex mask from the spectrogram using a small neural network.
  3. Apply the mask (complex multiplication) to the input spectrogram.
  4. Inverse STFT back to the time domain.

The mask is typically a complex ratio mask (cIRM) — it has both magnitude and phase components, and the network's task is to predict both. This is where Trainium's lack of native complex arithmetic matters: every step of the pipeline operates on complex values, and without trnfft.ComplexTensor the programmer ends up implementing complex multiply-and-add by hand everywhere.

docs.title: What trnfft covers
docs.text:
• trnfft.stft, trnfft.istft — windowed short-time Fourier transforms
  • trnfft.ComplexTensor — split real/imag storage, full arithmetic
  • trnfft.nn.ComplexLinear, ComplexConv1d, ComplexBatchNorm1d, ComplexModReLU — complex neural network layers for mask estimation

Together these are enough to express the full cIRM pipeline in PyTorch syntax. On CPU, it uses torch.stft and ordinary tensor ops; on Trainium with NKI enabled, it dispatches to the butterfly FFT and complex GEMM kernels.

docs.title: Why it matters for trnsci
docs.text:
Speech enhancement is an excellent test case for trnfft because:

  • The shapes are regular — fixed sample rate, fixed window size, fixed hop length. That's exactly the workload pattern the Neuron compiler handles best.
  • It exercises every part of the library: transforms, complex arithmetic, complex neural-network layers, and plan caching.
  • It's a real deployed workload (not just a benchmark), so regressions are detectable through end-to-end speech quality metrics (PESQ, STOI).

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A minimal, synthetic-signal version of the pipeline is in examples/speech_enhancement/. It constructs a synthetic clean signal + noise, runs STFT → complex mask network → iSTFT, and trains the mask for a handful of steps. No real speech data is used — this is a plumbing demo for the API surface. Production cIRM training needs a real dataset (noisy/clean pairs) and a longer schedule.

docs.title: Related CUDA samples
docs.text: The closest upstream NVIDIA sample is Samples/4_CUDA_Libraries/simpleCUFFT in the NVIDIA/cuda-samples repository. simpleCUFFT demonstrates a 1D complex FFT against a reference implementation — trnfft covers the same ground in examples/nvidia_samples/simple_cufft_2d_r2c.py. The speech-enhancement demo is the composition of simpleCUFFT + complex-valued neural network layers (which have no direct cuFFT analog; they would be written against cuBLAS in a CUDA implementation).
